title: Data Visualization
text:
Welcome


This educational resource aims to form a connected learning journey where each chapter introduces new principles and chart elements as a response to a limitation of what came before rather than simply presenting rules of which charts are good for what. The motivation for this is that learners can be apt at remembering that they should use one chart instead of another without understanding why that’s the case. Or they might remember why for a specific example, but fail to extend that into a general understanding that applies to previously unseen scenarios and charts.
Even more experienced visualized data workers might intuitively and implicitly make appropriate generalizations, without fully being able to articulate the reasoning behind their thought process. This resource strives to make such choices explicit through examples showing where previous techniques fall short so that students experience why a novel strategy is needed for a particular scenario.
Helping learners generalize their understanding can empower their agency and improve their ability to predict what is an effective visualization choice for a scenario not previously encountered. It is my hope that a deeper understanding for why and when certain visualization strategies are needed can contribute to and encourage learners’ critical thinking about any chart they might come across. In my personal experience, developing such an understanding and revealing the implicit reasons behind visualization choices also makes learning more fun.
This resource interleaves exercises throughout the chapters to encourage experiential learning and to make learners more active instead of leaving them to passively consume information. The exercises are largely focused on visualization principles rather than coding, since memorization of library APIs is an increasingly replaceable skill; although understanding the guiding principles of the grammatical framework those APIs implement can be informative and helpful.
To make the learning interactive, code is included for the learner to experiment on their own. Rather than focusing on any one particular library, this resource allows learners to choose their library of interest from a set of libraries implementing a grammar of graphics. These libraries where chosen because their predictable grammar encourages learners to interpolate from charts they have seen to charts they could potentially make based on understanding the rules of the grammar. Having multiple such libraries also allows learners to distinguish underlying visualization principles from library-specific API design. The grammar of graphics also provides a data-centric framework for reasoning about visualization choices and more clearly seeing similarities and difference between charts, rather than just memorizing names of different charts types.  

This resource also hopes to introduce students to some interesting data sets along the way, although this will likely be a work in progress over a longer time.

title: 1  Why visualize data?
text:
1.1 What is data visualization?
At its core, data visualization is about representing data with graphical elements such as the position of a point, the length of a bar, or the color of a line. We usually visualize data for two main purposes: to improve own understanding of a dataset or to improve someone’s else’s understanding by communicating what we have learned. While we often use visualization to answer a specific question about a dataset, it can also be more exploratory and help us generate new questions.
In this sense, we can think of data visualization as a human “data language” that helps us gain and communicate data insights effectively. This role is equally relevant when an analysis comes from another person or from a machine, such as a generative AI agent: in either case, the goal is to support human understanding. By supporting both exploration and communication, visualization is often where a data analysis begins and ends.

Summaries, such as the mean and standard deviation, are helpful statistical tools that are often useful for summarizing and detecting the differences between datasets. However, since they collapse the data into just a few numbers, statistical summaries can’t tell the whole story about the data and there can be important differences between datasets that summaries fail to reveal.






Ex-solutionSolution






So if you can’t really see any patterns in the table and the statistical summaries are nearly all the same, that must mean that the four sets are pretty similar, right? Sounds about right so let’s go ahead and plot them to have a quick look…








  
  
  
  
  


  
  








… what… how can they be so different… there must be something wrong, right? Well what is wrong is that humans are not good at detecting patterns in raw numbers, and we don’t have good intuition about which combination of numbers can contribute to the same statistical summaries. What do we excel at? Detecting visual patterns!
It is immediately clear to us how the four datasets differ once they are shown as graphical objects instead of textual objects. Sets A and C are roughly linearly increasing at similar rates, whereas set B reaches a plateau and starts to drop, and set D has a constant X-value for all numbers except one big outlier. We could only detect these patterns after visualizing the data. Importantly, if we only had looked at the raw data or the summary statistics, we would have come to the wrong conclusions about how the datasets differ, and any research or business level decision based on solely on our numerical analysis of this dataset would have been misinformed.

title: 1  Why visualize data?
section: 1.3 Why are visuals easier to interpret than numbers?
text:
1.3 Why are visuals easier to interpret than numbers?
To understand why visualizations are so powerful, it is helpful to remember that to answer a question, we often have to put the data in a format that is easy for us humans to interpret. Because our number systems have only been around for about 5,000 years, we need to assert effort and train ourselves to recognize structure in numerical data.
On the other hand, visual systems have undergone refinement during 500,000,000 years of evolution, so we can instinctively recognize visual patterns and accurately estimate visual properties such as colors and distances without much conscious cognitive effort.
In practice, this means that we can arrive at correct conclusions faster by studying graphical rather than numerical representations of the same data.

A modern take on Anscombe’s quartet
For a more recent and dynamic illustration of how graphical representations are much easier for us to interpret, check out the Datasaurus Dozen animation below. It displays several different datasets, all with nearly the same mean, standard deviation and correlation between X and Y, but looking at the data graphically shows us how different these datasets actually are:






Figure 1.2: The Datasaurus Dozen: Datasets with near identical summary statistics but widely different distributions.



Now that you have experienced the benefits of visualizing data, let’s figure out how to create such visualizations!

title: 2  The grammar of graphics
text:
2.1 Why bother?
Why do we need to know anything about visualization libraries and their underlying theory, such as the grammar of graphics? While there is a lot we can learn about visualization without coding, the act of implementing visualizations in code can help us understand their underlying principles, which makes the learning experience more interactive and memorable. The grammar of graphics also gives us a powerful theoretical framework to understand and reason about data visualizations.

title: 2  The grammar of graphics
section: 2.2 Which visualization library should we pick?

2.2 Which visualization library should we pick?
We will start by selecting which visualization library to use. To make an informed decision, it is helpful to understand that most visualization libraries can be classified as taking either a high-level declarative approach or a low-level imperative approach to creating visualizations.

To understand the difference between these two approaches, let’s start with an example, using the following small toy dataset:

A helpful way to illustrate the difference between the two approaches to syntax is to imagine that we want to create a chart where we color the points according to their group. Here is pseudocode1 that illustrates this difference:

Imperative syntaxDeclarative syntax



fig = create_figure()
colors = ['blue', 'orange']
for color, group in zip(colors, df['group'].unique()):
    tmp_df = df[df['group'] == group]
    fig.add_chart(tmp_df['x'], tmp_df['y'], label=group, color=color)





  
  
  
  
  


  
  








chart(
    x='x',
    y='y',
    color='group'
)





  
  
  
  
  


  
  








Although the same chart is created from both of these pseudocode examples, the syntax looks wildly different. Pause here and try to describe the differences between the two in your own words. Then, click on the hint and solution below to read our explanation of the two approaches.
Actively engaging with exercises like this one can help you remember and understand the information. The key is to activate your brain and try to come up with an answer yourself rather than skipping straight to passively reading the solution.






Ex-hintHint






Does one of the approaches focus more on the data and the other more on the plot-specific details?






Ex-solutionSolution






Based on the syntax of the exercise above, we can say that a declarative approach to visualization lets us express ourselves in terms of the data (color='group'), whereas an imperative approach to visualization focuses more explicitly on plot construction details such as choosing specific colors and then assigning them to groups by looping through the data.












A related way to understand declarative and imperative approaches is to consider the difference between giving an instruction in each:

Declarative instructionImperative instruction



“Color by the column group in the dataframe.”
Focus: Declaring links between data variables (e.g., group) and graphical properties (e.g., color). The rest of the plot details (such as which colors to use) are handled automatically.




“Loop over the dataframe and plot observations in group a in blue and observations in group b in orange.”
Focus: Being explicit with all the details for creating the chart via loops and low-level drawing commands.




In this book, we will learn about declarative visualization tools, since these allow us to code a high-level specification of what we want the visualization to include, rather than coding out the details of how to implement the visualization. Another way to state this would be that high-level libraries let our minds focus on data and relationships, which is the right level of abstraction for a data scientist. Low-level libraries focus more on plot construction details, which is often more appropriate when making a highly customized visualization, data art, or an application with complex plotting logic.
Among declarative visualization libraries, there are still a few different subcategories. In this book, we are going to learn about libraries that implement a so-called “grammar of graphics”, since this framework makes visualizations easy both to create and to reason about.

title: 2  The grammar of graphics
section: 2.3 What is the grammar of graphics?
text:
2.3 What is the grammar of graphics?
There is a plethora of names used to refer to specific types of chart. While referring to charts by name can be convenient in some contexts, it is often confusing. For example, a scatterplot, a dot plot, a strip plot, a bubble plot, and a forest plot all use points to represent data, but what’s the difference between them? Memorizing exactly which chart corresponds to which name is not as important as developing an understanding of the principles that form the foundations for building visualizations. Such an understanding can move us away from just creating charts from known templates to reflecting on what it is we’re trying to communicate and which graphical elements are the most suitable for this task.
The grammar of graphics lets us focus on understanding the common building blocks of all charts and how to combine them according to predictable rules to create bespoke visualizations. It parallels the grammars of natural2 and programming languages, but applies to visual components. While we’re all familiar with how the grammatical rules of natural languages describe how to compose meaningful sentences from words, it might not be as clear what grammatical structures look like in programming languages, so let’s see an example in the following exercise:


Grammatical origins
The idea of a grammar of graphics originates from Leland Wilkinson’s book The Grammar of Graphics.







Ex-promptExercise 2






What do you think the output of the following Python code would be?


1 + 2

As you might have expected, the output is 3 because Python uses the conventional rules of mathematics to add the two numbers together. Almost all programming languages follow this rule. But what does the + operator do if we are trying to add something other than numbers? What do you think the output of the following code would be? Do you think it differs between programming languages?


'one' + 'two'








Ex-hintHint






Adding two numbers gives their sum. Could adding two strings similarly combine their contents, producing a string with all the characters from both?






Ex-solutionSolution






In Python, the + operator performs concatenation when strings are added together, so the returned result would be "onetwo". In contrast, R does not support adding strings with +, so it would raise an error indicating that non-numeric arguments were passed to the + operator.
This example illustrates that the same expression can behave differently under the grammatical rules of different programming languages.

title: 2  The grammar of graphics
text:
2.4 Learning the grammar of graphics
So what does the grammar of graphics look like? Well, “it depends”. Just like linguistic grammars vary between languages, visualization grammars are implemented differently in different packages. However, there are some core steps which are present in most grammars of graphics:

Create a data-linked canvas: This step creates a background canvas that other graphical components are drawn upon and links it to the relevant dataset.
Encode visual aesthetics: This step defines how data will be mapped to graphical channels (e.g., the column 'group' might be mapped to the color of each mark).
Add geometric marks: This step selects the graphical elements used to represent the data (e.g., points or bars).

As a result of the predictable structure, a grammar of graphics allows you to create an impressive range of visualizations in an intuitive manner and aids in reasoning about these visualizations. It also makes it notably easier to change between different types of plots, as the code syntax follows a predictable structure and only parts of the specification change between charts. In fact, libraries that implement a grammar of graphics often require fewer changes in the code to create different types of visualizations.3


Implementations of the grammar of graphics
You can think of the grammar of graphics as an underlying theory of how to make visualizations. But to actually create a visualization, we need to use a package that implements this theory in code. This book shows several programmatic implementations and lets you choose which package you prefer to learn, while also allowing for quick comparisons between libraries. Before creating a visualization, let’s see how the structure of these implementations is similar to the general structure we described above.

 Stellar naming
Altair is built on Vega-Lite, which in turn is built on the JavaScript visualization library Vega. Vega was named after a star and the name “Altair” was picked because it represents another star in the same astronomical pattern.




 A nod in the name
The “gg” in ggplot2 is a reference to Wilkinson’s The Grammar of Graphics, which inspired the creation of the ggplot2 library.

Altairggplot


In the Python package Altair, a general representation of the core chart components would look like this:

alt.Chart(data).encode().mark()

alt.Chart(data) creates the data-linked canvas.
encode(...) encodes the visual aesthetics, such as x and y.
mark_*(...) adds geometric marks, such as points or bars.


Note that we wrote the Altair syntax in the same form as in our general grammar of graphics example above to help you see how it maps onto that structure. It is perfectly fine to keep writing this way if you prefer it, but the canonical way to write Altair chart specifications is in the form alt.Chart(data).mark().encode(). We will follow that order from now on since most examples you will see elsewhere follow this syntax.



In the R library ggplot2, a general representation of the core chart components would look like this:

ggplot(data) + aes() + geom()

ggplot(data) creates the data-linked canvas.
aes(...) encodes the visual aesthetics, such as x and y.
geom_*(...) A geom function adds geometric marks, such as points or bars.


Note that we wrote the ggplot syntax in the same form as in our general grammar of graphics example above to help you see how it maps onto that structure. It is perfectly fine to keep writing this way if you prefer it, but the canonical way to write ggplot chart specifications is in the form ggplot(data, aes()) + geom(). We will follow that order from now on since most examples you will see elsewhere follow this syntax.










Deep-diveDeep dive: The R and Python visualization ecosystems






There is a wide variety of high-level and low-level tools for visualizing data in R and Python. While we have already outlined the advantages of the libraries we chose, it can be helpful to be aware of which others are available since you are likely to encounter some of them in the wild. In this diagram, you can see an overview of the available tools and how they are connected.

title: 3  Individual observations
text:
3.1 Why bother?
Plotting each individual observation separately is one of the most direct ways to visualize data. Rather than summarizing groups of observations, we’re simply putting one graphical point in our chart for every record in our table. As we saw in the introductory chapter, even this simple form of visualization can reveal patterns that are difficult to spot in a table of numbers.

title: 3  Individual observations
text:
3.2 Creating our first chart
It’s time to start coding! First, we need some example data to visualize. Libraries that implement a grammar of graphics generally work with “tidy” data. In tidy data, each column represents a variable (also called a field), and each row represents an observation. We will start by loading a small historical dataset with information about cars’ design, performance, and fuel efficiency.

Looking at the table above, we might start to generate questions about our data. Perhaps the cars with the best fuel efficiency are also the cars with the least powerful engines (i.e. do the cars with the highest Miles_per_Gallon also have the lowest Horsepower)? This sounds reasonable since a more powerful engine generally uses more fuel. Let’s see if we can answer this question with a visualization. To see how these two variables relate to each other, we can map them to two visual channels in the chart, such as x and y.

Altairggplot


First, we create a canvas linked to the cars dataframe via alt.Chart(cars). Then, we indicate what kind of geometric mark we want to use to represent the data. Here, it is suitable to show the data as points using mark_point():

alt.Chart(cars).mark_point().encode(
    x='Miles_per_Gallon',
    y='Horsepower'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






First, we create a canvas linked to the cars dataframe via ggplot(cars). Then, we indicate what kind of geometric mark we want to use to represent the data. Here, it is suitable to show the data as points using geom_point():

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Miles_per_Gallon, y = Horsepower)) +
    geom_point()

Warning: Removed 14 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).















 Different defaults
You can see that there are some differences in the default choices made by each library.
Different styles have different advantages, and they are easy to customize to look however you want, which we will learn about later.
Including the origin (x = 0, y = 0) or zooming in on the data can both be sensible defaults in different contexts, which we will also learn more about in later chapters.
Observations with missing values in either Miles_per_Gallon or Horsepower are omitted because they cannot be positioned on both axes. Some libraries explicitly warn about this and others don’t.
Does the chart answer our question? That’s up to you to explore in the exercise below!






Ex-promptExercise 1






Study the chart above. What can you say about the relationship between Horsepower and Miles_per_Gallon? If you choose to use statistical terms such as correlation, also explain them in plain English, as if you were explaining what the chart means to someone unfamiliar with statistics. Finally, it’s always good to ask yourself if your interpretation of the chart makes sense, given your knowledge about how the world works.






Ex-hintHint






It can be helpful to start with a particular area of the chart. For example, look at the cars with the most powerful engines (highest horsepower). What is their fuel efficiency? Now do the same for the cars with the least powerful engines and compare the two.






Ex-solutionSolution






From the chart, we can see that Horsepower and Miles_per_Gallon are “negatively correlated”. In plain English, this means that cars with more powerful engines (higher Horsepower) tend to have lower fuel efficiency (lower Miles_per_Gallon). This makes sense, as more powerful engines often consume more fuel than less powerful ones. Note that we can’t make claims about a causal relationship from the chart alone, but in this case, the observed relationship in the chart supports our mechanistic understanding of the world.

What if one of the other variables also influences a car’s fuel efficiency? For example, it seems reasonable that the weight of the car could impact fuel efficiency, since more energy is needed to accelerate a heavier car to the same speed. To explore Weight_in_lbs together with the other two variables, we can use another visual channel in this chart, for example, by coloring the points according to this column. When using the color encoding channel, high-level visualization libraries will automatically figure out an appropriate color scale to use. Since the Weight_in_lbs column contains continuous numerical data, a continuous gradient will be used here.

Altairggplot


Here, we add the color encoding to the chart so that we can see how all three variables relate to each other. Note that the largest value in the Weight_in_lbs column is represented with a dark color, which contrasts strongly with the light background of the chart.

alt.Chart(cars).mark_point().encode(
    x='Miles_per_Gallon',
    y='Horsepower',
    color='Weight_in_lbs'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Here, we add the color encoding to the chart so that we can see how all three variables relate to each other. The default color gradient runs from dark blue for lower weights to light blue for higher weights, since light colors have the highest contrast to the chart’s dark background.

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Miles_per_Gallon, y = Horsepower, color = Weight_in_lbs)) +
    geom_point()

Warning: Removed 14 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).














 Making space
Notice the difference in how the legend is added in the two libraries. In Altair, the overall width of the figure increases to keep the dimensions of the chart area the same, whereas in ggplot, the width of the figure stays constant, so the chart area narrows to accommodate the legend. In general, we don’t want the chart area to shrink just because we are adding a legend, so here we would need to manually increase the width of the ggplot chart, which we will learn about in a future chapter. 






Ex-promptExercise 2






How does a car’s weight relate to its fuel efficiency?






Ex-hintHint






Use the color legend to find the heaviest cars. Where do they fall on the fuel-efficiency axis? Compare them with the lightest cars, then check how their horsepower differs too.






Ex-solutionSolution






We can see that Weight_in_lbs is positively correlated with Horsepower and negatively with Miles_per_Gallon. This aligns with our knowledge about the world: heavier cars generally need more energy to accelerate to the same speed, and the heavier cars in this dataset tend to have more powerful engines. However, remember that we can’t establish causation from the chart alone. We can only note that the correlation matches what we would expect based on our knowledge about the physics of moving objects.












Is the color or position easier to read?. You might already have noticed that it was harder to read exact values from the color scale than from the x- and y-axes. This is an important consideration, and we will dive deeper into which visual channels are the most effective at presenting information in the next chapter.

title: 4  Magnitude
text:
4.1 Why bother?
In the last chapter, we saw how we could visualize magnitude as either the position of a point along an axis or as the brightness of the point’s color. We can refer to these different ways of representing a quantity graphically as visual “channels”. There are many more visual channels than position and brightness, and when we visualize something, we want to think about which are the most effective channels that we can use to understand the data.
As in many cases, an efficient way to learn this topic is through personal experience, rather than just being told the answer. So let’s experience how some visual channels are more effective than others through a short exercise.

title: 4  Magnitude
text:
Ex-promptExercise 1






Take a few seconds to answer the following question. How many times larger is the bigger object as the smaller one in each of these two images?




Remember that we learn more effectively when we actively try to answer questions like these instead of viewing the solution right away.






Ex-hintHint






What do you think is meant by “bigger” when it comes to the circles? Are you supposed to compare the areas or the diameters?






Ex-solutionSolution






The larger circle has seven times the area of the smaller circle, and the longer bar has seven times the length of the shorter bar.1



Most people find that it is much easier to compare the length and position of the bars aligned to the same baseline than to estimate the areas of the circles. For bars, it is also immediately clear what to compare as long as their widths are kept constant, whereas for the circles we might hesitate between area and diameter. This is important to keep in mind, especially when communicating to others via visualization, but also when creating plots for yourself.
Even if you aced both comparisons yourself, the fact that many people tend to get one of them wrong more often means that in order for you to create effective visualizations you need to know which visual channels are the easiest for humans to decode.

title: 4  Magnitude
text:
4.2 Visual channel effectiveness
There has been plenty of research trying to determine which visual channels are the most effective when communicating different aspects of a dataset. The findings from these studies provide us with a useful guiding foundation that we should only stray from with good reason. The main findings are summarized in the schematic below, from the most to the least effective visual channel.






Figure 4.1: Classical visual-channel ranking for quantitative magnitude judgments. Adapted from Visualization Analysis and Design, Tamara Munzner, with illustrations by Eamonn Maguire (2014, CC BY 4.0).





What is regarded as visually salient might vary across cultures, geographic regions, and age groups. This is important to remember since much of this research has been carried out with college students in North America and Europe. More recent studies have shown that the chart’s purpose and the combination of visual channels affect which ways of depicting magnitude are most effective.2
Position along a common scale is generally the most effective visual channel for precise magnitude comparisons, so we should use it for our most important comparisons when possible. In a scatterplot, for example, position along the x- and y-axes represents two variables, but we can also use size or color to represent additional variables. Although it is harder to judge exact quantities from these channels (is this dot’s area exactly twice that of another?), they can still help us see trends in the data.

Unnecessary 3D makes plot interpretation harder
Three-dimensional plots are especially problematic when the extra dimension serves only as decoration, as in a 3D bar or pie chart. Even when depth represents data, as in a 3D scatterplot, positions can be difficult to compare. This is particularly challenging in a static image on paper, where the reader cannot rotate the plot to inspect it from different angles.






Ex-promptExercise 2






Which value do you think is represented by the bar labelled “B” in the 3D bar chart below?









Ex-solutionSolution






The bars appear to have values of approximately A = 0.7, B = 1.7, C = 2.7, and D = 3.7, but this is an illusion caused by the viewing angle of the “camera” in this 3D scene. The actual values of A, B, C, and D are 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. This plot would have been much easier to read without the unnecessary 3D effect.










Meaningful 3D can facilitate plot interpretation
Sometimes 3D can be useful, such as in a topographic map or a visualization of a protein’s structure. Below you can see examples created with the rayshader library that use 3D representations and camera rotation to help us interpret spatial relationships. The example on the right visualizes the curvature of spacetime via 3D position (depth), eliminating the need for the additional 2D plot shown in the example on the left.




Video

Figure 4.2: A useful application of 3D.



But be cautious: we will see in the next section that even for systems such as blood vessels, which are naturally organized in three dimensions, it can be more mentally demanding to interpret a 3D visualization accurately. Claus Wilke has written a helpful chapter on this topic if you are interested in learning more.

title: 4  Magnitude
section: 4.3 Well-designed visualizations can support clinical decisions
text:
4.3 Well-designed visualizations can support clinical decisions
The importance of these best practices might seem a bit abstract until you experience their effects yourself. Let’s look at a concrete example of how changing visualization methods improved performance on a medically relevant task.
Heart disease is the most common cause of death, killing almost 9 million people each year, or as many as diabetes, dementia, neonatal conditions, and respiratory infections combined. Low wall shear stress—the frictional force per unit area exerted by blood on an artery wall— is associated with the development of atherosclerosis. Identifying these regions can therefore help clinicians assess areas at risk.
To evaluate the shear stress in the arteries, one approach is to use a digital 3D representation of the artery colored according to the magnitude of shear stress, which is what you can see in the picture below. The colormap changes from blue for the areas of interest (low stress) to cyan, green, yellow, and red for higher stress.
In a 2011 study, Michelle Borkin and colleagues tested how effective this type of visualization was compared to alternatives using 2D representations and a diverging color scale.3 The experiment involved 21 Harvard medical students, who were asked to identify regions of low shear stress. When using the visualization you see below, they correctly identified an average of ~40% of these regions.




Changing the color scale almost doubled the accuracy
One comparison tested the effect of changing the color scale to one that is easier to interpret and makes the important areas of low shear stress stand out more, by highlighting them in bright red and showing the remaining areas in shades of gray. With this seemingly small modification, the percentage of low-shear-stress regions correctly identified almost doubled, from 40% to 70% for the 3D representations.
We will talk more about choosing appropriate color scales in later chapters.





Changing from 3D to 2D improved accuracy further
Another comparison tested changing from a 3D representation of the blood vessels to a 2D representation while using the diverging color scale. Although a 3D representation preserves more of the vessels’ anatomical geometry, it is also more cognitively demanding for us to process, and some areas can cover others so it is harder to get a quick overview of the vessels. In the 2D visualization, the blood vessels and their branching points are shown in a schematic that is less cognitively demanding to interpret. This representation was also shown to be more effective, as 90% of the low-shear-stress regions were correctly identified on average.
Overall, these two changes more than doubled the percentage of regions correctly identified, from 40% to 90%. That is a huge increase from modifications that might have seemed to be merely a matter of taste without knowledge of visualization theory! So, if anyone tells you that visualization of data is not as important as other components, you can tell them about this study and ask them what kind of visualization they want their doctor to look at when analyzing their arteries.



As with many things, there are situations where you can depart from these guidelines if you are sure about what you are doing and are trying to create a specific effect in your communication. But most of the time, it is best to adhere to the principles discussed above and we will dive deeper into some of them later in the book.

title: 4  Magnitude
section: 4.4 Choose the most effective channel for the most important comparison
text:
4.4 Choose the most effective channel for the most important comparison
Let’s apply what we have learned in the context of the dataset from last chapter.

Altairggplot



import altair as alt
import pandas as pd


url = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joelostblom/teaching-datasets/main/cars.csv'
cars = pd.read_csv(url)




library(ggplot2)


url <- 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joelostblom/teaching-datasets/main/cars.csv'
cars <- readr::read_csv(url)




If we are interested in visualizing the relationship between 'Miles_per_Gallon', 'Horsepower', and 'Weight_in_lbs'. If all pairwise relationships were of high importance, we could created three separate plots where each variable get to be on the x and y axis two times each, so that they can make use of the most effective channel, position on a shared scale.
However, if we would like to include all three variables in the same chart, then we would need to decide what the most important comparison is. If it is to compare fuel efficiency to weight, then we would make the following chart:

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(cars).mark_point().encode(
    x='Miles_per_Gallon',
    y='Weight_in_lbs',
    color='Horsepower'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Here, we add the color encoding to the chart so that we can see how all three variables relate to each other. The default color gradient runs from dark blue for lower weights to light blue for higher weights, since light colors have the highest contrast to the chart’s dark background.

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Miles_per_Gallon, y = Weight_in_lbs, color = Horsepower)) +
    geom_point()

Warning: Removed 8 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).












If we instead are mainly interested in comparing, engine power vs weight, then we would make the following chart:

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(cars).mark_point().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Weight_in_lbs',
    color='Miles_per_Gallon'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Here, we add the color encoding to the chart so that we can see how all three variables relate to each other. The default color gradient runs from dark blue for lower weights to light blue for higher weights, since light colors have the highest contrast to the chart’s dark background.

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Weight_in_lbs, color = Miles_per_Gallon)) +
    geom_point()

Warning: Removed 6 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).


















WarningAvoid blindly following a ranking



As with much of the other advice in this book, (and in life) context matters. If we think there is good reason to pick a lower ranking visual channel, then do that. For example, using size instead of color seems reasonable since area is more highly ranked than color brightness. However, if we try this, we immediately see that this is not an effective visualization since the additional size of the points leads to significant overlap in the chart and it is difficult to tell what is going on in the saturated area in the bottom left.

Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction by Kieran Healy; from “Visual tasks and decoding graphs” until the end of the chapter.

title: 5  Groups
text:
5.1 Why bother?
So far, you have created declarative visualizations by representing observations as point marks on a canvas, using position and color to represent quantitative variables. This is the foundation for all the visualizations we will make, but it is rarely sufficient on its own to give a complete picture of the data. In particular, real-world datasets might show overall trends that disappear or change when individual groups are explored more closely. The goal of grouping is to distinguish between groups by basing the visual appearance or placement of points in a chart on the value of a categorical variable. Let’s see this in action in the following exercise.
Did the pattern above match your expectations? Proceed to the next exercise to find out if there is more to this dataset than meets the eye!

title: 5  Groups
text:
Ex-promptExercise 1






Before making a chart, make a prediction: do you think that countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers tend to have higher or lower life expectancy? What makes you expect that?
We will investigate a country-level dataset containing the percentage of heavy drinkers and the average remaining life expectancy at age 65.1 In our scatterplot, each point represents a country. The x-axis shows the percentage of heavy drinkers, and the y-axis shows the average number of years a person reaching age 65 can expect to live beyond that age.2

Study the table and the tooltips in the previous chart. What do you think might be the reason that countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers also have higher remaining life expectancy at age 65? Suggest one visual change to the chart that would help you explore whether your suggested reason could influence the relationship between alcohol consumption and life expectancy.






Ex-hintHint






Could other variables in the dataset be related to both alcohol consumption and life expectancy? For example, consider the country’s income group or world region. Could you group the points by one of these variables using shape or color?






Ex-solutionSolution






Both a country’s income group and its region might help explain differences in alcohol consumption and life expectancy. Here, we will explore income group only; you can explore region on your own. To add this information to the chart, we could use different colors to group the points visually by income group:





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Notice how the data points form clusters by income group. Coloring reveals that both the percentage of heavy drinkers and remaining life expectancy at age 65 are associated with income group. High-income countries tend to have higher values for both measures. We see the opposite picture for most low-income countries, where both measures are lower.
This gives us a possible explanation for the surprising overall trend. Income level could be a confounding variable, influencing both alcohol consumption and life expectancy. The chart suggests this possibility but does not establish those causal effects. Crucially, the points represent countries, not people: we cannot conclude that the people who drink heavily are the same people who live longer. We would need individual-level data and an appropriate study design to investigate that relationship.
The data hasn’t changed, but our view of it has. Grouping turns a puzzling overall trend into a more granular question: does the relationship hold within comparable groups?

title: 5  Groups
section: 5.2 The two main purposes of grouping
text:
5.2 The two main purposes of grouping
As we have seen in the exercises above, grouping can have major benefits. We can divide these benefits into two main categories, both of which help us arrive at more accurate conclusions about our data:


Directly compare observations between groups.
Reveal patterns within individual groups that are obscured when viewing the data from all groups together.


These benefits are often connected and can be explored simultaneously. When we grouped the alcohol consumption data by income level, the positive relationship in the pooled data was much less apparent within groups. Grouping also made it easier to compare observations between groups.

Simpson’s paradox
Differences between overall and within-group relationships are central to Simpson’s paradox (named after the statistician Edward H. Simpson, rather than the TV series). In the classic form of this phenomenon, a trend within individual groups reverses when the groups are combined. Grouping can also reveal trends that are weak or absent in the pooled data.
Below we show a simplified illustration of this aggregation effect. Notice how the overall dataset shows little apparent relationship between X and Y, but when the observations are colored by group, you can see that both groups exhibit a negative trend between X and Y: larger values of X tend to be associated with smaller values of Y, and vice versa. This is a prime example of the utility of grouping in deepening our understanding of a dataset; without it, we would have missed the within-group relationships.

OverallBy group

title: 5  Groups
section: 5.3 What type of column can we use for grouping?
text:
5.3 What type of column can we use for grouping?
In general, we group data by “categorical” columns. If there is a natural order to the categories (e.g., education levels or letter grades), we can be more precise and call the column “ordinal”. If there is no such order, we say that the column is “nominal” (e.g., types of fruit or color names). As a general rule, we don’t group data by continuous variables or discrete variable with many values, but we could if we first turn them into interval categories e.g. converting age in years into the intervals 18–24, 25–34, and 35–44. In general, we want relatively few unique values when we group by a variable so that the visualization is easy to digest, but there are exceptions, particularly when creating faceted plots as we will see later.

title: 5  Groups
text:
5.4 Channels for grouping
Generally speaking, position and color are the two most effective visual channels to use for grouping. Shape can also be used, but often either in combination with one of the other two or for a specific purpose.






Figure 5.2: Classical ordering of static identity channels for grouping; effectiveness depends on the task and design. Adapted from Visualization Analysis and Design, Tamara Munzner, with illustrations by Eamonn Maguire (2014, CC BY 4.0); motion omitted.



Let’s take a look at a familiar example: the traffic light. Do you think that traffic lights are well designed? At first glance, their use of red and green presents a challenge for people with red–green color vision deficiency. Thankfully, signals can communicate their meaning through position and shape as well as color, as in the pedestrian signals below.






Figure 5.3: Traffic lights often use color, shape, and position to communicate meaning. Pedestrian Vectors by Achmad Saroju via Vecteezy





Shape up
Some regions also use shape to distinguish traffic signals for cars, as in this example from Nova Scotia in eastern Canada.

Using several visual channels for the same distinction gives viewers more than one cue to interpret. Even traffic signals for cars that lack distinct shapes typically use a consistent arrangement, so drivers can use position as well as color to distinguish the signals.

Applying grouping strategies
The grammar of graphics allows for the grouping strategies to be conveniently defined via an easily interchangeable syntax:

Altairggplot




ColorShapePosition


encode(color='category_column')


encode(shape='category_column')


encode(x='category_column')
encode(y='category_column')








ColorShapePosition


aes(color = category_column)


aes(shape = category_column)


aes(x = category_column)
aes(y = category_column)









Color
The human brain can detect color differences with little cognitive effort. Color is a preattentive feature3 which means that the brain can tell apart colors even without conscious attention. This is heightened when there is a high contrast, such as between the complementary colors blue and orange.
This is great news for grouping! By encoding our categorical variable as color, we can leverage the brain’s ability to infer groups. Conveniently, color doesn’t alter the layout or structure of the data visualization, so it’s an efficient way to compare the exact values of data points between groups.
In the second exercise of this chapter, we already saw how color could be used to group our life expectancy data by income group. Let’s now see what the code to create this chart looks like:

Altairggplot


Here we use color='income_group':

import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

income_df = pd.read_csv('data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv')

alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Here we use color = income_group:

library(tidyverse)

income_df <- read_csv('data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv')

ggplot(income_df, aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group
    )) +
    geom_point()

















WarningAvoid using color for more than 4-6 groups




Using too many colors or colors that are too similar can blur the differences between groups. There are also several other important aspects of using colors effectively, such as how to ensure accessibility, particularly for people with color vision deficiencies. We will learn more about these topics in a later chapter, but for now it’s enough to remember that when there are more than about 4–6 groups in the data, it might be better to break it down into separate charts instead of grouping by color. The more overlap, the fewer content




Shape
Shape is a less effective grouping strategy on its own, but it can be combined with color to provide an additional visual cue.
The syntax for mapping a variable to the shape channel is similar to that for color:

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='income_group'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Setting filled=True fills all the points with a solid color, making the shapes easier to distinguish:

alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(filled=True).encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='income_group'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group,
        shape = income_group
    ) +
    geom_point()











While this combined approach can make grouping clearer, there are some pitfalls. For instance, hollow symbols limit the total area that can be colored, reducing the impact of color. Filled shapes can make color easier to see when combining shape and color. Additionally, smaller shapes are difficult to distinguish, so when plotting a dense scatterplot of small marks, try restricting the number of unique shapes to three or fewer, or consider avoiding using shape altogether. 






WarningAvoid using color and shape for different variables



It is often difficult to interpret charts that map one variable to color and another to shape. This tends to lead to too much visual information and it is difficult to distinguish the many different combinations visually. The exception is if the chart is relatively simple with few observations and few combinations of the shape and color variable; then this combination might work.
The many combinations of income group and region in this chart are hard to separate visually, which makes this chart ineffective:

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(filled=True).encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='region'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  





How do lower middle income countries compare between Asia and Africa?



ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group,
        shape = region
    ) +
    geom_point()



















WarningAvoid using size to group by a categorical variable



Size is often used to represent the magnitude of quantitative data. Under limited circumstances, it can also be used for grouping data according to a categorical variable, but in general this is best avoided.
Since size has an inherent direction from small to large, it works better for ordinal than nominal categorical data. One example is the World Bank income levels, ranging from low to high. However, even when used for ordinal data, it is often difficult to tell different sizes apart, as you can see in the chart below.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  








Position

X and Y position
Grouping by position often creates the clearest separation between groups. Distributing the groups along the x- or y-axis gives each group its own visual lane, preventing observations from different groups from overlapping. This means that there is no risk for overlap between groups and we can generally visualize many more groups when we separate them by position rather than color or shape. However, the grouping column now occupies one positional visual channel, so there is only one positional channel left for encoding the values we want to compare between the groups.
Below, we distribute the regions along the y-axis. This leaves us with a choice of whether to use the x-axis for percentage_heavy_drinkers or life_expectancy_at_65. We cannot represent both quantitative variables with position in this chart.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='region',
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = region,
    ) +
    geom_point()

















WarningAvoid rotated category labels along the x-axis



We could swap the x and y variables above, but then the region labels would be rotated and harder to read. Short category labels that fit horizontally can work well on the x-axis. For longer labels, placing the categories on the y-axis usually makes the text easier to read.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  








Faceting
Faceting takes the concept of grouping to the next level. Instead of using different visual channels within a single chart, generates multiple charts (or “facets”), each dedicated to a grouped subset of the data. Faceting is particularly effective for highlighting distinct trends and patterns within each subset, as well as identifying extreme values or outliers within groups. We could think of faceting as a type of position grouping, but its advantage is that it keeps both the x- and y-axes free for other variables. Facetting generally supports comparison of many groups, just like grouping by x or y position.
Let’s create a separate facet for each income group, so that the relationship between percentage_heavy_drinkers and life_expectancy_at_65 within each group stands out. We can lay out the facets differently depending on what we are most interested in comparing. If the y-axis is the primary channel for comparison, we would spread the facets out horizontally in a single row. If the x-axis is the primary channel for comparison, we would spread the facets out vertically in a single column. In either case, the scales should be shared for direct comparisons. Neither axis is our sole focus here: we are interested in comparing the overall pattern within each group, so we will lay out the facets in a compact grid to save space.

Altairggplot


To facet by income group, we can append .facet('income_group') to our chart. We create a 2 × 2 grid of facets by using the columns parameter.

alt.Chart(income_df, height=150, width=150).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
).facet(
    'income_group',
    columns=2
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




In addition to faceting on a single variable in the data, faceting can also be done over two variables: one spread horizontally and one spread out vertically in the faceted charts. In Altair, we would use the column and row parameters to achieve this. For example, to have facets that are grouped by both income group and region, we could use facet(column='income_group', row='region'). This can be effective when we need to group our data further, but it can make the chart difficult to take in at a glance, so it is best used when there are fewer categories in the faceting variables.


To facet by income group, we can add + facet_wrap(vars(income_group)) to our chart. The vars() function specifies which columns to use for faceting, just as aes() specifies the mappings from variables to visual channels.
By default, facet_wrap() arranges these four groups in a 2 × 2 grid, which is appropriate for our visualization. Here, we set the ncol argument explicitly to illustrate how you can control the number of columns in the facet grid.

ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65
    ) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(vars(income_group), ncol = 2)








In addition to faceting on a single variable in the data, faceting can also be done over two variables: one spread horizontally and one spread out vertically in the faceted charts. In ggplot, we would replace facet_wrap() with facet_grid() to do this. For example, to have facets that are grouped by both income group and region, we could use facet_grid(rows = vars(region), cols = vars(income_group)). This can be effective when we need to group our data further, but it can make the chart difficult to take in at a glance, so it is best used when there are fewer categories in the faceting variables.



As you can see above, faceting makes it easier to observe the overall pattern for each income group and how tightly clustered the values are. It also reveals potential outliers in the upper-middle-income facet: we can easily spot two countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers than the others in that group. On the other hand, it is now harder to compare individual values between groups because the points are spread across different charts instead of being close together in a single chart.

title: 5  Groups
text:
5.5 Grouping within facets
All the previous grouping strategies can be used within each facet as additional layers of grouping. This nested grouping can be useful for dividing our data according to multiple categorical variables, but it can become confusing if we try to fit too much into a single visualization. How many grouping variables you can use depends on how well separated the groups are and how many observations you have. More observations and less separation between groups mean that you need to be more careful and may need fewer layers of grouping to keep the visualization easy to interpret.
Let’s try out an example of how we can use faceting together with other grouping strategies.






Ex-promptExercise 3






Let’s say you are primarily interested in the relationship between life expectancy and heavy drinking across different regions. As a secondary comparison, you would also like to see how different income groups vary within the same region. Which visual channels would you use to group the chart?






Ex-hintHint






You could e.g. use faceting and coloring, but which one should you use for which grouping variable?






Ex-solutionSolution






Since we are interesting in comparing the relationship between two variables, faceting is a suitable choice as it gives two free positional channels (x and y) to map the two variables to for each group. Since we are primarily interested in how this relationship changes between regions, we will create one facet per region. Then we use another visual channel, such as color (or color and shape) to highlight the income groups within each region.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df, height=200, width=200).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group'
).facet(
    'region',
    columns=2
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group
    ) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(vars(region), ncol = 2)

title: 6  Connections
text:
6.1 Why bother?
In Chapter 5, we learned how to distinguish groups of observations. In this chapter, we will explore how to connect observations, which is beneficial to highlight group membership and differences between conditions. Connections can follow a meaningful order, such as time of day or an increasing dose of a treatment. They can also link measurements of the same observational unit across unordered conditions, such as critics’ and audiences’ scores for the same movie. In either case, we need to decide which observations to connect and what those connections help us compare. We will begin with change over time.

title: 6  Connections
text:
Ex-promptExercise 1






In the chart below, we can see how CO₂ emissions per capita have changed over time for the world’s continents.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




As you can see, the chart applies the strategies we have learned so far and uses color to group observations from different continents. But the overlap between groups makes it difficult to follow changes over time for any particular continent, and the chart is a bit confusing even after studying it for a while. How could you change this chart to make it easier to see how CO₂ emissions per capita for each continent have changed over time?






Ex-hintHint






Do you think connecting the points belonging to the same continent would make it easier or harder to spot trends?






Ex-solutionSolution






Let’s see how it looks if we connect the points with a line:

points.mark_line() + points.mark_point(filled=True, strokeOpacity=1)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




We can use the natural order of the observations to connect the points that belong to the same continent with a line. Drawing a line from the earliest to the most recent year helps us with two things: it makes it easier to see changes over time for any single continent, and it makes it easier to see which points belong to which continent. As such, a line makes group membership explicit while helping us follow changes through an ordered sequence.

title: 6  Connections
text:
6.2 Connecting ordered observations
To explore how to create line charts, we will visualize population and fertility estimates at eight-year intervals from 1850 to 2018. The data comes from the Gapminder country-level dataset, and has been adapted for this textbook.

Altairggplot



import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

world = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_world_from_1850.csv')
world

library(tidyverse)

world <- read_csv('data/gapminder_world_from_1850.csv')
world

22 rows × 3 columns





When reading in a new dataset, it is always a good idea to have a look at a few rows as we did above, to get an idea of what the data looks like.
The world dataset has one row per sampled year, with the total population of the countries in the source dataset and the average of their fertility estimates (children_per_woman). Fertility here estimates the number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if the year’s age-specific birth rates persisted; it is not the number born per woman in a single year. Each country contributes equally to the average in our table, so this is a country average rather than a population-weighted global estimate. The regional dataset, which we will use later, applies the same summaries within each region.
Since the data reaches all the way back to the 1850s, it would be really interesting to plot how the world population grew over the period covered by the data. We can use a line plot to show this change over time.






Ex-promptExercise 2






Sketch a visualization for how you think the world population changed over time (by hand is better than in your mind, which is better than nothing…). Thinking about the data up front makes you more prepared to investigate the chart and notice if the output looks unexpected in some manner.






Ex-solutionSolution






If we sketched this visualization on paper, we might expect something like this: a single line that rises from the 1800s to the end of our dataset as the population increases.














Drawing of estimated world population growthNow we are ready to create our plot! By convention, time variables such as year tend to be laid out along the x-axis, while quantitative measures such as population tend to occupy the y-axis.

Altairggplot


In Altair, we use mark_line() to connect observations with a line.

alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x='year',
    y='population'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




You can see that the formatting on the x-axis includes a comma as a thousands separator. While this is desirable for regular quantitative variables, it is not how we are used to seeing years displayed. To deal with this, we can either change the underlying data type or the number formatting of the axis.
To change the axis formatting, we need to leverage the helper class alt.X (similar helpers exist for other channels, such as alt.Y and alt.Color). These classes help us customize many aspects of our charts. When using just x='year', we’re using shorthand for alt.X('year'); we just save ourselves some typing.
Here we are going to set alt.X('year').axis(format='d'), where the d is short for “decimal integer” (i.e., a base-10 integer).

alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='population'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Now the years are formatted as we are used to seeing them!


In ggplot, we use geom_line() to connect observations with a line.

ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_line()













 Population plateau
Although the historical curve might suggest that the population will keep growing rapidly, the UN’s 2024 projections suggest a peak of around 10.3 billion people before the end of the century, followed by a gradual decline.
Interestingly, the line in this example helps us notice a change in the slope. The world population increased more slowly numbers before around 1950, and more rapidly afterwards.
After making any chart, it’s beneficial to ask yourself: “Is this what I expected to see from the data?” and “Does it align with what I know about this topic?” If we think about what happened in the world around the time of the change in the population growth dynamics, a major event that stands out was the end of World War II in 1945. It seems reasonable that transitioning from a war involving many countries around the world to a time of peace and increased safety could lead to an increase in the number of babies born. Let’s explore whether the timing of the change coincides with an increase in the country-average fertility rate.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='children_per_woman'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = children_per_woman)) +
    geom_line()











The country-average fertility estimate does show a rise from the late 1930s to the early 1960s, followed by a decline. This “explosion” is what is commonly referred to as the “baby boom”. However, remember that this chart averages country-level fertility estimates rather than taking the population in each country into account, so it does not directly show the total number of babies born in the world.
Based on these charts, how would you explain the reason for the increase in the world population around the 1950?







Deep-diveDeep dive






One more important piece of the puzzle here would be to look at life expectancy data to see if people were also living longer lives during this period, which would also contribute to population growth. Historical life expectancy estimates vary in coverage and reliability, but you can explore available estimates at Our World in Data.










WarningAvoid claiming causation from visualizations alone



When commenting on a visualization, stick to non-causal language: variables are correlated, associated, or related.  You might have heard that “correlation is not causation”, and that applies here too. Although the end of World War II seems like a plausible contributor to some of the trends we have explored, it is important to understand that plausibility alone does not establish the cause of the observed patterns. Usually, several contributing factors interact to produce a more complex picture. This article about the baby boom elaborates on what we explored here. Among other things, it notes that many countries saw birth rates begin to rise even before World War II.

title: 6  Connections
text:
6.3 Indicating where the observations lie
Generally, it is helpful to add points on top of a line to indicate exactly where each observation from the data lies.

Altairggplot


In Altair, we combine lines and points through a concept called layering, where charts are superimposed on each other. The + operator means to “layer” a chart on top of another chart.  

line = alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='children_per_woman'
)
line + line.mark_point(filled=True)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Each basic Altair chart specification uses a single mark type, so line.mark_point() replaces the line mark with a point mark in the chart that we are layering on top of our original. 


In ggplot, we combine lines and points through a concept called layering, where charts (or “graphical layers”) are superimposed on each other. The + operator means to “layer” a geom on top of another geom.

ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = children_per_woman)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point()











This highlights something important: what does the line between the data points mean? Let’s find out in the next exercise.






Ex-promptExercise 3






In our data, there are only observations from every eighth year, but the line we have drawn is continuous and has a defined value for children_per_woman even between the points in the chart. For example, in this zoomed-in view we can see that the line at the year 1950 suggests a country-average fertility estimate of approximately 5.4 children per woman. But as we can see from the points in the chart, our data does not contain any observation from exactly this year. [What conclusions can we draw about the fertility estimate for year 1950]?





  
  
  
  
  


  
  










Ex-hintHint






Think about the purpose of the line: is it just a visual aid, or does it represent any feature of the underlying data?






Ex-solutionSolution






The line segments between two observations are there to guide the eye; they do not establish what the values are at every unobserved moment between two points. Although a simple linear interpolation between observations might seem harmless, it is important to consider whether the distance between two points represents a long enough period that important changes could be hidden by a straight line. To understand this more deeply, we can look at what would happen if the observations were closer or farther apart in time, as in the chart below.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




As you can see, drawing a line between the observations sampled 20 years apart misses the rise in the average fertility estimate: it decreased until around 1940, then increased until around 1960, after which it started to decrease again.
How closely observations need to be spaced for straight connecting lines to be a useful approximation depends on which question we are asking. For example, if we are interested in exploring seasonal variation within each year, then even a chart with one observation every year would be insufficient. We would need more frequent observations, such as monthly values.













Connecting observations across categories
Connections can also be useful when the positions on one axis represent categories. For ordinal categories, this might be intuitive, since there is often a natural progression throughout the categories. For example, drawing a line for a measurement over the days of the week would be natural and easy to understand.
We need to be careful when drawing a line between ordinal categories of unequal spacing. For example, if observations from January, February, and August of the same year are displayed at equally spaced categorical positions, the line’s slope reflects the difference between observations rather than change per month. Even a constant nonzero monthly rate would produce a steeper segment between February and August, because that interval covers more months.
In addition to connecting categories when they have a natural order, it can also be helpful to connect categories when the same observational unit is present in all of them. For example, we might measure the same patient before and after treatment, or compare evaluations of the same film by different reviewer groups. We say that such measurements are paired; a concept that extends to more than just two categories e.g. before, during, and after a treatment. Let’s explore this more closely with an exercise:






Ex-promptExercise 4






This data set that contains the names of a few movies together with their critic and general audience rating from Rotten Tomatoes:

Altairggplot



movie_scores = pd.read_csv('data/movie_scores.csv')
movie_scores

    Score Reviewer group               Movie
0      98        Critics          Inside Out
1      89       Audience          Inside Out
2      97        Critics  Mad Max: Fury Road
3      86       Audience  Mad Max: Fury Road
4      72        Critics      Jurassic World
5      78       Audience      Jurassic World
6      63        Critics     Mortal Combat 2
7      86       Audience     Mortal Combat 2
8      83        Critics                Dune
9      90       Audience                Dune
10     71        Critics       The Beekeeper
11     92       Audience       The Beekeeper





movie_scores <- readr::read_csv('data/movie_scores.csv')
movie_scores

# A tibble: 12 × 3
   Score `Reviewer group` Movie             
   <dbl> <chr>            <chr>             
 1    98 Critics          Inside Out        
 2    89 Audience         Inside Out        
 3    97 Critics          Mad Max: Fury Road
 4    86 Audience         Mad Max: Fury Road
 5    72 Critics          Jurassic World    
 6    78 Audience         Jurassic World    
 7    63 Critics          Mortal Combat 2   
 8    86 Audience         Mortal Combat 2   
 9    83 Critics          Dune              
10    90 Audience         Dune              
11    71 Critics          The Beekeeper     
12    92 Audience         The Beekeeper     





Say we’re interested in comparing which movies are more popular among critics and which are more popular among the general audience. We could plot the scores from the critics in one column and the scores from the general audience in another:

Altairggplot


We adjust the size of the chart, and rotate the labels so that they are easy to read.

points = (
    alt.Chart(movie_scores, height=250, width=150)
    .mark_circle(opacity=1)
    .encode(
        x=alt.X('Reviewer group').axis(labelAngle=0),
        y=alt.Y('Score').scale(zero=False),
        color='Movie',
    )
)
points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




How many movies have a higher scores from critics than from the audience?



movie_plot <- ggplot(
    movie_scores,
    aes(
        x = `Reviewer group`,
        y = Score,
        color = Movie,
    )
)
movie_plot + geom_point()











From this plot, are you able to quickly tell for which films the critics score is higher than the audience score? For which is it lower? Which films have the largest differences?






Ex-hintHint






Could connecting the points with a line help? What would we connect: points in the same reviewer group or points belonging to the same movie?






Ex-solutionSolution






Connecting the observations with a line makes it immediately obvious how the scores differ for each movie:

Altairggplot



points.mark_line() + points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







movie_plot +
    geom_line(aes(group = Movie)) +
    geom_point()











One of the reasons this comparison is difficult to make, is that it takes some cognitive effort to find the same movie in both column. We could make this task easier by connecting the points that are from the same movie with a line. In addition to showing which points belong to the same movie, the slope of this line also gives an indication of how the scores differ between the two reviewer groups.

If there are many observations, or we want to know more exactly how big the difference is between groups, it can be advantageous to spread out the movies along one of the positional axes:

Altairggplot



base = alt.Chart(movie_scores).mark_circle().encode(
    y=alt.Y('Movie').sort('x'),
    x=alt.X('Score').scale(zero=False),
)

(
    base.mark_line(color='lightgrey').encode(detail='Movie')
    + base.mark_circle(size=60, opacity=1).encode(color='Reviewer group') 
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Here we use the group aesthetic to group lines by Movie, without using a visual channel such as color or size.

ggplot(movie_scores, aes(x = Score, y = reorder(Movie, Score))) +
    geom_line(aes(group = Movie), color = 'grey') +
    geom_point(aes(color = `Reviewer group`), size = 2) +
    labs(y = 'Movie', color = 'Reviewer group')






























Deep-diveDeep dive








A related concept to what we just did is a parallel coordinates chart, Where several variables are plotted in the same plot, but on different axes next to each other. This is often used as an exploratory technique to detect clusters in the data. Like in the paired comparison, it is the same observation that is connected with the line across the variables. A difference between the two is that a paired comparison plots the same measurement (e.g. Movie score), between different groups (e.g. Reviewers group), whereas a parallel coordinate plot visualized different variables that all use different units or ranges. To be able to show these variables on a common scale, their ranges are often normalized










WarningAvoid arbitrarily connecting unordered categories



As we just saw, we need to be careful when interpreting a line between two observations along a quantitative axis. For the same reason, we should generally avoid using a line to connect observations along an axis of unordered categories. Here are two representations of the same population values:
The points show each continent’s population clearly. Connecting them also emphasizes comparisons between neighboring continents and creates a falling-and-rising pattern. However, the chosen ordering (Africa, Europe, Americas) does not represent a sequence we are interested in following. Rearranging the continents would change the line’s shape without changing the populations.
In the movie example, each connection helps us compare two evaluations of the same film. Here, the connections add an arbitrary sequence to a task that only requires comparing population values.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




It is also worth noting that a line between categorical values can be confusing because in contrast to how a line connecting two quantitative values can hint at what the value between them might have been, there is no meaningful numerical interval between unordered categories. For example, what does it mean that the line is at 1,000 million as it goes from Africa to Europe? That 1,000 million people lived somewhere between Europe and Africa?








Deep-diveDeep dive






Sometimes we want to show how the relationship between two quantitative variables has changed over time. We can do this by plotting the two variables of interest on the x- and y-axes, then connecting the points in chronological order.

Altairggplot


The order encoding controls the order in which observations will be connected by a line. Since there is no visible axis for the year, it would be difficult to know in which direction to read the chart; is the most recent year represented by the point in the top-left or bottom-right corner? To avoid this confusion, we add a tooltip so that you can see which year each point corresponds to when hovering over it with the mouse pointer.

line = alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x='children_per_woman',
    y='population',
    order='year',
    # Display the numeric year as an integer without a thousands separator
    tooltip=alt.Tooltip('year', format='d')
)
line + line.mark_point(filled=True)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






By default, geom_line() connects points in the order of the variable on the x-axis. To connect points in another order, we can use geom_path() instead. This geom connects observations in dataframe row order, so we need to make sure our data is sorted by the variable we want the connection order to represent.
