796        3200           The Mask of Zorro  ...          6.7      4789.0

[789 rows x 17 columns]





library(ggplot2)

movies <- readr::read_csv('data/movies.csv') |>
    dplyr::filter(`MPAA Rating` %in% c('G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R'))
movies

# A tibble: 789 × 17
    ...1 Title   `US Gross` `Worldwide Gross` `US DVD Sales` `Production Budget`
   <dbl> <chr>        <dbl>             <dbl>          <dbl>               <dbl>
 1   164 The Ca…   60240295         102825796             NA            47000000
 2   218 City H…   20278055          20278055             NA            40000000
 3   222 Courag…   59003384         100833145             NA            46000000
 4   234 Dante'…   67163857         178200000             NA           115000000
 5   248 Dragon…   51364680         104364680             NA            57000000
 6   307 From D…   25728961          25728961             NA            20000000
 7   325 First …      87264             87264             NA              300000
 8   356 The Fi…  105489203         181489203             NA            30000000
 9   400 Gone w…  198680470         390525192             NA             3900000
10   435 Happy …   38623460          38623460             NA            10000000
# ℹ 779 more rows
# ℹ 11 more variables: `Release Date` <date>, `MPAA Rating` <chr>,
#   `Running Time min` <dbl>, Distributor <chr>, Source <chr>,
#   `Major Genre` <chr>, `Creative Type` <chr>, Director <chr>,
#   `Rotten Tomatoes Rating` <dbl>, `IMDB Rating` <dbl>, `IMDB Votes` <dbl>





To show a joint distribution of counts, we often map the two categorical variables to the x and y channels in the chart, and then visualize the combined counts as color and/or size. Color and size then provide two cues to the same quantity.

Altairggplot


Mapping count() to color counts the films for each combination of the categories on the two axes.

alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x='MPAA Rating',
    y='Major Genre',
    color='count()',
    size='count()'
)




  
  
  
  


  
  






Computing and mapping count() to color counts the films for each combination of the categories on the two axes.

movies |>
    dplyr::add_count(`Major Genre`, `MPAA Rating`) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        y = `Major Genre`,
        x = `MPAA Rating`,
        size = n, color = n
    )) +
    geom_point()











Just like for other charts using counts we can sort the categoricals according to their count. This can be particularly effective when there are many categories. Here we don’t sort MPAA Rating by count since that category has a natural order to it from lowest to highest rating.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x=alt.X('MPAA Rating'),
    y=alt.Y('Major Genre').sort('color'),
    color='count()',
    size='count()'
)




  
  
  
  


  
  







movies |>
    dplyr::add_count(`Major Genre`, `MPAA Rating`) |>
    ggplot() +
        aes(
            y = reorder(`Major Genre`, -n),
            x = `MPAA Rating`,
            size = n, color = n
        ) +
        geom_point()











Visualizing counts as both size and color helps make large and small counts visually distinct. We could also have visualized the counts as a heatmap, where the size of each mark is a fixed rectangle and only the color varies by count. We will see this visualization further down for numerical distributions as it is more akin to a histogram with the bins more tightly together. For precise numerical comparisons, position and length are usually easier to judge than color or area, so a faceted or grouped bar chart can therefore be preferable (as we learned in Chapter 8). One drawback with such a chart is that it is harder to see patterns in the nested bars than the systematic 2D grid.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(movies).mark_bar().encode(
    y=alt.Y('Major Genre').sort('x'),
    yOffset=alt.X('MPAA Rating'),
    color='MPAA Rating',
    x='count()',
)




  
  
  
  


  
  







movies |>
    dplyr::add_count(`Major Genre`) |>
    ggplot(
        aes(
            y = reorder(`Major Genre`, -n),
            fill = `MPAA Rating`,
        )
    ) +
    geom_bar(position = 'dodge')












Counts or proportions?






Ex-promptExercise 1






There are 134 R-rated dramas and 60 R-rated horror films in this dataset. Does that mean the horror genre is less concentrated in R-rated films? What additional information do we need?






Ex-hintHint






The number of films in a genre and the proportion with a particular rating answer different questions.






Ex-solutionSolution






We need the genre totals: there are 275 dramas and 77 horror films. About 49% of the dramas are rated R, compared with about 78% of the horror films. Drama contains more R-rated films in absolute terms, but Horror has a larger R-rated share.
For example, the same count of 60 R-rated horror films can be divided by:








Denominator
Question answered
Result




All 789 included films
What share are both Horror and rated R?
7.6%


All 77 horror films
What share of Horror is rated R?
77.9%


All 262 R-rated films
What share of R-rated films is Horror?
22.9%



Dividing every cell by the grand total gives joint proportions. Dividing within a row or column gives a conditional distribution. State the denominator when displaying proportions: the appearance of a heatmap alone does not tell us which question it answers.

title: 12  Joint distributions
text:
12.3 Overplotting and binning quantitative variables
For numerical variables, a scatterplot shows the observed value pairs directly. But with many observations, overlapping marks can make regions with quite different numbers of observations look similarly crowded. Drawing every observation can saturate a scatterplot, making very different concentrations look equally dense.
We will use all 53,940 observations from the carat and price columns of a diamonds dataset. Carat measures diamond weight, and price is in US dollars.

Altairggplot



diamonds = pd.read_csv('data/diamonds-carat-price.csv')

alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_point().encode(
    x='carat',
    y='price',
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




Smaller, more transparent marks can help reveal some of the overlap.

alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_circle(size=10, opacity=0.3).encode(
    x='carat',
    y='price',
)




  
  
  
  


  
  







diamonds <- readr::read_csv('data/diamonds-carat-price.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_point()








Smaller points and a lower alpha make the marks less opaque.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.3)











Since there are so many observations, the chart becomes “saturated” or “overplotted”. Smaller or more transparent points help, but eventually even they saturate when there is enough overlap. To examine where observations are concentrated, we can extend the histogram idea from Chapter 9 to two dimensions.
A two-dimensional histogram bins both axes and maps the count in each rectangle to color. Each rectangular cell is the combination of one x interval and one y interval.

Altairggplot


Bin both position encodings and map count() to color. Here the bin widths are 0.1 carats and 500 dollars.

alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_rect().encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').bin(step=0.1),
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(step=500),
    color='count()'
)




  
  
  
  


  
  






geom_bin_2d() computes the two-dimensional bins and fills them by count. The two entries in binwidth set the widths along x and y, respectively.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_bin_2d(binwidth = c(0.1, 500))











The broad relationship between weight and price remains visible, and we can now distinguish concentrations that were difficult to compare in the crowded scatterplot. As with one-dimensional histograms, check more than one bin width when a pattern matters to your interpretation.






WarningAvoid saturated charts



When a scatterplot becomes so saturated that we can’t be sure how many individual observations there are in a specific area, we should consider a two-dimensional histogram or density estimate, depending on the question we want to answer.








Deep-diveDeep dive: Hexagonal bins






Hexagonal bins are another option for showing joint counts. Each hexagon has six edge-sharing neighbors, whereas square bins distinguish edge-sharing and diagonal neighbors. Hexagons are also more nearly circular. These properties can be useful, although either bin shape still requires a choice of bin size.
In ggplot, geom_hex() computes the counts in hexagonal bins. It requires the hexbin package. As with geom_bin_2d(), binwidth controls the resolution along the two axes.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_hex(binwidth = c(0.1, 500))









12.4 Two-dimensional density estimates
We can also extend the kernel density estimates from Chapter 10 to two dimensions. Each observation contributes a two-dimensional kernel rather than a one-dimensional bump. The resulting colors represent estimated density, rather than counts in bins. As with a one-dimensional KDE, the smoothing settings affect how much detail is retained.
The following ggplot example displays the estimated density as filled bands.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_density_2d_filled()








Contour lines show levels of equal estimated density, rather like elevation contours on a map. They can be useful, but an unfilled contour plot can be harder to interpret than a filled density plot. It does not automatically provide a colorbar, and the outermost contour does not necessarily cover the full extent of the observations.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_density_2d()

title: 12  Joint distributions
text:
12.5 Further reading

Overlapping points.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.1 Why bother?
[During data exploration, you are often the main person interpreting a chart.]{slide-bullet} For communication, a figure needs to make sense to someone who does not already know the data or the plotting code. That reader might encounter it without the surrounding text or a spoken explanation. Readable labels, an informative title, and an appropriate view of the data are therefore part of the explanation itself.
Many useful design recommendations are collected in the Cato Institute’s visualization style guide. Other collections include these style guidelines, this spreadsheet of visualization guides, and the Data Visualization Society’s resources. Another way to learn is from other people’s mistakes: the Economist’s review of its own charts contains useful examples.
These are guidelines, not rules that work independently of the audience and context. For example, a familiar association with a fruit or political party may matter more than using the default palette. This discussion of breaking visualization rules illustrates how a deliberate exception can sometimes make a visualization more memorable. The important question is whether the choice helps readers understand the data.
The examples below use (mostly) published figures to show how design choices affect what a reader notices and concludes. Treat them as prompts to ask what comparison the reader needs to make.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.2 Design shapes the message
Titles, colors, and graphical direction can emphasize different aspects of a dataset. Ask what message each design brings forward, and what important context it leaves behind. This first figure using red color and a reversed axis to draw parallels between the deaths in this war to the dripping of blood.



The same data set could have been presented with a more positive design, focusing on the recent decline in the death rate.



Both these messages are true and the complete data story includes both, but in a visulization we can what to highlight. This not only important to be aware of when making our own visualization, but also when reading a visualization from someone else.

title: 13  Communication
section: 13.3 Match the detail to the audience
text:
13.3 Match the detail to the audience
This chart of the evolution of the size of Napoleon’s army when they marched towards Moscow rewards careful study by combining several kinds of information. That richness can be useful for exploration, but may require more explanation than a reader has time for in a short presentation.



A simpler “take home” message of this chart presented to C-level executives in a short update meeting, might be much simpler and just focus on the outcome of the operation.



The simplified chart emphasizes the scale of the losses but discards route, timing, and conditions. Even a concise label needs checking: a reduction in army strength does not, by itself, establish how many soldiers died.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.4 Make category comparisons easy



Positions and lengths on a common scale are usually easier to compare than angles and areas. A bar chart can also place each category name beside the value it identifies.



Comparisons across several pies require the reader to mentally align angles. A shared baseline makes the intended comparison more direct.



With many categories, matching small wedges to a long legend becomes hard work. Extrusion and exploded pieces add visual complexity without making the values easier to compare.



A published chart can look polished while contradicting its own numerical labels. Check whether sector angles and areas represent the values proportionally, rather than trusting the visual finish.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.5 Use color to add information



When a chart shows one series, extra colors can imply distinctions that do not exist. A single color often provides a clear starting point.



Use a contrasting color to draw attention to the observation or series that matters for the current question. Keep the remaining observations as context.



If every series asks for attention, highlighting stops being selective. Consider smaller, separate views when a comparison becomes too crowded.



Make the foreground comparison easier to find by reducing the saturation or contrast of the background series. The context should remain visible and interpretable.



Use the same color for the same group across related figures. Reassigning a familiar color forces the reader to relearn the mapping; Chapter 14 develops these choices in more detail.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.6 Make long labels readable



Change the chart orientation when that gives category names room to be read naturally. Horizontal bars often preserve the comparison while avoiding rotated or heavily wrapped text.

title: 13  Communication
section: 13.7 Ask what a chart does not show
text:
13.7 Ask what a chart does not show



An increasing number of horror releases does not establish that horror’s share of all films is increasing. Ask what denominator would be needed to support that claim.



Adding total releases changes the question we can answer. To discuss relative popularity, examine the horror share alongside counts, and consider whether dataset coverage or reporting has changed.



A cumulative total of nonnegative sales cannot decrease. Its increasing height alone does not show that the current rate of sales is accelerating.



Quarterly sales correspond to increments in the cumulative total, not its height. Showing both can reveal changes in the rate that an ever-increasing total conceals.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.8 Avoid redundant 3D







Perspective and occlusion make both heights and colored segments harder to compare. Use a third spatial dimension when it represents something the reader needs to understand, rather than simply as decoration.



Textures, gradients, tilted axes, and competing colors can obscure the values. Readers should be able to answer the data question without first decoding the decoration.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.9 Axis label formatting
Choose number formats that your audience can read easily: units, currency symbols, and sensible rounding can be more useful than scientific notation. The same principle applies to legend values.
For the following formatting examples, we take a reproducible sample of 1,000 diamonds. The full dataset and the binning techniques are introduced in Chapter 12.

Altairggplot



diamond_sample = diamonds.sample(1000, random_state=1010)
sample_bins = alt.Chart(diamond_sample).mark_rect().encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').bin(maxbins=40),
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40),
    color='count()'
)

Altair uses D3 format strings. Useful format characters include % for percentages, $ for currency, e for scientific notation, and s for SI prefixes. Scientific notation can be useful internally, but may be unfamiliar to a general audience.

sample_bins.encode(y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40).axis(format='e'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




SI prefixes such as k for thousands are often easier to read.

sample_bins.encode(y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40).axis(format='s'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




A preceding ~ removes insignificant trailing zeros.

sample_bins.encode(y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40).axis(format='~s'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




Format characters can also be combined.

sample_bins.encode(y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40).axis(format='$~s'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




The legend accepts the same format strings. Here scientific notation demonstrates the syntax; ordinary counts would usually be easier to read.

sample_bins.encode(
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40).axis(format='$~s'),
    color=alt.Color('count()').legend(format='e')
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




Set a legend to None to remove it. Only do this when its meaning is conveyed elsewhere.

sample_bins.encode(color=alt.Color('count()').legend(None))




  
  
  
  


  
  




The tickCount setting requests a number of ticks on an unbinned axis. We switch to a small scatterplot to demonstrate this; binned axes determine their ticks differently.

sample_points = alt.Chart(diamond_sample.sample(100, random_state=1010)).mark_point().encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').axis(tickCount=40),
    y=alt.Y('price').axis(tickCount=2)
)
sample_points




  
  
  
  


  
  




As with a legend, an axis can be removed by setting it to None.

sample_points.encode(x=alt.X('carat').axis(None))




  
  
  
  


  
  




Themes control many styling choices at once. They are global settings rather than a change to only one chart.

alt.theme.names()

['carbong10', 'carbong100', 'carbong90', 'carbonwhite', 'dark', 'default', 'excel', 'fivethirtyeight', 'ggplot2', 'googlecharts', 'latimes', 'none', 'opaque', 'powerbi', 'quartz', 'urbaninstitute', 'vox']



alt.theme.enable('dark');
sample_points




  
  
  
  


  
  






The scales package supplies functions for formatting labels. Here we use the hexagonal bins introduced in Chapter 12.

diamond_hex <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_hex()


diamond_hex +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_scientific())









diamond_hex +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_si('')))









diamond_hex +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())








The label functions can be parameterized. For example, we can divide the displayed values by 1,000 and add a K suffix. This changes the labels, not the data used to draw the chart.

diamond_hex +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 0.001, suffix = 'K'))








The same functions can format the legend. Hexagons use the fill aesthetic, so we change the fill scale.

diamond_hex +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
    scale_fill_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_si('')))








In ggplot, tick locations are called breaks. pretty_breaks() requests an approximately specified number of readable breaks.

diamond_hex +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(), breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10))








An axis consists of several elements that can be removed independently.

diamond_hex +
    theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.x = element_blank())








Remove a legend, referred to as a guide in ggplot, with guides().

diamond_hex + guides(fill = 'none')








theme_void() removes all axis objects and much of the surrounding decoration.

diamond_hex + theme_void()








theme_classic() is another built-in theme. The ggthemes package supplies additional choices.

diamond_hex + theme_classic()

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.10 Figure, axis, and legend titles
Axis and legend titles should describe the values in language the reader understands, including units where appropriate. Replace variable names with underscores by readable labels.

Altairggplot


Channel titles are set inside the encoding.

titled_bins = sample_bins.encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').bin(maxbins=40).title('Carat'),
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40).title('Price (USD)')
)
titled_bins




  
  
  
  


  
  




The legend title is controlled by the channel whose values it explains.

titled_bins = titled_bins.encode(color=alt.Color('count()').title('Number of diamonds'))
titled_bins




  
  
  
  


  
  




An overall figure title should communicate the take-home message or pose a useful question, rather than simply repeat the axis names. For this chart, “Higher-carat diamonds are more expensive” is more informative than “Diamond carat versus price”.

titled_bins.properties(title='Higher-carat diamonds are more expensive')




  
  
  
  


  
  




A subtitle can qualify the main message or provide context. If the title asks a question, the subtitle can guide readers toward the answer rather than leaving them to infer it unaided. Depending on the publication, a longer subtitle may also serve some of the role of a caption.

titled_bins.properties(title=alt.Title(
    text='Higher-carat diamonds are more expensive',
    subtitle='But most diamonds have a low carat value'
))




  
  
  
  


  
  




anchor controls title alignment. frame='group' aligns it with the plotting area rather than the outer edge of all labels.

titled_bins.properties(title=alt.Title(
    text='Higher-carat diamonds are more expensive',
    subtitle='But most diamonds have a low carat value',
    anchor='start', frame='group'
))




  
  
  
  


  
  






Use labs() to name the axes and aesthetic scales.

titled_hex <- diamond_hex + labs(x = 'Carat', y = 'Price (USD)')
titled_hex









titled_hex <- titled_hex + labs(fill = 'Number of diamonds')
titled_hex








The same function sets the figure title and subtitle.

titled_hex +
    labs(title = 'Higher-carat diamonds are more expensive') +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())









titled_hex +
    labs(title = 'Higher-carat diamonds are more expensive',
         subtitle = 'But most diamonds have a low carat value') +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())








Title alignment is controlled through theme elements.

titled_hex +
    labs(title = 'Higher-carat diamonds are more expensive',
         subtitle = 'But most diamonds have a low carat value') +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.11 Axis ranges
The two-dimensional histograms show that many diamonds occupy a small part of the chart. We can inspect that area more closely, but filtering observations and zooming into a plot are different operations. Filtering changes which observations are available to summaries and statistical transformations. Zooming changes the displayed region.

Altairggplot


An explicit scale domain sets the displayed range. When marks extend beyond that range, clip=True keeps them inside the plotting area. The bins here are made smaller so that the restricted view retains detail. nice=False prevents the domain from being rounded to convenient endpoints.

alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_rect(clip=True).encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').bin(maxbins=400).scale(domain=[0, 1], nice=False),
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=400).scale(domain=[0, 2000], nice=False),
    color='count()'
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




For an analysis restricted to these observations, it is often simpler to filter first and let Altair choose scales for the remaining data. That also avoids sending unnecessary observations to the chart. However, the binning will then be calculated on the filtered data.

small_diamonds = diamonds.query('carat <= 1 and price <= 2000')
alt.Chart(small_diamonds).mark_rect().encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').bin(maxbins=40),
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=40),
    color='count()'
)




  
  
  
  


  
  






Scale limits remove out-of-bounds observations before the statistical calculation. For a binned chart, this can therefore change the bins and counts.

diamond_hex +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 2000))








If the purpose is to inspect part of a chart without removing observations before statistical calculations, use coordinate limits. This distinction also matters for fitted lines.

diamond_hex + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 2000))








The scale’s out-of-bounds behavior can also be changed explicitly with scales::oob_keep. This is useful when partially visible marks should be retained.

diamond_hex +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), oob = scales::oob_keep) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 2000), oob = scales::oob_keep)








expand controls padding around the limits. The two values in mult specify padding at the low and high ends as fractions of the range. For example, c(0, 0.05) keeps padding only at the high end.

diamond_hex +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 2000))











For communication, make a restricted view apparent through the labels and surrounding explanation. In particular, truncating the baseline of bars can mislead because their lengths encode values.

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.12 Reversing an axis
Reversing an axis is less common than changing its range, but useful to know. The same scale ideas also apply to color, size, and other channels.

Altairggplot


Set reverse=True on a scale.

zoomed_bins = alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_rect(clip=True).encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').bin(maxbins=400).scale(domain=[0, 1]),
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(maxbins=400).scale(domain=[0, 2000], reverse=True),
    color='count()'
)
zoomed_bins




  
  
  
  


  
  




Color can be reversed in the same way. We explore color choices in Chapter 14.

zoomed_bins.encode(color=alt.Color('count()').scale(reverse=True))




  
  
  
  


  
  






Apply the reverse transformation, and supply the limits in decreasing order. Other transformations include log10, with shortcuts such as scale_x_log10().

reversed_hex <- diamond_hex +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2000, 0), transform = 'reverse')
reversed_hex








Hexagon colors are controlled by the fill scale.

reversed_hex + scale_fill_continuous(transform = 'reverse')

title: 13  Communication
text:
13.13 Further reading

Figure titles and captions.
Small axis labels.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.1 Why bother?
Color can distinguish groups, communicate numerical magnitude, or draw attention to a particular observation. A color scheme should make those meanings easier to see, rather than introduce patterns that are not present in the data. This chapter builds on the grouping channels in Chapter 5 and the communication choices in Chapter 13.
A useful palette is not simply a collection of favorite colors. These lecture figures show how context, perception, and the meaning of a variable affect what a color choice communicates. The programming examples follow the visual examples later in the chapter.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.2 Color depends on context




The dress debate illustrates that perceived color depends on how we interpret illumination. Different readers can experience the same image differently, so a color choice that seems obvious to its creator may not be obvious to everyone.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.3 Surroundings change apparent lightness



Compare squares A and B before watching the next example. The surrounding checkerboard and cast shadow influence our judgment of their lightness. Illustration: Edward H. Adelson.



The animation reveals that the two squares use the same gray values. Apparent lightness is not determined by a pixel value alone; its surroundings help determine how we interpret it. Animation: Edward H. Adelson.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.4 Picking the right color palette








The distance is a continuous numerical variable, not a collection of distinct groups. Abrupt hue or lightness changes can nevertheless encourage us to see boundaries that were not defined in the data.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.5 Keep numerical gradients continuous



Rainbow


Viridis


Grayscale




An ordered progression in lightness helps readers follow increasing values. Grayscale can provide that order, while a carefully designed progression in hue can help readers distinguish additional detail without introducing abrupt bands.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.6 Test the ordering in grayscale









Converting a figure to grayscale reveals whether its lightness supports the intended order. Alternating light and dark regions can make a smooth numerical change look discontinuous.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.7 Check contrast for different color vision
text:
14.7 Check contrast for different color vision









A palette needs to remain interpretable when readers perceive its hue contrasts differently. Simulations are useful checks, but do not represent every viewer; ordered lightness, labels, and redundant encodings can provide additional support.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.8 RGB and HSL describe display colors
text:
14.8 RGB and HSL describe display colors







RGB and HSL models: SharkD, CC BY-SA 3.0.

RGB specifies red, green, and blue components; HSL describes hue, saturation, and lightness. These are ways to specify colors, not guarantees of perceptual uniformity: equal steps in their coordinates need not look equally different.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.9 Separate hue, saturation, and lightness



Hue answers roughly “which color?”, saturation describes how colorful or gray it looks, and lightness describes a dark-to-light dimension. The swatches from the Seaborn palette tutorial help separate these choices.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.10 Use hue to distinguish unordered groups
text:
14.10 Use hue to distinguish unordered groups


Source: Seaborn palette tutorial.

Distinct hues can separate categories without suggesting a low-to-high sequence. An ordered lightness palette can accidentally imply a ranking among otherwise unordered groups.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.11 Use lightness to communicate numerical order
text:
14.11 Use lightness to communicate numerical order


Source: Seaborn palette tutorial.

For numerical magnitude, the colors should support a recoverable order. An arbitrary set of category colors makes it harder to judge which values are larger.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.12 Sequential palettes need an ordered progression
text:
14.12 Sequential palettes need an ordered progression



A sequential palette represents movement along a numerical range. Check the lightness progression as well as the attractiveness of the color strip; plateaus or reversals can make some changes stand out more than others.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.13 Perceptual uniformity helps equal steps look equal
text:
14.13 Perceptual uniformity helps equal steps look equal



Perceptually designed palettes aim to make equal data steps look approximately equally different. These reference diagrams come from the Matplotlib colormap guide.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.14 Inspect uneven lightness changes



A colorful palette can have a highly uneven lightness profile. Those peaks and troughs can create artificial emphasis or obscure the ordering of values.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.15 The same values can look very different
text:
14.15 The same values can look very different



Changing the palette changes which features attract attention even when the values are unchanged. Choose a palette for the comparison it supports, rather than for visual excitement alone.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.16 Guessing a numerical sequence from hue
text:
14.16 Guessing a numerical sequence from hue






Where would you expect red to fall in this sequence before reading the legend? Hue alone does not provide an unambiguous numerical order; the legend and the palette’s lightness structure both matter.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.17 Cyclic data need a palette that wraps around
text:
14.17 Cyclic data need a palette that wraps around



Use a cyclic palette when the underlying variable wraps around, such as an angle or a position within a yearly cycle. Similar endpoint colors communicate that connection, but would be misleading for unrelated low and high endpoints on a linear scale.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.18 Diverging palettes need a meaningful midpoint
text:
14.18 Diverging palettes need a meaningful midpoint



Use a diverging palette when departures above and below a meaningful reference have different interpretations. Examples include change from a baseline or correlations centered on zero; the middle should not be chosen merely because it is halfway between the observed extremes.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.19 Categorical palettes distinguish groups



A categorical palette should make groups distinguishable without implying a numerical order. Its usefulness still depends on the number of categories, the background, and readers’ color vision.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.20 Too many colors become clutter








Coloring every country can create decoration rather than useful identification. Highlight selected comparisons, divide the display into smaller views, or use direct labels when that makes the intended question easier to answer.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.21 Work with familiar color associations








When colors have a strong existing association, working with it can reduce the reader’s effort. The bar values are unchanged, but using blue for water and green for land makes the categories easier to anticipate.

title: 14  Color
section: 14.22 Facilitate interpretation through informed color choices
text:
14.22 Facilitate interpretation through informed color choices
For continuous data, a perceptually uniform colormap is often a useful starting point. Equal steps in the data should produce approximately equal perceived changes in color. Lightness is especially important for conveying ordered magnitude: a sequential palette with steadily changing lightness makes low-to-high values easier to interpret than a palette with unrelated bright and dark patches. The Matplotlib colormap guide contains examples, and this talk about viridis explains many of the design principles.

Color vision and accessibility
Color vision deficiencies affect a substantial number of readers. Red–green deficiencies are more common among men than women, and their prevalence varies across populations. Do not rely on a color distinction that some readers cannot see. The same guidelines often improve a chart for readers with typical color vision too.
The Coblis simulator can simulate different color vision deficiencies for an uploaded image. The cividis palette was designed to give similar perceptual ordering to readers with and without common red–green deficiencies. For categorical groups, redundant shapes or direct labels can help in addition to choosing colors carefully.


Avoid artificial boundaries
The jet rainbow colormap has sharp changes in hue and uneven lightness. Yellow and cyan regions can attract disproportionate attention, creating apparent boundaries or features in otherwise smoothly varying data. Because higher values are not consistently lighter, the order is also hard to recover in grayscale.
Choose a palette whose perceptual changes support the comparison you want readers to make. For more examples, see How bad is your colormap? and The rainbow is dead … long live the rainbow. The turbo palette improves some shortcomings of jet, but does not make every rainbow palette perceptually uniform or suitable for every reader. Viridis or cividis are often better defaults for ordered values. For a broader discussion, see how color determines what we see.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.23 Categorical color schemes
Categorical palettes distinguish groups without implying a low-to-high order. We use iris measurements to compare the three species.

Altairggplot


Altair’s default categorical palette is tableau10, a sequence of ten colors beginning with blue, orange, and red.

iris_points = alt.Chart(iris).mark_circle(size=100).encode(
    x='petalWidth',
    y='petalLength',
    color='species'
)
iris_points




  
  
  
  


  
  




Set the palette by name with scheme inside alt.Scale. The Vega scheme reference lists categorical, sequential, diverging, and cyclic palettes.

iris_points.encode(color=alt.Color('species').scale(scheme='dark2'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




You can also supply colors explicitly, using names or hexadecimal codes. Here the order of the color range corresponds to the order of the species domain.

colors = ['coral', 'steelblue', 'rebeccapurple']
iris_points.encode(color=alt.Color('species').scale(
    domain=['setosa', 'versicolor', 'virginica'], range=colors
))




  
  
  
  


  
  






The default categorical scale in ggplot selects equally spaced hues from a color wheel.

iris_points <- ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +
    geom_point(size = 5)
iris_points








ColorBrewer palettes are available through scale_color_brewer() and scale_fill_brewer() for categories. The distiller scales interpolate these palettes for continuous values.

iris_points + scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Dark2')








The Tableau palette used by Altair is available through ggthemes. The R color palettes collection shows many other choices and the packages that provide them.

iris_points + ggthemes::scale_color_tableau()








Here we specify the same colors as the Altair example using their hexadecimal codes. Naming the values makes the mapping to species explicit.

iris_points + scale_color_manual(values = c(
    setosa = '#FF7F50', versicolor = '#4682B4', virginica = '#663399'
))











Experimenting with custom palettes can be useful, but well-designed existing palettes incorporate considerable research and testing. They are a good starting point for a final communication figure. Hexadecimal RGB codes range from #000000 for black to #ffffff for white. An image editor or online color picker can help recover the exact code for a color in an existing image.


The name rebeccapurple is a reminder of the people behind computational tools. Read the story of this color’s name.

title: 14  Color
text:
14.24 Sequential color schemes
Sequential palettes communicate increasing or decreasing magnitude. When working on a light background, it is often useful for low values to be closest to that background and larger values to be more visually prominent. Consider the background, the palette direction, and the meaning of high values together.

Altairggplot


Mapping petal width to color selects a continuous palette.

iris_points.encode(color=alt.Color('petalWidth:Q'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




The palette can be changed in the same way as for categories.

iris_points.encode(color=alt.Color('petalWidth:Q').scale(scheme='greenblue'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




Viridis was developed for Matplotlib and is now available in many visualization tools. It uses changes in lightness and hue while aiming to preserve perceptual ordering.

iris_points.encode(color=alt.Color('petalWidth:Q').scale(scheme='viridis'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




Reverse the palette with reverse=True, just as for the axis scales in Chapter 13.

iris_points.encode(color=alt.Color('petalWidth:Q').scale(scheme='viridis', reverse=True))




  
  
  
  


  
  






Mapping a numerical variable to color uses a continuous scale.

iris_numeric <- ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Petal.Length, color = Petal.Width)) +
    geom_point(size = 5)
iris_numeric








Use scale_color_viridis_c() for a continuous viridis palette. The _d variant is for discrete values.

iris_numeric + scale_color_viridis_c()








A reverse transformation reverses the numerical color scale, which also reverses the ordering of the legend values.

iris_numeric + scale_color_viridis_c(transform = 'reverse')








To reverse only the palette while preserving the legend’s numerical order, use direction = -1 instead.

iris_numeric + scale_color_viridis_c(direction = -1)

title: 14  Color
text:
14.25 Diverging color schemes
Diverging palettes distinguish departures on either side of a meaningful midpoint. For example, a correlation ranges from −1 to 1 and has a natural midpoint at zero. A sequential palette can make a value near zero look more important than a strongly negative correlation simply because zero is numerically larger.
We calculate a correlation matrix from the Gapminder example data. The numeric cluster identifier is excluded because its codes are categories, not a quantitative measurement. The point here is to compare color encodings, not to infer causal relationships from these correlations.

Altairggplot



numeric_gapminder = gapminder[['year', 'pop', 'life_expect', 'fertility']]
corr_df = (
    numeric_gapminder.corr()
    .rename_axis(index='variable_x', columns='variable_y')
    .stack().reset_index(name='correlation')
)

First, notice how the default sequential scale treats zero.

correlation_heatmap = alt.Chart(corr_df, width=240, height=240).mark_rect().encode(
    x='variable_x:N',
    y='variable_y:N',
    tooltip='correlation:Q',
    color='correlation:Q'
)
correlation_heatmap




  
  
  
  


  
  




Choose a diverging palette and set the domain to the full possible correlation range. The symmetric limits make equal-magnitude positive and negative correlations comparable.

correlation_heatmap.encode(
    color=alt.Color('correlation:Q').scale(domain=[-1, 1], scheme='purpleorange')
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




Alternatively, domainMid=0 identifies the midpoint and selects a default diverging palette.

correlation_heatmap.encode(color=alt.Color('correlation:Q').scale(domainMid=0))




  
  
  
  


  
  






The same correlation matrix can be computed directly in R.

corr_df <- gapminder |>
    select(year, pop, life_expect, fertility) |>
    cor(use = 'pairwise.complete.obs') |>
    as.table() |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    set_names(c('variable_x', 'variable_y', 'correlation'))


correlation_heatmap <- ggplot(corr_df, aes(x = variable_x, y = variable_y, fill = correlation)) +
    geom_tile()
correlation_heatmap








ggthemes provides a Tableau diverging palette.

correlation_heatmap + ggthemes::scale_fill_gradient2_tableau()








ColorBrewer offers alternatives through scale_fill_distiller(). The palette direction should agree with any relevant familiar association, such as red for warmer temperatures; the sign of a correlation has no inherent color.

correlation_heatmap + scale_fill_distiller(palette = 'PuOr')








Specify symmetric limits to make equal-magnitude departures from zero equally prominent.

correlation_heatmap + scale_fill_distiller(palette = 'PuOr', limits = c(-1, 1))

title: 14  Color
text:
14.26 Highlighting with colors
Color can also select a small part of a chart for attention. We use historical wheat prices after 1700, with fewer bars to keep the example readable. Give the observation of interest a distinct color while leaving the other observations as context.

Altairggplot


Create a Boolean column for the year to highlight.

wheat['highlight'] = wheat['year'] == 1810
bars = alt.Chart(wheat).mark_bar().encode(
    x='year:O',
    y='wheat:Q',
    color='highlight:N'
)
bars




  
  
  
  


  
  




The Boolean legend is not helpful unless the reader knows what True means. We can remove it and explain the selected year with text instead.

bars = bars.encode(color=alt.Color('highlight:N').legend(None))
bars




  
  
  
  


  
  






Bar interiors use fill, rather than the outline color aesthetic.

wheat <- wheat |> mutate(highlight = year == 1810)
bars <- ggplot(wheat, aes(x = year, y = wheat, fill = highlight)) +
    geom_col(color = 'white') + ggthemes::scale_fill_tableau()
bars








Remove the legend through the theme or guides(fill = 'none').

bars <- bars + theme(legend.position = 'none')
bars

title: 14  Color
text:
14.27 Text annotations
An exact value can make an important comparison easier to read. Text can also explain why an observation is highlighted. Keep in mind that labeling every observation may add more clutter than information.

Altairggplot


Layer a text mark above the bars.

bars + bars.mark_text(dy=-5).encode(text='wheat:Q')




  
  
  
  


  
  




The text inherited the bar chart’s color encoding. An encoding takes precedence over a color set directly in the mark. To override it, set a literal encoding value with alt.value(); otherwise a string in an encoding is interpreted as a data column name.

bars + bars.mark_text(dy=-5).encode(text='wheat:Q', color=alt.value('black'))




  
  
  
  


  
  






Use geom_text() with the label aesthetic.

bars + geom_text(aes(label = wheat), vjust = -0.3)








To match the text to the highlighted bar colors, map the color aesthetic and add a corresponding color scale. This is separate from the fill scale used by the bars.

bars +
    geom_text(aes(label = wheat, color = highlight), vjust = -0.3) +
    ggthemes::scale_color_tableau()








When a label represents a computed count rather than a precomputed value, use a layer with the same counting statistic, for example geom_text(stat = 'count', aes(label = after_stat(count))).




Remove unnecessary decoration
When exact labels already supply the values, some gridlines may be unnecessary. This is a design choice: gridlines can still help readers compare distant marks.

Altairggplot



bars = bars.encode(y=alt.Y('wheat:Q').axis(grid=False))
bars + bars.mark_text(dy=-5).encode(text='wheat:Q', color=alt.value('black'))




  
  
  
  


  
  




Without gridlines, the outline around the plotting area may stand out unnecessarily. Remove it with configure_view(stroke=None).

(bars + bars.mark_text(dy=-5).encode(
    text='wheat:Q', color=alt.value('black')
)).configure_view(stroke=None)




  
  
  
  


  
  






Remove the major and minor gridlines through theme elements.

bars +
    geom_text(aes(label = wheat, color = highlight), vjust = -0.3) +
    ggthemes::scale_color_tableau() +
    theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())













Annotate selected observations
Often only the highlighted observation needs a label. Filtering the annotation data leaves the other bars intact.

Altairggplot



bars + alt.Chart(wheat.query('year == 1810')).mark_text(dy=-5).encode(
    x='year:O', y='wheat:Q', text='wheat:Q'
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




For custom annotation text, use a literal value again.

bars + alt.Chart(wheat.query('year == 1810')).mark_text(dy=-5, dx=-30).encode(
    x='year:O', y='wheat:Q', text=alt.value('The record year')
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




For multiple annotations, either add a text column to the original data or create a separate annotation dataframe.

annot_wheat = pd.DataFrame({
    'year': [1730, 1810],
    'wheat': [26, 99],
    'text': ['The lowest year', 'The record year']
})
annot_wheat

   year  wheat             text
0  1730     26  The lowest year
1  1810     99  The record year



bars + alt.Chart(annot_wheat).mark_text(dy=-5).encode(
    x='year:O', y='wheat:Q', text='text:N'
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




If labels overlap bars or other labels, adjust their positions, alignment, or color. Separate annotation layers allow each label to have its own placement.


Supply filtered data to the text layer, rather than filtering the whole chart.

bars + geom_text(data = filter(wheat, year == 1810), aes(label = wheat), vjust = -0.3)








For a fixed annotation, annotate() avoids adding a data column.

bars + annotate('text', label = 'The record year', x = 1810, y = 102, hjust = 1)

title: 14  Color
section: 14.28 Direct labeling instead of using a legend
text:
14.28 Direct labeling instead of using a legend
A legend can make the reader repeatedly look away from the plotted marks. Matching the legend’s order to the visible order of the series reduces that effort; direct labels can remove the lookup entirely. The stock-price data provide an example where alphabetical order does not match the order of the line endpoints.

Altairggplot



stock_lines = alt.Chart(stocks).mark_line().encode(
    x='date:T', y='price:Q', color='symbol:N'
)
stock_lines




  
  
  
  


  
  




Calculate the series order at the final date.

stock_order = (
    stocks.loc[stocks['date'] == stocks['date'].max()]
    .sort_values('price', ascending=False)
)
stock_order

    symbol       date   price
436   GOOG 2010-03-01  560.19
559   AAPL 2010-03-01  223.02
245   AMZN 2010-03-01  128.82
368    IBM 2010-03-01  125.55
122   MSFT 2010-03-01   28.80


Pass that ordering to the color encoding’s sort parameter.

stock_lines.encode(color=alt.Color('symbol:N').sort(stock_order['symbol'].tolist()))




  
  
  
  


  
  




The title “symbol” provides little additional information here and can be removed.

stock_lines.encode(color=alt.Color('symbol:N').sort(stock_order['symbol'].tolist()).title(None))




  
  
  
  


  
  




To label the lines directly, add text at each endpoint and remove the legend. Use consistent color domains so the line and text layers identify the same series. The IBM and AMZN endpoints are very close together, so we give their labels small vertical offsets. Only the label positions change, not the line values.

lines = stock_lines.encode(
    y=alt.Y('price:Q').title('Price'), color=alt.Color('symbol:N').legend(None)
)
labels = stock_order.assign(
    label_price=stock_order['price'] + stock_order['symbol'].map({'IBM': 25, 'AMZN': -25}).fillna(0)
)
text = alt.Chart(labels).mark_text(align='left', dx=6).encode(
    x='date:T', y=alt.Y('label_price:Q').title('Price'), text='symbol:N', color='symbol:N'
)
lines + text




  
  
  
  


  
  







stock_lines <- ggplot(stocks, aes(x = date, y = price, color = symbol)) +
    geom_line() + ggthemes::scale_color_tableau()
stock_lines








Calculate the last-date ordering, then use it as the legend’s breaks.

stock_order <- stocks |>
    filter(date == max(date)) |>
    arrange(desc(price))
stock_order

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  symbol date       price
  <chr>  <date>     <dbl>
1 GOOG   2010-03-01 560. 
2 AAPL   2010-03-01 223. 
3 AMZN   2010-03-01 129. 
4 IBM    2010-03-01 126. 
5 MSFT   2010-03-01  28.8



stock_lines + ggthemes::scale_color_tableau(breaks = stock_order$symbol)









stock_lines + ggthemes::scale_color_tableau(breaks = stock_order$symbol, name = NULL)








To remove the legend altogether, set legend.position = 'none'. Then add geom_text() with the endpoint data. Some extra space on the right keeps the labels within the plotting area. As in Altair, only the labels for the closely spaced IBM and AMZN series are offset.

labels <- stock_order |>
    mutate(label_price = price + case_when(
        symbol == 'IBM' ~ 25, symbol == 'AMZN' ~ -25, TRUE ~ 0
    ))
stock_lines +

    scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.14))) +
    theme(legend.position = 'none')

title: 15  Exploratory data analysis
text:
15.1 Why bother?
In this chapter, several techniques from the book are combined to explore a dataset. When we receive a new dataset, we might start with a rather broad question of interest that gets more narrow as we learn which comparisons in the data reveal interesting features of the data. We also don’t know whether the data mean what we think they mean.
Early investigation of data is often called exploratory data analysis, or EDA: using inspection, visualization, and transformation to understand data and develop questions and explanations worth investigating. EDA usually involves being both curious and suspicious about the data, and a useful EDA cycle could look something like this:
An expectation could come from a known data-collection procedure, general knowledge about data, or ordinary knowledge of the subject. When something looks strange, either the data or our understanding of it could be wrong and we need to find out more. Let’s see an example in the following exercise.

title: 15  Exploratory data analysis
text:
Form an expectation → inspect the data → notice agreement or surprise → choose an informative next check.








Ex-promptExercise 1






The chart below shows the lowest recorded daily minimum temperature in each of four years of Seattle weather data.





  
  
  
  


  
  




All four minima are 1.1°C. Would you conclude that there were no freezing days? What would you check before making that claim?






Ex-hintHint






It seems a bit odd that each year has exactly the same minimum value. Remember that the minimum can only be calculated from the values that are available in the data. What kinds of missing measurements could make this summary misleading?






Ex-solutionSolution






The chart establishes that the lowest recorded values are above freezing. It does not establish that every day’s temperature was recorded. If colder measurements tend to be missing, the recorded minimum could be higher than the actual minimum. The identical values across years also deserve investigation: they might reflect rounding, a reporting threshold, or another processing step. We need to inspect the observations and their missingness before deciding.

title: 15  Exploratory data analysis
section: 15.3 Show an overview of the data
text:
15.3 Show an overview of the data
An overview is not just a quick route to a final chart. It gives us a chance to notice unexpected features across the dataset. We will inspect three complementary aspects:

The distribution of each variable.
Relationships between variables.
Where measurements are missing.

When doing EDA, we can automate some of the chart construction, but we still need to decide what the columns mean and how to interpret each chart we make. For example, a numerical storage type does not automatically guarantee that the column is worth putting in a histogram or correlation matrix, as it could e.g. contain IDs or phone numbers.

A grid of distributions
In Chapter 9 and Chapter 10, we examined one or a few distributions at a time. When we are doing EDA, we often want to explore multiple variables and tend to create many distributions charts at once to inspect several measurement columns together. We can create these grids using any of the distribution plots we have learned about so far; here we demonstrate it using histograms.

Altairggplot


repeat applies one chart specification to several columns. alt.repeat() indicates where each column should be substituted. This differs from faceting: each panel below shows a different variable, rather than multiple groups of observations for a single variable. Since we have multiple different variables with different scales, it is not possible to set a single value of step to set a suitable bin width for all the variables. Instead, we use maxbins to control the number of bins in the charts, and let Altair figure out what the bin width needs to be.

measurements = ['precipitation', 'temp_max', 'temp_min', 'wind']

alt.Chart(weather, height=200).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X(alt.repeat()).bin(maxbins=20),
    y=alt.Y('count()'),
).repeat(measurements, columns=2)




  
  
  
  


  
  




Since the construction of the plot grids in EDA tends to demand more complex syntax, we often use helper packages that allows us to focus on exploring the data rather than getting to bogged down with writing code. A related helper package for Altair is Altair Ally, and we could use it to visualize the distributions in the following way:

import altair_ally as aly

aly.dist(weather, bin=True)




  
  
  
  


  
  




The default is to show densities for each variables, which would be perfectly reasonable. Here we also demonstrate how to use bin=True to show histograms instead.


We can reuse the faceting grammar by putting the selected measurements in a long table with a column identifying the variable. The panels use independent scales so that each distribution’s shape is readable, despite differences in measurement units, ranges, and bin counts. Since we have multiple different variables with different scales, it is not possible to set a single value of binwidth to set a suitable bin width for all the variables. Instead, we use bins to control the number of bins in the charts, and let ggplot figure out what the bin width needs to be.

measurements <- c('precipitation', 'temp_max', 'temp_min', 'wind')
weather_long <- weather |>
    pivot_longer(all_of(measurements), names_to = 'variable', values_to = 'value')

ggplot(weather_long, aes(x = value)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
    facet_wrap(~variable, scales = 'free', ncol = 2)

Warning: Removed 121 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









Since the construction of the plot grids in EDA tends to demand more complex syntax, we often use helper packages that allows us to focus on exploring the data rather than getting to bogged down with writing code. A related helper package for ggplot is GGally and we could use it to visualize the distributions of each variable. By default, it also shows a lot of other information than just the histograms, which we turn off here, but will talk more about later.

library(GGally)

ggpairs(
  weather,
  diag = list(continuous = "barDiag"),
  upper = "blank",
  lower = "blank"
)

Warning: Removed 5 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).


Warning: Removed 116 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).









The default is to show densities for each variables, which would be perfectly reasonable. Here we also demonstrate how to use diag = list(continuous = "barDiag") to show histograms instead.



This grid of distribution plots bin settings provide a first look of our variables. We should still apply the best practices of each individual visualization, such as testing various bind widths and inspecting individual observations.
From the chart above, we can note that precipitation has many zero values and a long right tail. Here, zero precipitation is a plausible measurement: a dry day. That is different from a missing measurement of precipitation. The temperature distributions have a lower boundary worth investigating, especially given the suspicious minima in our opening chart.






Ex-promptExercise 2






Which of these would be useful follow-ups, and what would each check tell us?

Remove all zero precipitation values because they look unusual.
Check the frequency of zero precipitation against the meaning of the variable.
Inspect the records with the largest precipitation values.
Change the temperature bin width to see whether the lower boundary persists.







Ex-hintHint






Can we really just remove values from our data at this stage without first knowing more about the data?






Ex-solutionSolution






The last three are useful checks. A dry day is a valid zero, so a large spike at zero is not itself an error. Inspecting extreme records can reveal errors or genuine unusual days; their rarity alone does not distinguish those explanations. Changing bin width checks whether the apparent boundary depends on the display. It does not explain why values might be missing below it.












Just as we explored the distribution of our numerical variables above, we can explore the distribution of categorical variables as part of our overview visualization. We can think of the categorical distribution as simply the count of values for each categorical grouop. In this case, it could e.g. be interesting how many observations there are for each weather type.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(weather).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('count()'),
    y=alt.Y('weather').sort('-x'),
)




  
  
  
  


  
  







weather |>
    add_count(weather) |>
    ggplot(aes(y = reorder(weather, n))) +
    geom_bar()











In this chart we can see that there are some records described as snow days. How can there be snowy days if there were no negative temperatures in the data? This lends support to that there is something suspicious going on with this data that we should explore further.


An overview of bivariate relationships
In addition to viewing the univariate distributions above, we might also be interesting in the bivariate or joint distributions. Creating a grid of usch distributions is often referred to as a a scatterplot matrix or a pairs plot and lets us scan multiple relationships effectively. Usually, we are on the lookout for clusters, straight and curved relationships, and changes in spread.

Altairggplot


We can use the repeat-syntax to create a scatterplot matrix; each row selects a y variable and each column selects an x variable.

alt.Chart(weather).mark_point(size=9, opacity=0.2).encode(
    x=alt.X(alt.repeat('column'), type='quantitative'),
    y=alt.Y(alt.repeat('row'), type='quantitative'),
).properties(width=110, height=110).repeat(
    column=measurements,
    row=measurements,
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




As you can see the diagonal compares each variable with itself, why we see a straight line for all those relationships, and it redundant to include. Likewise, the lower and upper diagonal are mirrors of each other and we really only need to include one of them. It would be a tedious manual process to modify this, so instead we can use a Altair ally, which also let’s us easily bin the points to avoid saturation.

aly.pair(weather, mark='rect')




  
  
  
  


  
  






It would be tedious and laborious to try to create a scatterplot matrix directly in ggplot. Instead, GGally supplies a convenient pairs-plot constructor that we will use. Here we request points for the lower triangle and histograms on the diagonal. We include the densities on the diagonal, but we could have excluded them if we wanted to just show the bivariate relationships. GGally also let’s us easily use a 2D density instead of plotting the points directly to avoid saturation.

GGally::ggpairs(
    weather,
    columns = measurements,
    upper = 'blank',
    lower = list(continuous = "density")
)

Warning: Removed 5 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density2d()`).


Warning: Removed 5 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density()`).


Warning: Removed 116 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density2d()`).
Removed 116 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density2d()`).

(`stat_density()`).


Warning: Removed 5 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density2d()`).


Warning: Removed 116 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density2d()`).












From the chart, we can see a positive association between minimum and maximum temperature, which is rather unsurprising, since these likely vary together depending on whether a single day is warm or cold.


Use correlations to navigate bivariate relationships
A correlation heatmap compresses many relationships into one display. That can help us choose which pairs to inspect, but it leaves out the distributional detail visible in a pairs plot.

Altairggplot


aly.corr(weather)



  
  
  
  
  





GGally::ggcorr(weather)

Warning: data in columns date and weather are not numeric and were ignored












Pearson correlation tends to be the default and summarizes linear association. It’s good to also visualize Spearman correlation which uses ranks and summarizes monotonic associations: whether larger values of one variable tend to accompany larger or smaller values of another. It can capture some nonlinear relationships, but not arbitrary curves. For example, a strong U-shaped relationship can have little correlation for both the Pearson and Spearmean metrics. Relationships that depend on a combination of predictors can also be missed by inspecting each predictor separately.
Correlation values are defined from -1 for a perfect negative correlation to +1 for a perfect positive correlation.  We therefore use a colorscale with two different colors diverging from a midpoint.

title: 15  Exploratory data analysis
section: 15.4 Missing values are part of the data story
text:
15.4 Missing values are part of the data story
We have seen a pattern that might involve missing measurements. Even without that clue, missingness should be part of our initial inspection. There are two separate questions: how much is missing, and which observations are affected?

Altairggplot



weather.info()

<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 1461 entries, 0 to 1460
Data columns (total 6 columns):
 #   Column         Non-Null Count  Dtype         
---  ------         --------------  -----         
 0   date           1461 non-null   datetime64[us]
 1   precipitation  1461 non-null   float64       
 2   temp_max       1456 non-null   float64       
 3   temp_min       1345 non-null   float64       
 4   wind           1461 non-null   float64       
 5   weather        1461 non-null   str           
dtypes: datetime64[us](1), float64(4), str(1)
memory usage: 73.8 KB





weather |> summary()

      date            precipitation       temp_max        temp_min     
 Min.   :2012-01-01   Min.   : 0.000   Min.   : 1.10   Min.   : 1.100  
 1st Qu.:2012-12-31   1st Qu.: 0.000   1st Qu.:10.97   1st Qu.: 5.600  
 Median :2013-12-31   Median : 0.000   Median :15.60   Median : 8.900  
 Mean   :2013-12-31   Mean   : 3.029   Mean   :16.50   Mean   : 9.054  
 3rd Qu.:2014-12-31   3rd Qu.: 2.800   3rd Qu.:22.20   3rd Qu.:12.800  
 Max.   :2015-12-31   Max.   :55.900   Max.   :35.60   Max.   :18.300  
                                       NAs    :5       NAs    :116     
      wind            weather    
 Min.   :0.400   Length   :1461  
 1st Qu.:2.200   N.unique :   5  
 Median :3.000   N.blank  :   0  
 Mean   :3.241   Min.nchar:   3  
 3rd Qu.:4.000   Max.nchar:   7  
 Max.   :9.500                   
                                 





There are 116 missing minimum temperatures and five missing maximum temperatures. The meaning of a missing value also requires context. It might represent a failed measurement, a survey question that was never asked, a refusal to answer, or a field that does not apply to that observation. A missing value can also be introduced by an unsuccessful join between tables, so the issue could like in the data processing rather than the data collection step. All these situations can all end up encoded as NA, but they require different interpreatations and actions. Conversely, an unknown value might be encoded as a number such as 999 and therefore escape a simple missing-value count (this is not good practice but can still happen).

Make the missingness pattern visible
We can create a table of indicators describing whether each cell is missing, then visualize those indicators with the same heatmap grammar used for other data. Here the horizontal axis represents actual dates, not an arbitrary row order.

Altairggplot



missing_cells = (
    weather.set_index('date').isna().reset_index()
    .melt(id_vars='date', var_name='variable', value_name='is_missing')
    .assign(
        end_date=lambda d: d['date'] + pd.Timedelta(days=1),
        status=lambda d: d['is_missing'].map({True: 'Missing', False: 'Recorded'}),
    )
)

alt.Chart(missing_cells, width=560, height=130).mark_rect().encode(
    x=alt.X('date:T', title='Date').axis(format='%Y', tickCount='year'),
    x2='end_date:T',
    y=alt.Y('variable:N', title=None),
    color=alt.Color('status:N', title=None).scale(
        domain=['Recorded', 'Missing'], range=['#dedede', '#c44e52']
    ).legend(orient='bottom'),
    tooltip=['date:T', 'variable:N', 'status:N'],
)




  
  
  
  


  
  








missing_cells <- weather |>
    mutate(across(-date, is.na)) |>
    pivot_longer(-date, names_to = 'variable', values_to = 'is_missing') |>
    mutate(status = if_else(is_missing, 'Missing', 'Recorded'))

ggplot(missing_cells, aes(x = date, y = variable, fill = status)) +
    geom_tile(width = 1, height = 0.9) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Recorded = '#dedede', Missing = '#c44e52')) +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = '1 year', date_labels = '%Y') +
    labs(x = 'Date', y = NULL, fill = NULL)











The missing temperatures seems to occur in colder parts of the year. This supports further investigation as we don’t yet know the mechanism. A device problem, a reporting procedure, and a processing rule could all produce seasonally patterned missingness.






Ex-promptExercise 3






Suppose we suspect that low minimum temperatures are more likely to be missing. We cannot inspect a missing minimum temperature directly. Which observed variable could help us investigate that suspicion? What would you expect to see?






Ex-hintHint






Think about the relationship between the daily minimum and maximum temperatures in the pairs plot.






Ex-solutionSolution






We can compare maximum temperatures on days with and without a recorded minimum. If missing minima tend to occur on cold days, we would expect lower maximum temperatures on those days.














Follow the clue with a focused comparison
We create a new categorical variable that records whether the minimum is missing. That lets us compare the distributions of maximum temperature between the two groups. The five rows without a maximum temperature cannot contribute to this comparison; they remain accounted for in our missingness summary.

Altairggplot



weather_status = weather.assign(
    minimum_status=weather['temp_min'].isna().map(
        {True: 'Minimum missing', False: 'Minimum recorded'}
    )
)

alt.Chart(weather_status.dropna(subset=['temp_max']), height=100).mark_boxplot().encode(
    x=alt.X('temp_max:Q', title='Recorded daily maximum (°C)').scale(zero=False),
    y=alt.Y('minimum_status:N', title=None),
)




  
  
  
  


  
  







weather_status <- weather |>
    mutate(minimum_status = if_else(
        is.na(temp_min), 'Minimum missing', 'Minimum recorded'
    ))

weather_status |>
    drop_na(temp_max) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = temp_max, y = minimum_status)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(x = 'Recorded daily maximum (°C)', y = NULL)











The recorded maxima are generally lower when the minima are missing. So maybe something is going wrong with the sensor on cold days?


Inspect combinations of categories
The weather description gives us another way to investigate missing minima. We can count the combinations of weather type and recording status, then compare the counts with proportions within each weather type. These answer different questions, as we saw in Chapter 8.

Altairggplot



status_counts = (
    weather_status.groupby(['weather', 'minimum_status']).size()
    .reset_index(name='days')
)
status_counts['proportion'] = (
    status_counts['days'] / status_counts.groupby('weather')['days'].transform('sum')
)

tiles = alt.Chart(status_counts, width=210, height=150).mark_rect().encode(
    x=alt.X('minimum_status:N', title=None).axis(labelAngle=0),
    y=alt.Y('weather:N', title=None),
    tooltip=['weather:N', 'minimum_status:N', 'days:Q',
             alt.Tooltip('proportion:Q', format='.1%')],
)
counts = tiles.encode(
    color=alt.Color('days:Q', title='Days').scale(scheme='blues').legend(orient='bottom')
).properties(title='Counts')
proportions = tiles.encode(
    color=alt.Color('proportion:Q', title='Share within weather type')
        .scale(domain=[0, 1], scheme='blues').legend(format='%', orient='bottom')
).properties(title='Within-type proportions')
alt.hconcat(counts, proportions).resolve_scale(color='independent')




  
  
  
  


  
  







status_counts <- weather_status |>
    count(weather, minimum_status, name = 'days') |>
    group_by(weather) |>
    mutate(proportion = days / sum(days)) |>
    ungroup()

tiles <- ggplot(status_counts, aes(x = minimum_status, y = weather)) +
    geom_tile() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = 'bottom')
counts <- tiles +
    aes(fill = days) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = '#f7fbff', high = '#08519c') +
    labs(title = 'Counts', fill = 'Days')
proportions <- tiles +
    aes(fill = proportion) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = '#f7fbff', high = '#08519c',
                        limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_percent()) +
    labs(title = 'Within-type proportions', fill = 'Share within weather type')
patchwork::wrap_plots(counts, proportions, nrow = 1)

















Ex-promptExercise 4






There are more missing minima on days described as sunny than on snow days: 62 versus 19. Does that mean a sunny day’s minimum is more likely to be missing?






Ex-solutionSolution






No. There are 640 sunny days but only 26 snow days. The proportions are about 10% and 73%, respectively. Sunny days account for more missing values in total, while snow days have a much higher missingness rate. The relevant denominator depends on the question. Neither comparison establishes that the weather description caused the missingness.














WarningAvoid drawing premature conclusions about the cause of the missingness



In real data, we would now consult the collection procedure, processing code, or people who produced the measurements. The pattern is consistent with preferential loss of cold measurements, but it does not prove a faulty sensor. Likewise, failing to see a pattern would not prove that missingness is harmless.
Formal distinctions such as missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random describe assumptions about how missingness depends on observed and unobserved values. We generally cannot establish those assumptions from a missingness plot alone.




Reveal the teaching modification
For this example, we know the mechanism because we created it: both minimum and maximum temperatures at or below 0.6°C were replaced with missing values. This simulates a reporting failure that removes low measurements, e.g. due to a faulty sensor that can’t record low temperatures.
Even though only about 8% of minimum temperatures were removed, they came from one part of the distribution. Whether missingness matters depends on which values are missing and which question we are asking, not just on the overall percentage. Replacing the missing temperatures with zero would also be misleading: zero Celsius is a particular temperature, not a way to represent missingness. Handling missing data requires a justified decision for the analysis at hand; this example does not establish a universally correct replacement rule.

title: 15  Exploratory data analysis
text:
15.5 Turn patterns into questions
The weather mystery is one example of a broader strategy: follow a surprising pattern with a check that could change your interpretation. Generating another plot is useful when you can explain what it will help you learn. Here is an example of some common scenarios and what a helpful next step could be.








Observation in an overview
Possible explanations
A useful next check




Two peaks
Subgroups, rounding, or display settings
Compare subgroups, inspect values, and vary bin width or bandwidth


An extreme value
A genuine unusual case, a unit mismatch, or an entry error
Inspect the record, related variables, and source documentation


A tall distribution for one group
More observations, not necessarily a different shape
Compare counts and within-group normalized distributions


A pooled association
Within-group relationships or differences between groups
Color or facet by a plausible grouping variable


More rows after a transformation
New observations or repeated memberships
Check distinct units as well as row counts



There need not be a single correct follow-up. Its usefulness depends on which explanation you want to investigate. Sometimes the next step is to ask the data provider a question rather than draw a chart.






Ex-promptExercise 5






An overview of a movie catalog suggests that one genre has higher revenues. For each question below, identify what you would need to inspect next.

Is the apparent advantage mostly due to one blockbuster?
Does the genre offer the largest number of films above a revenue threshold?
Would licensing that genre produce the most profit for a streaming service?







Ex-solutionSolution







Inspect the underlying revenues and the extreme film’s record. Compare the conclusion with and without that observation as a sensitivity check, rather than silently deleting it.
Compare qualifying counts, not just central values or normalized shapes. An ECDF can show the qualifying proportion; group size is also needed for a count.
The available revenue comparison does not establish streaming profit. We would also need information such as licensing costs and expected streaming demand.

The three questions require different evidence, even though they begin with the same chart.














WarningAvoid “fixing” an anomaly without first investigating it



An unusual value can be an error, but it can also be the observation that teaches us something important. Use units, definitions, related measurements, and provenance to investigate. Record any exclusions and their reasons. Do not remove a value simply because the resulting chart looks cleaner or the association becomes stronger.








NoteWhen EDA precedes machine learning



An outcome-focused overview helps us understand a prospective target and candidate predictors, but it does not establish future predictive performance. Ask whether a feature would actually be available when a prediction is made. For example, using the measured precipitation for a day to predict whether that day had rain would reveal the answer rather than provide a useful forecast.
Once evaluation data have been held out, use the training data for exploratory choices that influence feature selection, transformations, or fitted preprocessing. For time-dependent prediction, also consider whether a chronological split is needed. Later modeling courses develop these evaluation decisions in more detail.

title: 15  Exploratory data analysis
section: 15.6 What have we learned, and what remains unresolved?
text:
15.6 What have we learned, and what remains unresolved?
EDA does not have to end with a striking discovery. Finding a data limitation, ruling out an explanation, or recognizing that the available variables cannot answer the question can be a useful result.
For our weather investigation, a short record could be:







Stage
What we learned




Initial observation
Every year’s lowest recorded minimum is 1.1°C.


Broad inspection
The lower temperature range is absent, although all dates are present.


Missingness overview
Missing temperature measurements are concentrated in colder months.


Focused comparison
