Missing minima tend to occur on days with lower recorded maxima.


Mechanism check
The teaching preparation removed temperatures at or below 0.6°C.


Revised conclusion
The incomplete data cannot establish that freezing days were absent; their temperature summaries describe a selected subset of measurements.



In a real investigation, the mechanism-check row might still say “unresolved”. That is more informative than quietly assuming a cause and proceeding.
You do not need to publish every chart made during exploration. Keep enough of the analysis history to explain important decisions, and communicate the evidence relevant to the final question. Useful stopping points include having enough evidence for the current decision, or discovering that the next step requires information outside the dataset.
For your next dataset, try leaving a short trail of reasoning:

What did I expect? What did I observe? What could explain it? What did I check next? What can I now conclude?

title: 15  Exploratory data analysis
text:
15.7 Further reading

Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund, R for Data Science, Chapter 10: Exploratory data analysis. A question-driven cycle of visualization, transformation, and follow-up, with R examples.
Peng and Matsui, The Art of Data Science, Chapter 4, especially “Always be Checking Your n’s” and “Challenge Your Solution.”
Wongsuphasawat, Liu, and Heer (2019), Goals, Process, and Challenges of Exploratory Data Analysis: An Interview Study. Describes how analysts combine data-quality assessment, discovery, and automated overviews.
Emerson and colleagues, The Generalized Pairs Plot. Explains how a matrix of appropriate displays can reveal relationships among mixed variable types.
Waskom, Visualizing distributions of data and Building structured multi-plot grids. Python examples connecting representation choices with exploratory tasks.

title: 16  Trends
text:
16.1 Why bother?
In Chapter 6, lines connected observations to show relationships and changes. Here we use lines to summarize a pattern rather than connect every observation. A trendline can make a general pattern easier to see when individual observations or multiple groups obscure it. Trendlines are also called fitted lines or lines of best fit. The choice of line determines which features of the data are emphasized. Here we focus on the summaries themselves and keep the observations visible. In Chapter 17, we add intervals and distinguish the spread of observations from uncertainty in an estimated mean.
We use automobile specifications from the Vega datasets collection, with missing acceleration or horsepower observations omitted. Acceleration records the time in seconds to accelerate from 0 to 60 mph: a larger value means the car takes longer to reach that speed. We first examine how horsepower varies with acceleration time across all cars, using one trendline. Near the end of the chapter, we compare this pooled relationship with separate fits by origin.
Connecting every observation without any aggregation does not provide a useful summary of the trend.

title: 16  Trends
text:
Altairggplot



points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle(opacity=0.2, color='black').encode(
    x=alt.X('Acceleration:Q').scale(zero=False),
    y='Horsepower'
)
points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







car_points <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Acceleration, y = Horsepower)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = 'black')
car_points













Altairggplot



points + points.mark_line()




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







car_points + geom_line()

















Ex-promptExercise 1






The four panels below show the same cars on the same axis scales, but summarize the relationship in different ways. Before learning how to construct the lines, consider what each might be estimating.

Altairggplot







  
  
  
  
  


  
  
























Ex-hintHint






Think about whether the prediction is constant, changes at a constant rate, or changes its behavior across the x-axis.




Keep your proposed explanations in mind as you work through the chapter. We will revisit the same figure and identify the four methods in Section 16.4.





Averaging at each exact value
A simple summary is the mean horsepower at each acceleration time. Some acceleration times occur repeatedly, but others have very few observations, resulting in a noisy appearance of the line with many spikes that makes it hard to see the overall trend

Altairggplot



points + points.mark_line().encode(y='mean(Horsepower)')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







car_points + geom_line(stat = 'summary', fun = 'mean')











Each mean is calculated separately from the observations at that acceleration time. Connecting the estimates helps us follow the pattern, but does not change the estimates or fit a shared model across the x-range.


Binned means
For a continuous x variable, we could instead divide its range into bins and calculate the mean response within each bin. A histogram uses these intervals to count observations; here we use them to average a response variable. The example below uses three-second acceleration intervals.

Altairggplot



points + points.mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('Acceleration:Q').bin(step=3),
    y='mean(Horsepower)'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






We use stat = 'summary_bin' to allow us to define a custom summary function with the bin instead of counting the observations.

car_points + geom_line(stat = 'summary_bin', fun = mean, binwidth = 3)











Binned means give a first view of the pattern, but depend on the width and placement of the bins. Bins can contain very different numbers of cars, and a single mean hides any pattern within its interval. Connecting these summaries adds interpolation between them, not a fitted model for the whole dataset.
We will now explore two ways to estimate the pattern more systematically: fit one model across the full range, or fit simple models within moving neighborhoods.

title: 16  Trends
text:
16.2 Fitting a global model
Another way to summarize the data is to fit one shared equation across the observed range. Here, a model is a rule that uses an input value to produce a predicted response. The simplest model returns the same prediction for every input. We will build up the flexibility of that equation in three steps:


One mean for all observations: give every car the same predicted horsepower.
Allow the line to tilt: let the prediction change with acceleration time.
Allow the relationship to curve: add a squared acceleration feature.


We use least-squares fitting throughout this progression. Unlike separate means at each acceleration time, a regression links estimates across acceleration times through shared coefficients. Changing observations in one part of the x-range can change fitted values throughout the range. This pooling can stabilize estimates, but it can also hide abrupt changes or impose an unsuitable shape; a shared model is not automatically better.

One mean for all observations
If we had to predict every car’s horsepower using the same value, which value would minimize the sum of squared errors? Unlike the earlier means at individual acceleration times or within bins, this estimate uses all cars to make one prediction shared by every observation.
The mean is the constant that minimizes the sum of squared deviations. In graphical terms, it is the best-fitting horizontal line under squared-error loss. Here \(i\) indexes cars, \(\hat{y}_i\) is predicted horsepower, and \(w_0\) is the fitted constant:

\[
\hat{y}_i = w_0 = \bar{y}
\]


Altairggplot



global_mean = alt.Chart(cars).mark_rule().encode(y='mean(Horsepower):Q')
points + global_mean




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







car_points + geom_hline(yintercept = mean(cars$Horsepower))













Allow the model to tilt
Can we improve the predictions by allowing them to depend on acceleration time? Linear least-squares regression fits a straight line by minimizing the sum of squared vertical deviations from the observations to the line. Linear regression allows that line to tilt by estimating a slope in addition to the intercept. The horizontal mean line is a special case where the slope is constrained to zero. For the straight-line fit, we estimate

\[
\hat{y}_i = w_0 + x_{i1}w_1
\]

where \(i\) indexes cars, \(x_{i1}\) is car \(i\)’s acceleration time in seconds, and \(\hat{y}_i\) is its predicted mean horsepower. The fitted weights \(w_0\) and \(w_1\) are the intercept and slope. The first subscript in \(x_{i1}\) identifies the observation; the second identifies the feature.

Altairggplot



points + points.mark_line().transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Set the smoothing method to lm for a linear model. se = FALSE hides ggplot’s default confidence band, which we will instead talk about in Chapter 17.

car_points + geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE)












Tilt the line around the sample means
For ordinary least squares with an intercept, the fitted line passes through the point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\): mean acceleration time and mean horsepower. For any chosen slope \(w_1\), the least-squares intercept is \(w_0 = \bar{y} - w_1\bar{x}\). We can therefore think of moving from the constant model to a straight line as tilting the line around this fixed point. The intercept changes with the slope; the pivot is the sample means, not necessarily the visual midpoint of the x-axis.
Use the slider below to change the slope. Start at zero to see the global mean line, then try negative and positive slopes. Watch how the equation changes while the line continues to pass through the diamond.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




The slider explores candidate slopes, with the intercept adjusted for each one. They all pass through the sample means, but they do not fit the observations equally well. OLS chooses the slope that minimizes the sum of squared vertical residuals. The fixed axis limits make the change in tilt visible without rescaling the chart.






Deep-diveDeep dive: Which is the “best” line?






To be able to quantify how well a model “fits” the data, we need to quantify some type of metric that indicates how good the fit is. A common way of doing this is to use the distance from each observation to the model’s prediction for an observation at that location. For each observation, the prediction error —also called a residual when comparing observed and fitted values— is the observed value (the point) minus the predicted value (the line). In the chart below, the orange segments show the magnitudes (i.e. the absolute value) of these discrepancies.
There are different ways to combine these residuals into an overall error. An intuitive one might be to simply sum up all the magnitudes of the prediction errors, i.e. add the length orange lines together. This is a perfectly reasonable thing to do, but often the squared distance is used instead. Squaring gives large misses disproportionately more influence than taking the absolute distance (just like the mean vs the median). Squared error therefore encourages the model to avoid large misses, even if this means accepting several smaller ones. It also targets the mean (i.e. the mean is the best fit of all possible horizontal lines) and makes linear regression particularly convenient to fit using linear algebra since optimizing the squared error instead of the absolute error is more computationally efficient. Absolute error remains a valid alternative which targets the median and gives extreme residuals less influence. The choice should reflect what we want to estimate and which kinds of prediction errors matter.








Fitting objective
Error displayed below
What large residuals contribute to the error




Least absolute deviations (LAD)
Mean absolute error (MAE): average of absolute residuals
A residual twice as large contributes twice as much


Ordinary least squares (OLS)
Mean squared error (MSE): average of squared residuals
A residual twice as large contributes four times as much



As you can see in the table, these error metrics are defined as averages, but we talked about sums of residuals above. Minimizing the sum or the mean of either kind of error gives the same fit for a fixed dataset: dividing by the number of observations only rescales the objective. Using means makes it easier to communicate how wrong the line is on average. To facilitate communication, we might also avoid MSE since results in really large numbers and squared units (e.g. squared horsepowers) and instead take the square root of the MSE, which is called the Root Mean Squared Error (notably similar to standard
As in the preceding example, the slider changes the slope while the intercept adjusts to keep the line passing through this sample’s means. The title shows the resulting equation, with MSE and MAE directly below it. This lets us compare the losses for the same candidate lines. However, note that a freely fitted LAD line need not pass through the sample means (or median), it could be shifted up or down (whereas the OLS line is guranteed to be rotated around the mean).





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Start with slope zero: the horizontal line is at the sample mean. Then adjust the slope: can you find a line with smaller MSE? Does the same candidate slope also give the smallest MAE? Watch how one long orange segment can dominate MSE even when many other segments are short. The axes remain fixed; at steep slopes, parts of the line and residual segments are clipped to the plotting area, but both error values include the full residuals.
If we were free to move a horizontal line vertically, the height minimizing MSE would be the sample mean, and a height minimizing MAE would be a sample median. With both intercept and slope freely fitted, OLS targets a conditional mean relationship, while LAD, also called median regression, targets a conditional median relationship.







Allow the model to curve
What if one constant slope does not capture the pattern? Regression is not restricted to straight lines. For the degree-two polynomial below, we add a feature \(x_{i2} = x_{i1}^2\):

\[
\hat{y}_i = w_0 + x_{i1}w_1 + x_{i2}w_2
\]

The weight \(w_2\) on squared acceleration time allows the relationship to curve rather than have a constant slope. All three examples estimate their coefficients using all cars by minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals. The quadratic fit is still a linear model in its weights \(w_0\), \(w_1\), and \(w_2\), even though its graph can be curved in the original feature space.

Altairggplot



points + points.mark_line().transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower', method='poly', order=2
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







car_points +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), se = FALSE)

title: 16  Trends
text:
16.3 Fitting local models
Sometimes one equation is a poor description of the whole dataset. Instead of fitting one model across the full range, we can fit simple models repeatedly to nearby observations. We will follow the same progression as before: start with a constant, then allow each local fit to tilt.
Binning uses fixed, non-overlapping neighborhoods. A rolling mean instead averages observations within overlapping neighborhoods that move along the axis. We can think of a rolling mean as local constant regression: at each target x-value, fit a horizontal line to nearby observations and retain its height as the estimate. The resulting curve can bend even though each individual fit is horizontal, because the observations contributing to the estimate change as the neighborhood moves.
Here we sort the individual cars by acceleration time and average neighboring observations across all origins. Each included car receives equal weight. Unlike fixed bins, the neighborhoods overlap; however, equal-weight windows can still produce jumps as observations enter or leave.

Altairggplot


frame=[-30, 30] starts with the preceding 30 observations, the current observation, and the following 30 observations in acceleration-time order. At the endpoints, it uses the available observations. By default, Altair expands window boundaries to include ties in the sorting variable, so a window can include more than 61 cars when acceleration times repeat.

alt.Chart(cars).transform_window(
    rolling_hp='mean(Horsepower)',
    frame=[-30, 30],
    sort=[alt.SortField('Acceleration')]
).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('Acceleration:Q'),
    y='rolling_hp:Q'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






There is no built-in way to plot a rolling mean in ggplot, so instead we calculate the means before plotting. slider::slide_dbl() averages the preceding 30 rows, the current row, and the following 30 rows, using the available rows at the endpoints. Unlike Altair’s default, this uses strict row boundaries rather than expanding for ties, so the curves can differ where acceleration times repeat.

rolling_cars <- cars |>
    arrange(Acceleration) |>
    mutate(rolling_hp = slider::slide_dbl(
        Horsepower, mean, .before = 30, .after = 30
    ))
ggplot(rolling_cars, aes(x = Acceleration, y = rolling_hp)) +
    geom_line()












Choosing a rolling window
The width of 30 observations on either side is an illustrative starting point, not a generally optimal choice. Compare narrower and wider windows to see which features persist. A fixed observation count spans different ranges of acceleration times where cars are more or less densely represented. Repeated acceleration times can also receive different estimates as the row window moves, producing vertical segments when those estimates are connected at the same x-value.
Three window types answer different questions:


Expanding ([None, 0], the default in Altair): average everything up to the current position in the sort order. This estimates a cumulative level rather than a local trend.
Trailing (for example, [-30, 0]): use observations at or before the current position. Common in e.g. finance. With a chronological sort, this is useful for monitoring as observations arrive.
Centered ([-30, 30]): use observations on both sides to describe a local pattern. Common in e.g. statistics.




Allow each local fit to tilt
Local linear regression instead fits a line with a slope, then evaluates that line at the target x-value. Moving the neighborhood and repeating these fits produces the curve. LOESS (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing), also called LOWESS (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing), uses local fits with distance-based weights. Nearby observations receive more influence, and the local fits can be linear or quadratic. The animation builds up the red fitted curve from local fits.




A local regression curve is assembled by moving a fitting window across the observations. Animation by Rafael Irizarry, from Simply Statistics.




Altairggplot


Altair fits linear regression locally in each neighborhood in transform_loess.     

points + points.mark_line().transform_loess(
    'Acceleration',
    'Horsepower',
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






For computational efficiency, geom_smooth() automatically changes the method based on the number of data points. To ensure that we use LOESS, we therefore set it explicitly although it is the default for datasets up to 1000 observations per group. By default, ggplot fits quadratic regressions locally for each neighborhood.

car_points + geom_smooth(method = 'loess', se = FALSE)

















Deep-diveDeep dive: Choosing the smoothing neighborhood size









Setting
Altair
ggplot




Local fit
Linear
Quadratic


Neighborhood fraction
bandwidth=0.3
span=0.75



The examples start with each library’s defaults. Changing the neighborhood fraction does not by itself make the fits equivalent.
We can control the fraction of observations included in each neighborhood. Larger fractions usually give a smoother, more general curve. Note that even if we were to include all observations in each neighborhood, this would not generally be identical to a single global linear regression since all observations do not have the same weight.

Altairggplot


The bandwidth parameter controls the fraction of observations included in each neighborhood. By default, it is set to 0.3.

points + points.mark_line().transform_loess(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower', bandwidth=0.75
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






The span parameter changes the fraction of observations in each neighborhood. By default, it is set as 0.75.

car_points + geom_smooth(
    method = 'loess', span = 0.3, se = FALSE,
    method.args = list(degree = 1, family = 'symmetric')
)











The following animations illustrate the qualitative effect of narrower and wider weighting neighborhoods in a different LOWESS implementation. Its Gaussian-width parameter, \(\sigma\), is not the same parameter as Altair’s bandwidth or ggplot’s span.
















A narrower weighting neighborhood follows more local variation. Source: .A wider weighting neighborhood produces a smoother curve. Source: .





Deep-diveDeep dive: Kernels connect density estimation and local regression






In Chapter 10, kernels let observations contribute gradually to nearby locations rather than placing them entirely inside one fixed bin. The same distance-based weighting idea can be used to estimate a relationship.
At a target x-value, a rectangular kernel gives equal weight to observations inside a window and zero weight outside it. A Gaussian kernel gives the greatest weight to nearby observations, with smoothly decreasing weights at greater distances. Its weights are technically nonzero everywhere. The bandwidth controls the distance over which those weights decrease.
What we do with the weights determines what we estimate:

KDE: add the kernel contributions and normalize to estimate the density of x.
Local weighted mean: average the corresponding y-values, dividing by the sum of the weights.
Local linear regression: use the weights to fit a nearby line, then evaluate it at the target.

With rectangular weights, the local weighted mean is a moving-window average. With smoothly decreasing weights, it is often called a kernel smoother. A KDE needs only the x-values; regression also needs a response variable y. More observations near a location increase its estimated density, but do not by themselves increase its estimated mean response.
LOESS commonly uses tricube weights, which decrease with distance and reach zero at the edge of a nearest-neighbor neighborhood. Its span specifies a fraction of observations, whereas a KDE bandwidth commonly specifies a distance in the variable’s units. These settings therefore share an idea but are not directly interchangeable. Likewise, a rolling window of 61 rows is not a fixed interval of acceleration times when observations are unevenly spaced along the x-axis.






Ex-promptExercise 2






Suppose every car has exactly 100 horsepower, but many more cars have acceleration times near 15 seconds than near 10 or 20 seconds. Would a KDE of acceleration times and a local weighted mean of horsepower both have a peak near 15 seconds?






Ex-hintHint






One calculation estimates where the x-values are concentrated; the other averages the y-values associated with nearby x-values.






Ex-solutionSolution






The KDE can have a peak where acceleration times are densely represented, depending on its bandwidth. The local weighted mean remains 100 wherever the total weight is positive: its weighted sum is 100 times the sum of its weights, so dividing by that sum returns 100. The same kernels can therefore reveal a changing density and a constant response.


















Why fit a local slope?
Near the left edge of an increasing trend, most available neighbors lie to the right. A rolling mean averages their higher responses and can overestimate the response at the target. A local linear fit can account for the slope and evaluate the line at the target instead For observations lying exactly on a straight line, it recovers that line wherever the neighborhood contains enough distinct, positively weighted x-values. A local mean can also reproduce a straight trend in a symmetric neighborhood, but generally not at the boundaries or when the x-values are unevenly spaced.
In our examples, the rolling mean and regression both use individual cars as observations, so densely represented acceleration ranges contribute more observations to their fits. The rolling mean uses a centered observation window with equal weight per included car (with boundary ties expanded in the Altair example); LOESS instead selects a fraction of nearby cars and weights them by distance. To isolate the effect of a local constant versus a local slope, we would need to use the same input observations, neighborhoods, and weights.

title: 16  Trends
section: 16.4 Compare the questions answered by different summaries
text:
16.4 Compare the questions answered by different summaries
Return to the opening exercise. The same four panels now illustrate a progression from a global constant to a global line, and from a local constant to local regression. The top row uses all cars to fit one shared model; the bottom row uses moving neighborhoods.

Altairggplot







  
  
  
  
  


  
  


















Following more local variation is not automatically better: the useful summary depends on the question and on which features persist across reasonable modeling choices.









Panel and summary
Observations used
What is fitted?




A: Overall mean
All cars
One shared constant


B: Global linear regression
All cars
One shared straight line


C: Rolling mean
Moving, overlapping window
A local constant


D: Local smoothing regression (LOESS)
Nearby cars, weighted by distance
A local line at each target




For this comparison, the rolling mean uses 30 observations on either side, with the boundary-tie handling described earlier for each library. Both LOESS examples use a neighborhood fraction of 0.5; the R fit explicitly uses local linear, robust fitting to more closely match Altair. The implementations can still give slightly different curves.
Trend estimators differ in which observations they use, how they weight them, and how flexible a function they fit.

title: 16  Trends
text:
16.5 When to choose which trendline?


Means and rolling means are useful when the summarized values should have a straightforward interpretation. It is poorly suited to extrapolation beyond the data range but can be particularly accessible to a general audience.
Regression models are useful when a simple equation is a reasonable description of the relationship and it is advantageous to describe the relationship with a known equation. Predictions beyond the observed range are generally more accurate than for models fitted using a local neighborhood, but they still rely on that the fitted equation hold beyong the observed range, and become more uncertain as they move further from the data.
LOESS is useful for describing patterns within the observed data without choosing one global equation. It often resembles the trend a reader would sketch by eye, and it generally usable for communication purposes although they are not as straightforward to understand as a rolling mean. It is poorly suited to extrapolation beyond the data range.

title: 16  Trends
text:
16.6 Extension: comparing trends within groups
So far, each trend has summarized all cars together. The pooled fit describes the overall relationship between acceleration time and horsepower. Separate fits by origin ask whether that relationship also describes the cars within each group. As in Chapter 5, the overall pattern can reflect both differences within groups and differences between groups.
In the following comparison, the colored lines are separate linear regressions for each origin, and the dashed black line is the pooled regression from earlier. Using the same fitting method lets us focus on the effect of grouping.

Altairggplot



grouped_points = points.encode(color='Origin:N')
grouped_lines = grouped_points.mark_line().transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower', groupby=['Origin']
)
pooled_line = points.mark_line(color='black', strokeDash=[6, 4]).transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower'
)
grouped_points + grouped_lines + pooled_line




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(cars, aes(x = Acceleration, y = Horsepower, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE) +
    geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = 'lm', se = FALSE,
                color = 'black', linetype = 'dashed')











The pooled line need not coincide with any group’s line. Ask whether the groups occupy different parts of the x-range and whether their slopes or fitted levels differ. The pooled and grouped fits answer different questions; choose according to the comparison you want to make, rather than automatically adding groups to every trend plot.

title: 16  Trends
text:
16.7 Further reading

Visualizing trends.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.1 Why bother?
A point or a line can look precise even when it represents an uncertain estimate. Showing uncertainty helps readers judge which conclusions the data support, but the visual representation also matters: an interval that is familiar to a statistician may convey something quite different to a general audience. We will first explore how to communicate uncertainty, then create interval plots in Altair and ggplot.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.2 Framing probabilities as frequencies
The lecture’s historical example compares three forecasts of Donald Trump’s chance of winning the 2016 US presidential election. These percentages describe the probability of winning, not the predicted share of votes.






Figure 17.1: Three historical forecasts assign Trump approximately 28%, 15%, and 2% chances of winning. The slide credits Justin H. Gross, Washington Post.





When called upon to judge probability, people actually judge something else and believe they have judged probability – Daniel Kahneman








Ex-promptExercise 1






Trump won the election. Does that result alone establish that all three models were bad? How could we make the probabilities more intuitive to an audience unfamiliar with forecasting?






Ex-hintHint






An outcome with a probability below 50% is less likely than its alternative, but is it impossible? Think about rolling a particular number on a fair six-sided die.






Ex-solutionSolution






No. A probabilistic forecast is not a promise that the most likely outcome will occur. Rolling a six does not establish that a die is unfair merely because that outcome had only a one-in-six chance. The models assigned different probabilities, so they did not express the same degree of uncertainty. A scoring rule can reward a forecast that assigned more probability to the observed outcome, but one election cannot establish a model’s long-run calibration.
We can make the probabilities easier to imagine by expressing them as frequencies: roughly 28, 15, or 2 wins out of 100 comparable hypothetical elections under each forecast. These are model-implied scenarios, not a claim that we observed 100 elections.












Frequency framing expresses a probability as a share of a collection of outcomes. In the theater-seat version below, imagine choosing a seat without seeing its color first. Dark seats represent scenarios in which Trump wins. Even in the first forecast, a dark seat is less likely than a light one, but selecting one would hardly be extraordinary.






Figure 17.2: The same forecasts represented by dark seats among 1,000 seats: 286, 150, and 20 winning scenarios. The first panel uses a finer value than the rounded percentage above. Credit: Justin H. Gross, Washington Post, as cited in the lecture.



The format can show more than a binary win or loss. FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 forecast displayed both a distribution of simulated electoral-vote outcomes and a sample of 100 scenarios. The scenario display combines a frequency statement with the possible margin of victory.






Figure 17.3: Historical FiveThirtyEight forecast distributions for electoral votes.









Figure 17.4: A historical FiveThirtyEight screenshot summarizes 100 scenarios: 10 Trump wins, 89 Biden wins, and one scenario without an Electoral College majority.



These are snapshots from the 2020 forecast, not current predictions. Each dot represents a simulated scenario, not a voter. Frequency displays can make unlikely outcomes more tangible, but labels must explain what the marks represent and how they were generated. Too many tiny marks can also become difficult to count.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.3 Reading error bars and bands
Error bars are compact and useful when comparing many estimates, but their appearance alone does not tell us what they represent.






Ex-promptExercise 2
















What information would you need before interpreting these intervals? Could you tell whether they show the spread of penguin body masses or uncertainty in a mean?






Ex-solutionSolution






We need to know what the point estimates and intervals represent: for example, means with standard deviations, confidence intervals for means, or some other summary. For confidence intervals, we also need the confidence level and an explanation of how they were calculated. The same point-and-line marks can display all these quantities, so we cannot infer the interval definition from their shape.








Figure 17.5: An intentionally unlabeled interval example from the lecture.In Chapter 7, we combined measures of central tendency with indications of how the observations vary. But the spread of the observations and the uncertainty in an estimated mean answer different questions. In Chapter 16, we used lines to summarize horsepower without displaying intervals. Here we group the cars by model year and origin, then add intervals to the annual means. For example, cars can have very different horsepower values even when we have enough observations to estimate their mean relatively precisely.








Display
What it describes




Mean ± one standard deviation (SD)
Spread of the individual observations around their mean


Mean ± one standard error (SE)
Uncertainty in the estimated mean; approximately a 68% CI under a normal approximation


95% confidence interval (CI) for the mean
An interval targeting 95% coverage; often approximately mean ± 1.96 SE, or calculated using another interval method










Figure 17.6: Different intervals for the same chocolate-rating sample. The labels distinguish standard deviation, standard error, and three confidence levels. Adapted from Claus O. Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization, Figure 16.5; data credit: Brady Brelinski, Manhattan Chocolate Society.



A shorter bar does not by itself mean that the data or model are better. Changing from SD to SE changes the question being answered; changing the confidence level changes the interval’s intended coverage. Choose the quantity that addresses the question and label it explicitly.
A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimate, in this case the population mean. The interval gives a range of population estimates reasonably compatible with the observed data. For a 95% confidence interval, the precise interpretation is that if we repeatedly sampled data and constructed intervals in the same way, about 95% of those intervals would contain the population quantity, provided the method’s assumptions hold. Note that this is not the same as saying that the true population mean has a 95% chance to be contained within a single CI. The population mean is fixed, and it is our construction of the CI that varies depending on the values in our observed data (i.e. our sample from the entire population).
The standard error describes uncertainty in the estimated mean. When its sampling distribution is approximately normal—as is often the case for sufficiently large samples—mean ± one SE is approximately a 68% confidence interval, and mean ± two SE is approximately a 95% confidence interval.
It’s common to compute the confidence interval and standard error using bootstrapping. Bootstrapping is a procedure for estimating the distribution of an estimator (such as the mean) by resampling the observed data. The underlying idea in bootstrapping is that since we don’t have access to data of the entire population and we cannot repeatedly collect new samples from that population, we treat the data we have as the closest approximation of the distribution of the population and draw new samples from our observed data to build a confidence interval for our population mean estimate. You can read more detail about this technique and play around with an interactive chart in the deep dive below.






Deep-diveDeep dive: Building a confidence interval by bootstrapping






The bootstrapping technique resamples observations with replacement from the observed data, calculates the mean for each resample, and uses the resulting distribution of means to construct an interval. We refer to each generated dataset as a bootstrap resample, and its mean as the bootstrap resample mean or just resample mean for short. Together, these estimates form the bootstrap distribution of the mean. The percentile-bootstrap method uses a range of resample means to construct a confidence interval for the population mean: for example, the 5th–95th percentile interval of the resample mean distribution gives a nominal 90% confidence interval. The standard deviation of the resampled means can similarly be used to construct the standard error of the sample mean (SEM).
As an example, suppose that our observed sample contains the horsepower of 20 cars and we want to estimate the population mean and its confidence interval. These are the steps we would follow to construct that interval via bootstrapping:

Resample with replacement: draw 20 observations from the observed sample. A car can appear more than once, and others may not appear at all.
Calculate the resample’s mean: each resample contributes one value to the distribution of resample means.
Repeat and take percentiles: choose the middle fraction corresponding to the desired confidence level. At 95%, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resample means form a 95% percentile-bootstrap confidence interval for the population mean.

You can see this process depicted graphically below, and play around with some of the parameters.







  
  
  
  
  


  
  







The bootstrap distribution describes how the estimated mean varies when we resample the observed data. We use it to approximate how the sample mean would vary if we could repeatedly collect new samples from the population. At the default 95% level in the percentile-bootstrap method, we take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of these resample means and use those same endpoints as an approximate 95% confidence interval for the population mean. In SD / SE mode, the standard deviation of the accumulated resample means estimates the standard error of the original sample mean. A one-SE interval is approximately a 68% confidence interval when the estimator’s sampling distribution is approximately normal and bias is small (which is increasingly likely as the sample size grews larger as per the central limit theorem).




Figure 17.7: Interactive chart for construction CI via bootstrapping. After clicking a slider you can either drag with the pointer or use the arrow keys to step through the values. The slider reveals a fixed sequence of resamples generated with a random seed, so returning to the same position gives the same result. Notice that every resample still contains 20 observations, even when the histogram contains 500 means. Increasing the number of resamples makes the bootstrap calculation more stable; it does not add new information to the original sample.
Interval endpoints are not walls
Readers can interpret the endpoints of an error bar as the limits of what is possible. This is sometimes called a deterministic construal error: treating an uncertainty display as a hard constraint. An interval summarizing part of a distribution need not contain all its possible values. For a confidence interval, remember that the coverage statement concerns repeated sampling; a particular interval can miss the population quantity.






Figure 17.8: A schematic distribution continues beyond the displayed interval. The drawing illustrates why an interval should not automatically be read as the full range of possible values; it does not specify a confidence level.



Nor should we assume that every kind of error bar must exclude observations: a minimum-to-maximum interval includes the observed range by construction. The interpretation depends on what the interval actually represents.


Overlap is not a general significance test






Figure 17.9: The lecture’s overlap schematic illustrates that overlapping intervals can accompany a statistically significant difference under particular assumptions. Its printed p-values are not universal thresholds for interpreting error bars.



The amount of overlap alone does not establish whether two estimates differ significantly. The answer depends on the interval definition and the relationship between the estimates, including whether observations are paired. If the question concerns a difference, calculate and visualize an interval for the difference itself, using a method appropriate to the data.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.4 Showing alternative outcomes
A single line and shaded band can make one fitted curve seem inevitable, with uncertainty appearing only as a little movement up or down. Showing alternative curves makes the possible variation in shape more explicit.






Figure 17.10: A fitted spline and interval band compared with alternative curves drawn from a posterior distribution. Source: Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization, Figure 16.18, using Motor Trend car data.



A hypothetical outcome plot (HOP) cycles through sampled possibilities, rather than drawing them all at once. In this example, each frame shows an alternative fitted curve from the model’s posterior distribution. The animation shows uncertainty in the fitted relationship, not a time sequence in which the cars change.






Figure 17.11: An animated hypothetical outcome plot of alternative fitted curves. Source: Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization, Figure 16.22.



The static comparison above remains useful for print and for readers who prefer to inspect several alternatives at once. For an animation, outcomes should be sampled to represent the modeled uncertainty, rather than selected to exaggerate stability or variation. Rare but important outcomes may need explicit annotation or a separate view, since a short animation can easily omit them.

title: 17  Uncertainty
section: 17.5 Forecast uncertainty is not physical size
text:
17.5 Forecast uncertainty is not physical size






Ex-promptExercise 3
















What might an unfamiliar reader think the widening shaded region represents? How could the alternative tracks help, and what explanation would they still need?






Ex-hintHint






Does the widening cone describe a growing storm, or growing uncertainty about the location of its center?






Ex-solutionSolution






A forecast cone can be mistaken for the storm’s physical size. Its widening instead represents increasing uncertainty about the future position of the storm’s center. Its boundary is not a line separating dangerous from safe locations: the center can move outside the cone, and hazardous weather can extend beyond it.
Alternative tracks make the uncertainty about location more explicit, but viewers still need to know what the tracks represent and how they were generated. A collection of different models is not automatically a set of equally probable outcomes. For decisions such as evacuation, pair the uncertainty display with information about the relevant hazards and guidance, rather than asking readers to infer risk from the center line or cone alone.












Figure 17.12: A hurricane forecast shown as a cone and as a collection of possible tracks, reproduced from the lecture.The same general lesson applies to statistical bands: explain what is uncertain, what the displayed region means, and which conclusions its boundaries do and do not support. We now turn to constructing intervals with the plotting libraries.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.6 From trend summaries to intervals
We will use the cars dataset from Vega, available here as a local CSV. Each row describes a car, including its model year, horsepower, and origin. We omit rows with missing horsepower for these examples.

Altairggplot



import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

cars = pd.read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv', parse_dates=['Year']).dropna(subset=['Horsepower'])
cars['Year'] = cars['Year'].dt.year

points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_point(opacity=0.3).encode(
    x=alt.X('Year:Q').scale(zero=False).axis(format='d'),
    y='Horsepower:Q',
    color='Origin:N'
)
points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







library(tidyverse)

cars <- read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv') |>
    drop_na(Horsepower) |>
    mutate(Year = lubridate::year(Year))

points <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Year, y = Horsepower, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1970, 1982, by = 2))
points












A band describing the spread of observations
First, show the mean plus or minus one sample standard deviation for each combination of origin and year. This describes the spread of horsepower values, not uncertainty in the mean. It is not guaranteed to contain a particular percentage of observations.

Altairggplot



mean_line = points.mark_line().encode(y='mean(Horsepower):Q')
points.mark_errorband(extent='stdev', opacity=0.3) + mean_line




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






mean_sdl returns the mean plus or minus a multiple of the standard deviation. Its default multiplier is two, so we explicitly set mult = 1 to match Altair.

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Year, y = Horsepower, color = Origin, fill = Origin)) +
    geom_ribbon(stat = 'summary', fun.data = mean_sdl,
                fun.args = list(mult = 1), alpha = 0.3, color = NA) +
    geom_line(stat = 'summary', fun = mean)













A band describing uncertainty in the mean
To summarize the uncertainty in the mean horsepower for each origin and year, we can draw a confidence band. At each year, the lower and upper edges show the endpoints of an interval; shading connects those intervals across years.

Altairggplot


mark_errorband() calculates and draws the interval. Setting extent='ci' requests a 95% bootstrap confidence interval for the mean, calculated separately for each combination of year and origin. The default extent is 'stderr', which instead shows the mean plus or minus one standard error. Use 'stdev' to show one standard deviation. These choices have different meanings, so specify the extent explicitly.

band = points.mark_errorband(extent='ci', opacity=0.3)
band




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






In ggplot, we can create confidence bands with geom_ribbon(). Previously we passed summary functions such as mean to fun. Here we use fun.data, because a ribbon needs both a lower and an upper bound.
The mean_cl_boot function returns three values: y, ymin, and ymax. These are the mean and the lower and upper endpoints of its bootstrap confidence interval. The ribbon uses the two endpoints. This function requires the Hmisc package, which is included in the textbook’s R environment.

set.seed(531)

band <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Year, y = Horsepower, color = Origin, fill = Origin)) +
    geom_ribbon(stat = 'summary', fun.data = mean_cl_boot,
                fun.args = list(conf.int = 0.95), alpha = 0.3, color = NA)
band








color = NA removes the ribbon’s boundary lines, leaving only the shaded area. The random seed makes the R bootstrap reproducible. Both libraries use bootstrap intervals, but their endpoints can differ slightly because the resamples are random and are generated separately.





Adding the estimated mean
A band shows the interval, but it is also helpful to show the estimate itself. We can add a line for the mean, using the same grouping as the band.

Altairggplot



band + mean_line




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







set.seed(531)
band + geom_line(stat = 'summary', fun = mean)











These are pointwise intervals: each interval is calculated separately for one origin in one year. Connecting them does not turn them into a simultaneous 95% confidence band for the entire trajectory. Similarly, the connecting segments do not establish the mean or its uncertainty at unobserved times, as discussed in Chapter 6.
These intervals summarize each year’s observations independently; they are not confidence bands around a fitted regression or LOESS curve.
The cars provide a convenient illustration of the plotting tools. Interpreting these intervals as uncertainty about a broader population would also require justifying how the cars were sampled and whether resampling individual rows is appropriate.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.7 Confidence bands around fitted trends
We can also show uncertainty around the fitted relationships from Chapter 16. Here we return to horsepower versus acceleration time, fitting a separate relationship for each origin. Acceleration time is measured in seconds to reach 60 mph, so larger values indicate slower acceleration.
Unlike the separate annual means above, a fitted relationship uses observations across x-values to estimate its curve. The confidence band should describe uncertainty in that fitted curve, using the same model as the line.

Altairggplot


Altair’s built-in regression and LOESS transforms return fitted curves, but do not calculate their confidence bounds. We would need to calculate the fit and interval endpoints with a statistical library first, then draw the line and shaded area in Altair. For example, scikit-learn fits could be bootstrapped by repeatedly resampling the observations and refitting the model, but scikit-learn does not supply these confidence bands automatically. We use ggplot for the compact examples here.
Adding mark_errorband(extent='ci') to the raw data would instead calculate separate bootstrap intervals at each acceleration time; those would not be confidence intervals for the fitted regression or LOESS curve.


For linear regression, geom_smooth(method = 'lm') can display both the fitted line and a confidence band. We explicitly set se = TRUE and level = 0.95, although these are the defaults. Despite the argument’s name, se = TRUE enables a confidence band; it does not request a band of plus or minus one standard error. Mapping both color and fill to origin gives each line and its band matching colors.

trend_points <- ggplot(
    drop_na(cars, Acceleration),
    aes(x = Acceleration, y = Horsepower, color = Origin, fill = Origin)
) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    labs(x = 'Acceleration time (seconds)')

trend_points + geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = TRUE, level = 0.95)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









The shaded region is a pointwise 95% confidence interval for the fitted mean horsepower. It is not a standard-deviation band or a prediction interval for individual cars. These intervals use the linear model’s estimated standard errors and a t-distribution, rather than the groupwise bootstrap calculation used earlier.
We can also show a confidence band around a LOESS curve. Here we use R’s local quadratic, non-robust fit and a span of 0.75, making those defaults explicit.

trend_points + geom_smooth(method = 'loess')

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









For LOESS, ggplot uses an approximate pointwise confidence interval based on the smoother’s estimated standard errors and a t-based approximation. The curve and band depend on the chosen span and fitting settings; the band does not account for uncertainty about which smoothing settings to choose.



In both charts, the bands describe uncertainty in the fitted mean relationship, not the spread of the underlying observations. Keeping the points visible helps distinguish those two quantities. As with the annual-mean intervals, pointwise 95% coverage does not imply 95% simultaneous coverage of the entire curve.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.8 Confidence intervals around individual estimates
For comparisons between categories, an interval around a point can be easier to read than a band. Here we pool the years and estimate mean horsepower separately for each origin. This answers a different question from the preceding year-by-year comparison.

Altairggplot


mark_errorbar() displays an interval around a single estimate. As with the band, extent='ci' requests a 95% bootstrap interval for the mean.

err_bars = alt.Chart(cars).mark_errorbar(
    extent='ci', rule=alt.LineConfig(strokeWidth=2)
).encode(
    x='Horsepower:Q',
    y='Origin:N'
)
err_bars




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




We can add the mean as a point.

mean_points = err_bars.mark_point(color='black', filled=True).encode(
    x='mean(Horsepower):Q'
)
err_bars + mean_points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






geom_pointrange() displays both the mean and its interval. It uses all three values returned by mean_cl_boot. With horsepower on the x-axis and origin on the y-axis, the intervals are horizontal.

set.seed(531)

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Origin)) +
    geom_pointrange(stat = 'summary', fun.data = mean_cl_boot)

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.9 Showing the observations alongside uncertainty
A mean and its confidence interval can still hide the distribution of the data. Adding faded marks for individual observations lets the reader distinguish the spread of the cars’ horsepower values from uncertainty in their mean.

Altairggplot


Draw the observations as light ticks first, so that the interval and mean remain visible on top.

observations = err_bars.mark_tick(color='lightgrey', opacity=0.5)
observations + err_bars + mean_points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






We can use a vertical bar as the point shape to create the same kind of display.

set.seed(531)

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Origin)) +
    geom_point(shape = '|', color = 'grey', alpha = 0.5, size = 5) +
    geom_pointrange(stat = 'summary', fun.data = mean_cl_boot)








As a ggplot-specific alternative, a faded violin can provide an overview of each distribution. The point here represents the mean, unlike the median often shown inside a violin.

set.seed(531)

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Origin)) +
    geom_violin(color = NA, fill = 'steelblue', alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_pointrange(stat = 'summary', fun.data = mean_cl_boot)

















Ex-promptExercise 4






Most of the individual cars fall outside the confidence interval for their origin’s mean. Does this indicate that the interval was calculated incorrectly? What would you expect to happen to the interval if we collected more independent observations from the same population, with a similar spread of horsepower values?






Ex-hintHint






Is the interval describing variation among individual cars, or uncertainty in the mean horsepower?






Ex-solutionSolution






No. A confidence interval for the mean is not intended to contain 95% of the cars. The ticks and violin show the spread of individual observations; the interval describes uncertainty in the estimated mean. With more independent observations and similar variability, we generally expect the confidence interval to become narrower, even though the spread of individual horsepower values remains similar.












Always identify what an interval represents in its caption or accompanying text. Standard deviations, standard errors, and confidence intervals can be drawn with the same marks, but they answer different questions.

title: 17  Uncertainty
text:
17.10 Further reading

Fundamentals of Data Visualization: Visualizing uncertainty.
When(ish) is My Bus? User-centered Visualizations of Uncertainty in Everyday, Mobile Predictive Systems.
The lecture’s videos on communicating uncertainty and hurricane forecasts.

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
text:
18.1 Why bother?
A single plot may not answer every part of a question. Combining complementary views can show a relationship alongside its distributions, or let readers compare how the same response relates to different predictors. The layout should make those comparisons easier, rather than simply fit more plots onto a page.
After composing a figure, we also need to choose how to share it. A PNG is convenient in a document, a vector image stays sharp when resized, and an HTML file can preserve browser interactions. We introduce the export workflow here, then develop the interactions themselves in Chapter 19.

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
text:
18.2 Preparing complementary panels
We will reuse the cars dataset. We keep observations with recorded fuel economy, horsepower, and weight so that both panels show the same cars. If a variable is shared between panels, placing it on the same axis makes the relationships easier to compare. Here, weight stays on the y-axis. The short titles identify panels while we experiment with layouts; for a communication figure, a title explaining the message may be more useful.

Altairggplot



import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

cars = pd.read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv').dropna(
    subset=['Miles_per_Gallon', 'Horsepower', 'Weight_in_lbs', 'Origin']
)
mpg_weight = alt.Chart(cars, title='Fuel economy and weight').mark_point().encode(
    x='Miles_per_Gallon:Q', y='Weight_in_lbs:Q', color='Origin:N'
)
hp_weight = alt.Chart(cars, title='Horsepower and weight').mark_point().encode(
    x='Horsepower:Q', y='Weight_in_lbs:Q', color='Origin:N'
)
mpg_weight




  
  
  
  
  


  
  





hp_weight




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

cars <- read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv') |>
    drop_na(Miles_per_Gallon, Horsepower, Weight_in_lbs, Origin)
mpg_weight <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Miles_per_Gallon, y = Weight_in_lbs, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point() + labs(title = 'Fuel economy and weight')
hp_weight <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Weight_in_lbs, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point() + labs(title = 'Horsepower and weight')
mpg_weight









hp_weight

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
text:
18.3 Arranging panels horizontally and vertically

Side-by-side panels

Altairggplot


Use the pipe operator, |, for horizontal concatenation. Set the dimensions of the individual panels before composing them. Here the two x-axes represent different measurements, but the y-axis represents weight in both panels, so we explicitly share its scale.

mpg_weight = mpg_weight.properties(width=250, height=220)
hp_weight = hp_weight.properties(width=250, height=220)
(mpg_weight | hp_weight).resolve_scale(y='shared')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






patchwork composes ggplot objects with layout operators. As in Altair, | places panels side by side.

mpg_weight | hp_weight








Patchwork aligns panel geometry automatically, but each ggplot retains its own scales. These panels use the same cars and y-variable, so their default y-ranges agree. When data or scale settings differ, specify common limits if direct comparison requires them.





Stacked panels

Altairggplot


Use & for vertical concatenation.

mpg_weight & hp_weight




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Use / to stack panels vertically. This differs from Altair’s & operator.

mpg_weight / hp_weight








In patchwork, & instead applies a setting to every panel. For example, (mpg_weight / hp_weight) & theme(legend.position = 'none') hides both legends.





Overall titles and panel labels

Altairggplot


Parentheses make it clear that properties() applies to the composed figure, not just the second panel.

(mpg_weight | hp_weight).properties(title='Two views of vehicle weight')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




The functions alt.hconcat() and alt.vconcat() are alternatives to | and &. For example, the following also adds an overall title:

alt.hconcat(mpg_weight, hp_weight, title='Two views of vehicle weight')



plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A') adds automatic panel tags A, B, and so on. Use tag_levels = list(c('A', 'B')) to supply an explicit sequence of tags.

(mpg_weight | hp_weight) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A')








The same function adds an overall title to the composed figure. Here we also collect the matching legends into a single guide.

(mpg_weight | hp_weight) +
    plot_layout(guides = 'collect') +
    plot_annotation(
        title = 'Two views of vehicle weight',
        tag_levels = 'A',
        theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = 'bold'))
    )








guides = 'collect' consolidates matching legends. It does not make different color scales equivalent, so check that shared colors retain the same meaning.

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
text:
18.4 Unequal widths and nested layouts
Complementary panels do not always need equal space. A scatterplot may need a wide plotting area, while a categorical count chart can remain readable in a narrower panel.

Altairggplot


A short histogram can show the distribution of fuel economy, and a narrow strip of ticks can show weights within each origin.

mpg_hist = alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Miles_per_Gallon:Q').bin(), y='count()'
).properties(width=250, height=80)
mpg_hist




  
  
  
  
  


  
  





weight_ticks = alt.Chart(cars).mark_tick().encode(
    x='Origin:N', y='Weight_in_lbs:Q', color='Origin:N'
).properties(width=90, height=220)
mpg_weight | weight_ticks




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Combining operators without parentheses may produce a different arrangement than intended. Python evaluates & before |, so this puts the histogram above the scatterplot and then places the tick plot alongside that entire column:

mpg_hist & mpg_weight | weight_ticks




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Parentheses can instead group the scatterplot and ticks into the bottom row:

mpg_hist & (mpg_weight | weight_ticks)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Check which axes should align when arranging marginal distributions. The histogram’s x-variable matches the scatterplot’s x-variable, and the tick plot’s y-variable matches the scatterplot’s y-variable. Sharing a variable does not make every possible arrangement equally easy to read.


First create a count chart of origins. This is a categorical summary of the same cars, rather than a marginal distribution of either scatterplot axis.

origin_count <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Origin)) + geom_bar()
origin_count








An equally wide panel can give a three-category count chart more space than it needs. plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1)) allocates three times as much panel width to the scatterplot. Axes, titles, and legends need additional space, so the full plot widths need not have exactly that ratio.

mpg_weight | origin_count









(mpg_weight | origin_count) + plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1))








Here the scatterplot legend falls between the panels. Reordering them keeps that legend at the outside edge:

(origin_count | mpg_weight) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 3))








We can also nest layouts with parentheses and control the relative heights of rows. This deliberately repeats the count plot to make the layout structure easy to see. Automatic tags continue through the nested panels.

top_row <- origin_count | origin_count
nested_figure <- (top_row / mpg_weight) +
    plot_layout(heights = c(1, 2)) +
    plot_annotation(title = 'Vehicle weight and sample composition', tag_levels = 'A')
nested_figure

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
text:
18.5 Choosing an output format








Format
Useful for
What to consider




PNG
Slides, documents, previews
Raster image: enlarging it reveals pixels; choose sufficient resolution


SVG or PDF
Resizable diagrams and publication figures
Vector output stays sharp, but dense plots can create large files


HTML
Interactive charts
Preserves supported browser interactions; decide whether dependencies and data must work offline


Vega-Lite JSON
Storing or reusing an Altair specification
Describes the chart; needs a compatible renderer to display it



Saving a static image preserves the displayed view, not its tooltips, selections, or controls. Exporting a notebook or book page is also different from saving an individual figure.

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
text:
18.6 Saving static figures
The following save commands are intended to be run when you want to create files; they are not executed automatically while rendering this chapter.

Altairggplot


The filename extension selects the output format. PNG, SVG, and PDF export use vl-convert-python, included in the textbook environment through Altair’s optional dependencies.

mpg_weight.save('mpg_weight.png')
mpg_weight.save('mpg_weight.svg')
mpg_weight.save('mpg_weight.pdf')

scale_factor scales the exported image dimensions. For example, this produces three times as many pixels along each dimension of a PNG:

mpg_weight.save('mpg_weight-hires.png', scale_factor=3)

Altair also offers ppi for specifying PNG pixel density. The chart’s width and height determine its layout; exporting more pixels does not automatically make small labels proportionally larger within the figure.

mpg_weight.save('mpg_weight-print.png', ppi=300)
mpg_weight.save('mpg_weight.json')



ggsave() can save the most recent plot when its plot argument is omitted. Passing the object explicitly avoids accidentally exporting a different plot. Specify physical size and pixel density when preparing a raster image.

ggsave('mpg_weight-r.png', plot = mpg_weight, width = 6, height = 4, units = 'in', dpi = 300)

At six by four inches, 300 dpi produces a 1,800 by 1,200 pixel image. Using 96 dpi at the same size gives fewer pixels, not a higher-resolution image. Vector formats do not use dpi to determine the resolution of their vector elements. SVG export uses the svglite package.

ggsave('mpg_weight-r.pdf', plot = mpg_weight, width = 6, height = 4)
ggsave('mpg_weight-r.svg', plot = mpg_weight, width = 6, height = 4)

The plot argument can also be a composed patchwork figure:

ggsave('vehicle-layout.svg', plot = nested_figure, width = 6, height = 7)

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
section: 18.7 Saving interactive figures, including offline HTML
text:
18.7 Saving interactive figures, including offline HTML

Altair: include both the data and JavaScript
This chart has tooltips and supports panning and zooming. Its data comes from a local dataframe, so Altair embeds the values in the specification.

interactive_cars = mpg_weight.encode(
    tooltip=['Name:N', 'Origin:N', 'Horsepower:Q', 'Miles_per_Gallon:Q']
).interactive()
interactive_cars




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Saving HTML preserves these client-side interactions: the recipient does not need a running Python process or Jupyter session. However, the default HTML export loads JavaScript libraries from an online CDN.

interactive_cars.save('cars-interactive.html')

For an HTML file that can be opened without an internet connection, use inline=True. It bundles the JavaScript dependencies into the file, making it larger but self-contained for this dataframe-based example.

interactive_cars.save('cars-interactive-offline.html', inline=True)

inline=True bundles the rendering libraries; it does not automatically download arbitrary externally referenced datasets, map tiles, or images. For example, a chart built with a data URL may still need the network to retrieve its data. Load the data into a dataframe before constructing the chart, as we do here, and check the exported file with the network disabled.
You can send the resulting HTML file as an attachment or host it on a static website such as GitHub Pages. Naming it index.html makes it the usual landing page for its directory. The lecture’s Altair demos provide examples of this kind of sharing. For integration into a larger report, interactive_cars.to_html(inline=True) returns the HTML as a string instead of writing a file.


R: save the HTML widget
Wrapping a ggplot in plotly::ggplotly() creates an interactive HTML widget. This preview has hover details, zooming, and a clickable legend; we will explore those interactions in Chapter 19.

interactive_cars_r <- plotly::ggplotly(mpg_weight)
interactive_cars_r





Use htmlwidgets::saveWidget() to preserve the widget’s interactivity.

htmlwidgets::saveWidget(interactive_cars_r, 'cars-interactive-r.html', selfcontained = TRUE)

selfcontained = TRUE bundles local widget dependencies into one HTML file, using Pandoc. It is suitable for this chart, whose data is included in the widget. As with Altair, externally requested resources such as online map tiles still need their own offline solution. For a multi-file export, use selfcontained = FALSE and distribute the accompanying dependency directory together with the HTML.
An HTML page containing widgets plus other elements, such as headings or filter controls, is a container rather than one HTML widget. Save the container with htmltools::save_html(), then bundle its local dependencies with rmarkdown::pandoc_self_contained_html():

widget_page <- htmltools::tagList(
    htmltools::tags$head(htmltools::tags$title('Vehicle explorer')),
    htmltools::h2('Vehicle explorer'), interactive_cars_r
)
htmltools::save_html(widget_page, 'vehicle-page.html', libdir = 'vehicle-page_files')
rmarkdown::pandoc_self_contained_html('vehicle-page.html', 'vehicle-page-offline.html')

The final file includes the local widget dependencies; the intermediate HTML and dependency directory are useful if you prefer a multi-file website. This is the same workflow we will use for a page of linked plots and controls in Chapter 19.

title: 18  Figure composition and saving
section: 18.8 Notebook display formats and static previews
text:
18.8 Notebook display formats and static previews
A notebook can store several representations of one output, such as a Vega-Lite specification, HTML, and a PNG. The viewer chooses which representation it can display. GitHub’s notebook viewer does not run arbitrary interactive JavaScript, so a chart that works in JupyterLab may need a static fallback there.
In a compatible Jupyter frontend, Altair’s MIME renderer supplies a Vega-Lite representation that the frontend can render and may save with a PNG fallback:

alt.renderers.enable('mimetype')

Run the plotting cells again and save the notebook so the outputs are stored. The frontend must support the chart’s Vega-Lite version; the Python MIME bundle alone does not guarantee that a PNG has been stored. For an explicitly static notebook output, use the PNG renderer instead:

alt.renderers.enable('png')
mpg_weight

Return to interactive HTML display with alt.renderers.enable('default'). A PNG fallback is a static preview; sharing the HTML export preserves interactive exploration. Notebook display settings and exported-file formats are separate choices.
