title: 19  Interactivity
text:
19.1 Why bother?
An interactive figure lets readers ask questions that a static view cannot answer all at once. They might examine a particular region, inspect an observation, compare selected groups, or change which variable is displayed. Interactivity can help us explore data ourselves and let others explore a figure without writing code.

title: 19  Interactivity
text:
19.2 Navigating views

Panning and zooming
Panning and zooming is useful changes the viewing window or the state we are examining. This is useful when there is additional detail that cannot be seen in a chart’s initial view, but might be of interest to the reader. While it would be possible to present a single static zoomed in view of the chart, it would quickly become unwieldley to show multiple zoom levels in separate panels.
This basic type of interaction also illustrates a key features of interactivity, it enables the audience of the visualization to activiley explore the data an ask questions of their own; including questions that the chart creator might not have thought of including in a static chart.

Altairggplot


Altair extends the concepts of a grammar of graphics to a grammar of interactivity, where interactive elements are composed together in a predictable manner. We could have built up the panning and zooming through fundamental interactive building blocks, but since it is such a common operation, we can use the method .interactive() as a shortcut that binds an interval selection to the position scales. Scroll over the plot to zoom and drag to pan; double-click to reset.

import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

cars = pd.read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv')
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower:Q', y='Miles_per_Gallon:Q'
).interactive()




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






ggplot does not have interactivity built-in to the library, so we will need to use a few different libraries to be add interactive features to it. Plotly provides the ggplotly convenience function which convert a ggplot figure to a plotly figure and adds basic interactive features to it. It would be sufficient to just use the ggplotly function and its toolbar to access most functionality, but here we show how to enable zooming and panning by default without having to click in the panel. You will also notice that there is a tooltip enabled by default, more on that later. Click the little house icon in the toolbar to reset the axes.

library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

cars <- readr::read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv')
car_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon)) +
    geom_point()

ggplotly(car_plot) |>
    layout(dragmode = 'pan') |>
    config(scrollZoom = TRUE)





Note that while plotly provides many useful interactive feature to ggplot its API does not aim to implement a grammar of interactivity, but follows a more traditional design approach, so the code we learn here will look slightly different from the ggplot code we have used so far.





Overview and detail
Another helpful interaction tool it to use one chart as a navigation overview for another chart that displays more detail. The example below shows how a time series can be examples below use the same S&P 500 time series. Drag an x-interval in the lower overview to set the upper panel’s scale domain.

Altairggplot


We are using the layout operators from Chapter 18 to compose a view of the navigation overview togeher with the more detailed chart. Here we first define a selection and add it to the chart. You can click and drag in the chart (also called “brushing”) to create the selection rectangle (a “brush”), but it is not yet linked to any functionality. encodings=['x'] means that our brush is only selecting on the x-axis (i.e. the height of the brush is constant).

sp500 = pd.read_csv('data/vega-sp500.csv', parse_dates=['date'])

overview = alt.Chart(sp500, height=50).mark_area().encode(x='date', y='price')
brush = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])
overview.add_params(brush)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




To make another chart respond based on the selection we make with the brush, we set the domain of our detailed chart’s scale to the brush’s endpoints. Now brushing in the lower overview chart will change the scale min and max of the detailed upper chart:

details = alt.Chart(sp500, height=120).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('date').scale(domain=brush),
    y='price'
)
details & overview.add_params(brush)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Not that we can also scroll when hovering over the brush to expand and shrink the selection.


Due to the lack of a grammar of interactivity, we cannot reuse what we learned in Chapter 18 to compose together the navigation overview and the detailed chart. Instead, plotly has a function named rangeslider() that supplies an overview with draggable handles used to create a selection (also called a “brush”). hovermode = 'x' means that our brush is only selecting on the x-axis (i.e. the height of the brush is constant).

sp500 <- readr::read_csv('data/vega-sp500.csv')

sp500_plot <- ggplot(sp500, aes(x = date, y = price)) + geom_area()
ggplotly(sp500_plot, dynamicTicks=TRUE) |>
    rangeslider() |>
    layout(hovermode = 'x')

title: 19  Interactivity
text:
19.3 Tooltips
Tooltips is an effective way to supply additional information when a data point is hovered. This can prevent overlaoding a visualization with text labels while still providing these details on demand when a reader asks for them.

Altairggplot


Enabling the tooltip of a mark, includes all mapped encodings in the text that pops up when hovering a point in the chart.

alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle(tooltip=True).encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Modifying the tooltip involves passing a dataframe column to the tooltip encoding channel instead.

alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
    tooltip='Name'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




In contrast to most other encoding channels, a tooltip can contain multiple fields, passed as a list.

alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
    tooltip=['Name', 'Origin']
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




The Altair documentation also has examples of how to show images in the tooltip.


By default, the tooltip includes all mapped aesthetics in the text that pops up when hovering a point in the chart.

car_tooltip_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(car_tooltip_plot)





ggplotly() uses the text aesthetic from ggplot for custom tooltip content, so we must first map a dataframe column to text in ggplot

car_tooltip_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(
    x = Horsepower,
    y = Miles_per_Gallon,
    color = Origin,
    text = Name
)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(car_tooltip_plot, tooltip = 'text')





Including multiple fields involves manually pasting together columns with newlines in ggplot.

car_tooltip_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(
    x = Horsepower,
    y = Miles_per_Gallon,
    color = Origin,
    text = paste(Name, Origin, sep = '<br>')
)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(car_tooltip_plot, tooltip = 'text')

title: 19  Interactivity
text:
19.4 Creating and responding to selections
A selection identifies observations of interest in a chart, and can then trigger an effect such as highlighting or filtering of that data. We already saw how to set up a chart’s scale domain to respond to a selections range, and here we will see a few other ways to respond to selections as well.

Highlighting observations
Highlighting observations means that all data is retained in the chart but the visual styling of the selected observations differ from that of the unselected ones.

Altairggplot


Let’s start by creating an empty brush again. Drag’n drop to see the brush selection rectangle.

brush = alt.selection_interval()
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin'
).add_params(brush)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




To add a response to the condition, we can define a condition via alt.when(test).then(if_true).otherwise(if_false), where the “test” condition would be if the brush is over a point or not. In the example below, we let the selected cars retain their origin colors while other cars become light gray. Note that empty selections match all observations by default.

brush = alt.selection_interval()
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.when(brush).then('Origin').otherwise(alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Plotly supports rectangular and lasso selections through its toolbar. highlight_key() assigns a stable key to each car; highlight() specifies how selected observations should be emphasized. The original observations remain visible.

cars <- cars |> mutate(car_id = dplyr::row_number())
highlight_cars <- highlight_key(cars, ~car_id, group = 'single-car-highlight')
highlight_plot <- ggplot(highlight_cars,
                        aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin, text = Name)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(highlight_plot, tooltip = 'text') |>
    layout(dragmode = 'select') |>
    highlight(on = 'plotly_selected', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.15)









Click and hover selections
A point selection chooses discrete items or values rather than a continuous interval. Here we select origins by interacting with bars representing their counts.

Altairggplot


Click a bar; Shift-click to select several origins.

click = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'])
alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.when(click).then(alt.value(0.9)).otherwise(alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(click)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Changing the event to mouseover lets hovering drive the selection instead. toggle=False keeps one hovered origin selected at a time.

hover = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'], on='mouseover', toggle=False)
alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.when(hover).then(alt.value(0.9)).otherwise(alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(hover)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






In Plotly, the on event makes the same distinction between click and hover. These bars use the same origin counts as the Altair examples.

origin_keys <- cars |> dplyr::count(Origin) |>
    highlight_key(~Origin, group = 'origin-count-selection')
origin_bars <- plot_ly(origin_keys, x = ~n, y = ~Origin, color = ~Origin,
                       type = 'bar', orientation = 'h')
origin_bars |> highlight(on = 'plotly_click', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.2)






hover_keys <- cars |> dplyr::count(Origin) |>
    highlight_key(~Origin, group = 'origin-count-hover')
plot_ly(hover_keys, x = ~n, y = ~Origin, color = ~Origin, type = 'bar', orientation = 'h') |>
    highlight(on = 'plotly_hover', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.2)











Coordinating selected observations across views
Referencing the same selection in several views lets us compare the selected observations across different encodings. This is linked brushing. It is one use of coordination; the earlier overview/detail example instead coordinated scale domains.

Linked scatterplots

Altairggplot


The first view shows fuel economy and the second weight, both against horsepower. Brush either view and inspect those cars in the other.

brush = alt.selection_interval()
linked_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.when(brush).then('Origin').otherwise(alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs:Q')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Both ggplots use the same highlight_key() object, so their car identifiers link the marks. Use the selection tool in either panel. This widget will also serve as an example of a self-contained R dashboard to export later in the section.

linked_cars <- highlight_key(cars, ~car_id, group = 'linked-car-views')
linked_plot <- ggplot(linked_cars,
                      aes(Horsepower, Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin, text = Name)) + geom_point()
linked_mpg <- ggplotly(linked_plot, tooltip = 'text')
linked_weight <- ggplotly(linked_plot + aes(y = Weight_in_lbs), tooltip = 'text') |>
    style(showlegend = FALSE)
car_dashboard <- subplot(linked_mpg, linked_weight, shareX = TRUE, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |>
    layout(dragmode = 'select') |>
    highlight(on = 'plotly_selected', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.15)
car_dashboard










Combining selections
Altair’s default resolve='global' maintains one brush: drawing in the other panel replaces it. With resolve='union', each panel can retain its brush and observations selected in either view are highlighted.

brush = alt.selection_interval(resolve='union')
linked_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.when(brush).then('Origin').otherwise(alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




With resolve='intersect', observations must satisfy all participating brushes. These are specific Altair selection-resolution options; the R example above uses one shared selection rather than implementing these per-view combinations.

brush = alt.selection_interval(resolve='intersect')
linked_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.when(brush).then('Origin').otherwise(alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Linking views with different encodings
Linking is based on data values or identifiers, not a requirement that both charts use the same visual channels. An origin selected in a bar chart can also identify cars in a scatterplot.

Altairggplot



brush = alt.selection_interval()
click = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'])
selected_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.when(brush).then('Origin').otherwise(alt.value('lightgray')),
    opacity=alt.when(click).then(alt.value(0.9)).otherwise(alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars, height=80).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.when(click).then(alt.value(0.9)).otherwise(alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(click)
selected_points & bars




  
  
  
  
  


  
  


























These panels show the same cars and origin counts. Suppress duplicate legend entries in the bars and toggle matching legend groups together. This coordinates trace visibility; it does not turn the precomputed ggplot counts into a statistic that responds to arbitrary point selections.

count_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(y = Origin, fill = Origin)) + geom_bar(width = 0.6)
count_widget <- ggplotly(count_plot) |> style(showlegend = FALSE)
car_legend_plot <- car_plot + aes(color = Origin)
car_legend_widget <- ggplotly(car_legend_plot, tooltip = 'text')
subplot(count_widget, car_legend_widget, widths = c(0.3, 0.7), titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |>
    layout(legend = list(groupclick = 'togglegroup'))











Filtering observations
Highlighting changes the visual emphasis without changing the observations used in the view. Filtering restricts which observations enter a layer or calculation. We introduce this distinction before the controls, because the same control can drive either effect.
An interactive query can change not just which marks appear, but the values being summarized. The summary must be calculated from the filtered observations in the browser.

Altairggplot


The brush filters the bar chart’s input before counting, so the bars show the number of selected cars in each origin. The legend still controls only opacity.

brush = alt.selection_interval()
selected_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.when(brush).then('Origin:N').otherwise(alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars, height=80).transform_filter(brush).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N'
)
selected_points & bars




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






For this R example we use a horsepower filter to drive both views. Plotly’s native histogram trace counts the filtered rows in the browser. This differs from converting a ggplot bar chart whose counts were already calculated in R.

count_cars <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(cars, key = ~as.character(car_id), group = 'car-filter-counts')
count_scatter <- plot_ly(count_cars, x = ~Horsepower, y = ~Miles_per_Gallon,
                         color = ~Origin, text = ~Name, type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers')
dynamic_counts <- plot_ly(count_cars, y = ~Origin, color = ~Origin, type = 'histogram',
                          showlegend = FALSE)
htmltools::tagList(
    crosstalk::filter_slider('car-count-hp-filter', 'Horsepower range', count_cars, ~Horsepower, step = 5),
    subplot(count_scatter, dynamic_counts, nrows = 2, heights = c(0.75, 0.25), titleX = TRUE)
)


Horsepower range












Driving selections from legends
A legend can be used instead of another chart as the input element that drives the selection.

Altairggplot


Click a legend entry, or Shift-click several, to highlight origins. In this example, we bind the legend to an opacity condition, but it could also have been used to filter the data.

legend = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'], bind='legend')

alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
    opacity=alt.when(legend).then(alt.value(0.9)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(legend)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Plotly legends are interactive by default. Clicking an entry highlights that group and make the other points invisible.

car_legend_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(car_legend_plot)










Driving selections from widgets
Widgets are another type of input mechanisms that can drive a selection. A dropdown, radio button, slider, legend, or plotted mark can define a selection; and then the chart can respond with highlighting or filtering observations, just like with non-widget selections.

Movie data for category and numeric controls
We use the full Vega movies snapshot here, rather than the smaller distribution-example dataset. Both languages apply the same missing-value filters and create a unique row identifier. The snapshot contains suspicious future release dates for some historical films; inspecting a year control can expose this issue, but changing axis formatting cannot correct it.

Altairggplot



movies = (
    pd.read_csv('data/vega-movies-interactivity.csv', parse_dates=['Release_Date'])
    .drop(columns=['US_DVD_Sales', 'Director', 'Source', 'Creative_Type'])
    .assign(Release_Year=lambda df: df['Release_Date'].dt.year,
            Title=lambda df: df['Title'].fillna('Untitled').astype(str))
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
movies['movie_id'] = movies.index + 1
movie_points = alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating:Q', y='IMDB_Rating:Q', tooltip='Title:N'
)
movies.head()

1      First Love, Last Rites    10876.0  ...          1998         2

3        Let's Talk About Sex   373615.0  ...          1998         4
4                        Slam  1009819.0  ...          1998         5

[5 rows x 14 columns]



movies.info()

RangeIndex: 3201 entries, 0 to 3200
Data columns (total 14 columns):

---  ------                  --------------  -----

 5   MPAA_Rating             2596 non-null   str

 8   Major_Genre             2926 non-null   str

 10  IMDB_Rating             2988 non-null   float64       
 11  IMDB_Votes              2988 non-null   float64

movies <- readr::read_csv('data/vega-movies-interactivity.csv') |>
    dplyr::select(-c(US_DVD_Sales, Director, Source, Creative_Type)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(Release_Year = lubridate::year(Release_Date),
          # Title = replace_na(Title, 'Untitled'),
           movie_id = dplyr::row_number())

Dropdowns, radio buttons, and initial states

Altairggplot


A legend selection works for genres too, but many genre colors make the view busy.

select_genre = alt.selection_point(fields=['Major_Genre'], bind='legend')
movie_points.encode(
    color='Major_Genre:N', opacity=alt.when(select_genre).then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




A dropdown can select a genre without assigning a color to every category.

genres = sorted(movies['Major_Genre'].dropna().unique())
dropdown = alt.binding_select(name='Genre: ',options=genres)
select_genre = alt.selection_point(fields=['Major_Genre'], bind=dropdown)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.when(select_genre).then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Give the control a readable label and specify an initial value to make the starting state explicit.

select_genre = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Major_Genre'],
    bind=alt.binding_select(name='Genre: ', options=genres),
    value=[{'Major_Genre': 'Comedy'}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.when(select_genre).then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Bind different fields of a selection to different controls. Here a film must match both the chosen genre and rating. The age ratings use their conceptual order rather than alphabetical order.

mpaa_ratings = ['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R', 'Not Rated']
select_genre_and_mpaa = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Major_Genre', 'MPAA_Rating'],
    bind={
        'Major_Genre': alt.binding_select(name='Genre: ', options=genres),
        'MPAA_Rating': alt.binding_radio(name='MPAA rating: ', options=mpaa_ratings)
    },
    value=[{'Major_Genre': 'Comedy', 'MPAA_Rating': 'PG-13'}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.when(select_genre_and_mpaa).then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre_and_mpaa)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






These Crosstalk dropdowns operate on the same movies and fields. They start with all movies and filter the points; the Altair examples above instead highlight matches. Choose a genre and rating to see the difference in response. Using a new shared-data group keeps this example independent of other widgets on the page.

movie_categories <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(movies, key = ~as.character(movie_id), group = 'movie-category-controls')
movie_category_plot <- ggplot(movie_categories,
                             aes(Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, IMDB_Rating, text = Title)) + geom_point()
category_controls <- crosstalk::bscols(
    crosstalk::filter_select('movie-genre-filter', 'Genre', movie_categories, ~Major_Genre, multiple = FALSE),
    crosstalk::filter_select('movie-rating-filter', 'MPAA rating', movie_categories, ~MPAA_Rating, multiple = FALSE),
    widths = c(6, 6)
)
htmltools::tagList(category_controls, ggplotly(movie_category_plot, tooltip = 'text'))





Genre








MPAA rating

















Sliders: equality, thresholds, and ranges

Altair


A point selection bound to a slider matches an exact value.

select_rating = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating'],
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer: ', min=0, max=100, step=1),
    value=[{'Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating': 50}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.when(select_rating).then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_rating)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




For a threshold, a scalar parameter is simpler. alt.datum refers to a field of the current observation inside an expression.

rating_cutoff = alt.param(
    value=50,
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer below: ', min=0, max=100, step=1)
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.when(alt.datum.Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating < rating_cutoff)
        .then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(rating_cutoff)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Range, step, and initial value are separate choices.

rating_cutoff = alt.param(
    value=15,
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer below: ', min=10, max=60, step=5)
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.when(alt.datum.Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating < rating_cutoff)
        .then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(rating_cutoff)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







The same pattern can select movies released before a chosen year. This highlights matches rather than removing the remaining movies.


Moving through time
We can use filtering to navigate through a sequence of data states. Both examples use the same local Gapminder snapshot: country fertility, life expectancy, and population from 1955 to 2005. A year control chooses the observations to display; the x- and y-scales remain fixed so that frame changes are comparable.

Altairggplot


A scalar parameter stores the chosen year. This example lets the reader scrub through the frames with a slider rather than playing them automatically.

gap = pd.read_csv('data/vega-gapminder.csv')
frame_year = alt.param(
    value=int(gap['year'].min()),
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Year: ', min=int(gap['year'].min()),
                           max=int(gap['year'].max()), step=5)
)
alt.Chart(gap).transform_filter(alt.datum.year == frame_year).mark_circle(opacity=0.7).encode(
    x=alt.X('fertility:Q').scale(domain=[0, 9]).title('Children per woman'),
    y=alt.Y('life_expect:Q').scale(domain=[20, 90]).title('Life expectancy (years)'),
    size=alt.Size('pop:Q').scale(domain=[0, float(gap['pop'].max())], range=[10, 600]).title('Population'),
    tooltip=['country:N', 'year:O', 'fertility:Q', 'life_expect:Q']
).add_params(frame_year)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Plotly interprets frame as the frame variable and ids as the identity to track between frames. Use Play or choose a year on its slider.















frame and ids are Plotly extensions, not ordinary static ggplot aesthetics. Playback emphasizes movement; choosing a frame lets the reader stop and inspect it. For comparing several years at once, small multiples may be easier than relying on memory.
A range control selects both endpoints. Here it filters the same movie ratings, illustrating another response to a numeric selection.

movie_ratings <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(movies, key = ~as.character(movie_id), group = 'movie-rating-range')
movie_rating_plot <- ggplot(movie_ratings,
                           aes(Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, IMDB_Rating, text = Title)) + geom_point()
htmltools::tagList(
    crosstalk::filter_slider('movie-rating-range-filter', 'Tomatometer range',
                            movie_ratings, ~Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, step = 1),
    ggplotly(movie_rating_plot, tooltip = 'text')
)


Tomatometer range












Building a search widget

Altairggplot



search_input = alt.param(
    value='',
    bind=alt.binding(
        input='search',
        placeholder="Car model",
        name='Search ',
    )
)
search_matches = alt.expr.test(alt.expr.regexp(search_input, "i"), alt.datum.Name)

alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    tooltip='Name',
    opacity=alt.when(search_matches).then(alt.value(.9)).otherwise(alt.value(0.05)),
).add_params(search_input)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







searchable_cars <- highlight_key(cars, ~Name)

p <- ggplot(
    searchable_cars,
    aes(Horsepower, Miles_per_Gallon, text = Name)
) +
    geom_point()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = 'text') |>
    highlight(selectize = TRUE, opacityDim = 0.05)














Deep-diveDeep dive: A widget or a chart?






We could design charts as more small, more informative widgets by removing elements from the charts and styling them accordingly.

Altairggplot


The multidimensional legend encodes genre and rating by position, and their count by size. The year and runtime plots provide additional brushes. A movie must satisfy all three selection predicates to be highlighted. & between predicates means AND; between charts it means vertical composition.

movies_fewer_years = movies.query('1994 < Release_Year < 2030') 
top_genres = movies_fewer_years['Major_Genre'].value_counts().head(5).index
movies_clean = movies_fewer_years.query(
    "Major_Genre in @top_genres and MPAA_Rating in ['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R']"
)
select_categories = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Major_Genre', 'MPAA_Rating'], nearest=True
)
select_year = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])
select_runtime = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])
category_legend = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Genre and rating').mark_circle().encode(
    x=alt.X('MPAA_Rating:N').sort(['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R']).title(''),
    y=alt.Y('Major_Genre:N').title('').axis(orient='right'),
    size=alt.Size('count()').legend(None), color=alt.Color('Major_Genre:N').legend(None),
    opacity=alt.when(select_categories).then(alt.value(1)).otherwise(alt.value(0.2))
).properties(width=130, height=140).add_params(select_categories)
year_control = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Production year').mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('year(Release_Date):T').title('').axis(grid=False), y=alt.Y('count()').title('').axis(None)
).properties(width=130, height=35).add_params(select_year)
runtime_control = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Running time').mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running_Time_min:Q').title('').axis(grid=False), y=alt.Y('count()').title('').axis(None)
).properties(width=130, height=35).add_params(select_runtime)
scatter = alt.Chart(movies_clean).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating:Q', y='IMDB_Rating:Q', color=alt.Color('Major_Genre:N').legend(None),
    tooltip='Title:N',
    opacity=alt.when(select_categories & select_year & select_runtime)
        .then(alt.value(0.7)).otherwise(alt.value(0.1))
).properties(width=300, height=300)
movie_dashboard = (scatter | (year_control & runtime_control & category_legend)).configure_view(stroke=None)
movie_dashboard.properties(usermeta={'embedOptions': {'renderer': 'canvas'}})




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Empty selections match all movies. Double-click a brush to clear it, or Shift-click category combinations to retain several. The controls summarize the fixed subset; they do not recompute each other’s distributions.


This same idea is not possible to express in plotly, but crosstalk can combine standard controls over the same fields and movies. Here the controls filter the plot rather than fading nonmatching points. All active conditions must be satisfied.

movies_fewer_years <- movies |> dplyr::filter(Release_Year > 1994, Release_Year < 2030)
top_genres <- movies_fewer_years |> dplyr::count(Major_Genre, sort = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |> dplyr::pull(Major_Genre)
movies_clean <- movies_fewer_years |>
    filter(Major_Genre %in% top_genres, MPAA_Rating %in% c('G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R'))
explorer_movies <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(movies_clean, key = ~as.character(movie_id), group = 'movie-explorer')
movie_controls <- htmltools::tagList(
    crosstalk::bscols(
        crosstalk::filter_select('explorer-genre', 'Genre', explorer_movies, ~Major_Genre),
        crosstalk::filter_select('explorer-rating', 'MPAA rating', explorer_movies, ~MPAA_Rating),
        widths = c(6, 6)
    ),
    crosstalk::bscols(
        crosstalk::filter_slider('explorer-year', 'Release year', explorer_movies, ~Release_Year, step = 1),
        crosstalk::filter_slider('explorer-runtime', 'Runtime (minutes)', explorer_movies, ~Running_Time_min, step = 5),
        widths = c(6, 6)
    )
)
explorer_plot <- ggplot(explorer_movies,
                        aes(Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, IMDB_Rating, text = Title)) + geom_point()
movie_explorer <- htmltools::tagList(movie_controls, ggplotly(explorer_plot, tooltip = 'text'))
movie_explorer





Genre








MPAA rating












Release year






Runtime (minutes)

title: 19  Interactivity
text:
19.5 Changing encodings and parameters
Interactivity can also change the question or representation rather than select observations. Choosing a genre asks which movies to emphasize; choosing a y-variable asks which measurement to display. The same dropdown mechanism can implement either task.

Choosing the displayed variable
Both examples return to the same cars and let us choose fuel economy, weight, or acceleration time as the response to horsepower.

Altairggplot


A parameter stores the chosen column name, and a calculated field retrieves that column’s value for each car. The observations remain the same.

measurement = alt.param(
    value='Miles_per_Gallon',
    name='car_measurement',
    bind=alt.binding_select(name='Y variable: ', options=['Miles_per_Gallon', 'Weight_in_lbs', 'Acceleration'])
)
alt.Chart(cars).transform_calculate(measurement='datum[car_measurement]').mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower', y=alt.Y('measurement:Q').title('Selected measurement'),
    color='Origin:N', tooltip=['Name', 'Origin', 'measurement:Q']
).add_params(measurement).properties(
    title=alt.TitleParams(text=alt.ExprRef(expr="'Horsepower versus ' + car_measurement"))
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Plotly can switch among prepared traces. We prepare three measurements for each origin, then choose which traces are visible. The metadata identifies the measurement of every trace, so the visibility mask covers all nine traces rather than assuming one trace per variable.

metrics <- c('Miles_per_Gallon', 'Weight_in_lbs', 'Acceleration')
metric_plot <- plot_ly(cars, x = ~Horsepower, color = ~Origin, text = ~Name)
for (metric in metrics) {
    metric_plot <- add_trace(
        metric_plot, y = cars[[metric]], type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers',
        meta = metric, visible = metric == 'Miles_per_Gallon'
    )
}
metric_plot <- plotly_build(metric_plot)
trace_metrics <- vapply(metric_plot$x$data, function(trace) unique(trace$meta), character(1))
buttons <- lapply(metrics, function(metric) list(
    method = 'update', label = metric,
    args = list(list(visible = trace_metrics == metric), list(yaxis = list(title = metric)))
))
layout(metric_plot,
       updatemenus = list(list(type = 'dropdown', active = 0, buttons = buttons)),
       yaxis = list(title = 'Miles_per_Gallon'), legend = list(title = list(text = 'Origin')))










Changing a calculation or display parameter
We have already used this kind of interaction in earlier chapters: changing histogram bin width, changing a candidate line’s slope in Chapter 16, and changing the confidence level or interval multiplier in Chapter 17. Those controls change a calculation or representation, not which observed cases are of interest.
Before adding a control, ask what it should change: the viewing window, the selection, the observations entering a calculation, the encoding, or the calculation’s parameters. Then choose a gesture or widget that makes that effect understandable. Keep reset behavior and the current state clear so readers can tell what they are looking at.

title: 19  Interactivity
text:
19.6 Saving and sharing interactive visualizations
All the examples in this chapter run client-side, in the browser. That means that they don’t require a server that keeps running in the background and the examples work after the Python or R session that created them has ended. This also means that we can share them without someone else without the need for that person to know how to use R or Python. We will use the composition and self-contained HTML export techniques from Chapter 18 to assemble and share them as offline explorers.

Altairggplot



movie_dashboard.save('movie-explorer-offline.html', inline=True)



Save the linked Plotly widget directly, or save and bundle the HTML container that includes the movie filters as well as the plot.

htmlwidgets::saveWidget(car_dashboard, 'car-dashboard-offline.html', selfcontained = TRUE)
movie_page <- htmltools::tagList(
    htmltools::tags$head(htmltools::tags$title('Movie explorer')), movie_explorer
)
htmltools::save_html(movie_page, 'movie-explorer.html', libdir = 'movie-explorer_files')
rmarkdown::pandoc_self_contained_html('movie-explorer.html', 'movie-explorer-offline-r.html')

title: 20  Geospatial
text:
20.1 Why bother?
A map makes geographic patterns visible: where observations occur, which regions are similar, and how nearby places differ. But geographic position also constrains the layout. A small region can be almost invisible even when its population or contribution to a total is large. Choosing the boundaries, projection, and visual encodings is therefore part of answering the question, not just decorating a chart.
We will combine the layout techniques from Chapter 18 with the selections and linked views from Chapter 19. The examples use local snapshots of the lecture’s data; their dates and sources are documented in the data notes.

title: 20  Geospatial
text:
20.2 GeoJSON: geometry alongside attributes
So far, most of our datasets have been tables of rows and columns. To represent country boundaries, flight paths, or subway lines, we also need geometries. GeoJSON stores these geographic features in JSON.
A Feature has a geometry and a set of properties. For example, the following deliberately simplified rectangle approximates Colorado’s outline:
{
  "type": "Feature",
  "properties": {"name": "Colorado"},
  "geometry": {
    "type": "Polygon",
    "coordinates": [
      [[-109.05, 37.00], [-109.05, 41.00], [-102.05, 41.00],
       [-102.05, 37.00], [-109.05, 37.00]]
    ]
  }
}
Coordinates are ordered longitude, latitude, in degrees. A polygon ring closes by repeating its first coordinate. A MultiPolygon can represent a country with islands, while points and lines represent locations and routes. A FeatureCollection groups multiple features into one dataset.
The properties can contain anything we might otherwise put in a table: a name, identifier, population, or link. We do not need to write the coordinates ourselves, but recognizing this structure helps us inspect a downloaded file. See Tom MacWright’s GeoJSON primer for more detail.

Finding boundaries and choosing detail
Natural Earth provides geographic data at several scales:

Cultural data includes countries, administrative regions, and populated places.
Physical data includes coastlines, rivers, and lakes.
Admin 0 represents countries; Admin 1 represents states and provinces.
1:110 million is useful for an overview of the world. 1:50 million and 1:10 million provide more detail for regional maps.

Here, m means million in the map scale, not meters of positional accuracy. More detail means larger files and slower drawing. Zooming into an overview map does not recover coastline detail that was omitted from its data.
Natural Earth’s download archives contain shapefiles, rather than GeoJSON. GeoPandas can read both formats. These are direct download URLs for the two archives used to prepare our local GeoJSON files:
https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/110m/cultural/ne_110m_admin_0_countries.zip
https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/50m/cultural/ne_50m_admin_1_states_provinces.zip
If a website’s download button uses a redirect, the browser’s Network tab can help identify the actual file URL. For detailed local work, also look for data from the relevant national or regional mapping agency.

title: 20  Geospatial
text:
20.3 Working with geographic data
Both language versions use the same local GeoJSON boundaries and statistical tables. Python keeps attributes and geometry in a GeoDataFrame. In R, we read the GeoJSON as a list and extract its properties into a table for Plotly.

Altairggplot


GeoPandas extends pandas with geometry types and spatial operations. read_file() reads a local file or a supported URL, including zipped shapefiles. Here we use a local snapshot, so rendering does not require downloading boundaries.

import altair as alt
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd

world_countries = gpd.read_file('data/geospatial-world-countries.geojson')
world_countries.head()

                       NAME  ...                                           geometry
0                      Fiji  ...  MULTIPOLYGON (((180 -16.06713, 180 -16.55522, ...
1                  Tanzania  ...  POLYGON ((33.90371 -0.95, 34.07262 -1.05982, 3...
2                 W. Sahara  ...  POLYGON ((-8.66559 27.65643, -8.66512 27.58948...
3                    Canada  ...  MULTIPOLYGON (((-122.84 49, -122.97421 49.0025...
4  United States of America  ...  MULTIPOLYGON (((-122.84 49, -120 49, -117.0312...

[5 rows x 10 columns]


The geometry column contains the country outlines. The local file keeps a subset of Natural Earth’s attributes. We lowercase their names, calculate an approximate GDP per person, and remove Antarctica for the following comparisons. GDP_MD is GDP in millions of US dollars, so we multiply by one million before dividing by population.

world_countries = world_countries.rename(
    columns=lambda name: name.lower()
).assign(
    gdp_per_capita=lambda frame: frame['gdp_md'] * 1e6 / frame['pop_est']
).query('continent != "Antarctica"')
world_countries[['name', 'continent', 'pop_est', 'pop_year', 'gdp_year']].head()

                       name      continent      pop_est  pop_year  gdp_year
0                      Fiji        Oceania     889953.0      2019      2019
1                  Tanzania         Africa   58005463.0      2019      2019
2                 W. Sahara         Africa     603253.0      2017      2007
3                    Canada  North America   37589262.0      2019      2019
4  United States of America  North America  328239523.0      2019      2019


These attributes are historical estimates, not current statistics. Their reference years can differ; inspect pop_year and gdp_year before making a substantive comparison.

Quick static and interactive views
GeoPandas has a convenient plot() method for an initial look at the geometries.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

world_countries.plot(figsize=(9, 4))
plt.show()








Its explore() method creates a Leaflet map with panning, zooming, and tooltips. This uses Folium, Matplotlib, and mapclassify, which are included in the textbook’s Python environment. The OpenStreetMap background tiles require a network connection.

world_countries.explore(
    tiles='OpenStreetMap',
    tooltip=['name', 'continent'],
    popup=False,
    height=400
)

Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


Zoom in and compare the background tiles with the country outlines. The tiles can show finer detail than our 1:110 million boundaries. Changing the zoom level changes the view; it does not change the resolution of the overlaid polygons.



For interactive geographic marks in R, we use Plotly. jsonlite::read_json() reads the feature collection, and map_dfr() combines the properties into a table. The geometry remains in world_geojson; the country names will connect it to the table when we draw a map.

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

world_geojson <- jsonlite::read_json('data/geospatial-world-countries.geojson')
world_countries <- map_dfr(world_geojson$features, 'properties')
head(world_countries)

Use the same attributes, normalization, and Antarctica filter as in Python:

world_countries <- world_countries |>
    rename_with(tolower) |>
    mutate(gdp_per_capita = gdp_md * 1e6 / pop_est) |>
    dplyr::filter(continent != 'Antarctica')

title: 20  Geospatial
text:
20.4 Drawing geographic marks

Altairggplot


Altair accepts a GeoDataFrame directly. mark_geoshape() draws its geometries, and the usual encoding channels map attributes to color, tooltips, and so on.

alt.Chart(world_countries, width=550).mark_geoshape()




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Plotly’s choropleth trace draws filled regions. locations supplies a key from the table, and featureidkey identifies the matching property in the GeoJSON. The constant z value gives all matched countries the same fill.

world_map <- plot_ly(
    world_countries, type = 'choropleth', geojson = world_geojson,
    featureidkey = 'properties.NAME', locations = ~name,
    z = rep(1, nrow(world_countries)), text = ~name,
    colorscale = list(c(0, 'lightgray'), c(1, 'lightgray')),
    showscale = FALSE, hoverinfo = 'text',
    marker = list(line = list(color = 'white', width = 0.3))
) |>
    layout(margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, b = 10, t = 30),
           geo = list(projection = list(type = 'equal earth'), visible = FALSE)) |>
    config(topojsonURL = 'data/plotly-geo/')
world_map





~ references a column in the table. We explicitly choose Equal Earth to match the Altair map. Plotly’s supporting TopoJSON files are also local, so the map does not need geographic downloads from Plotly’s CDN.




Choosing a projection
A projection turns positions on the curved Earth into positions on a flat page. Every flat map distorts something: area, shape, distance, or direction.
Altair’s default geographic projection is Equal Earth, which preserves relative areas. Web maps commonly use Web Mercator, which greatly enlarges high-latitude regions. Africa is about 14 times Greenland’s area, despite how similar their sizes can appear on a Mercator world map.
Compare the same data under the two projections:

Altairggplot



projection_map = alt.Chart(world_countries, width=260, height=200).mark_geoshape(
    fill='lightgray', stroke='white', strokeWidth=0.3
)
projection_map.project('equalEarth').properties(title='Equal Earth') | \
    projection_map.project('mercator').properties(title='Mercator')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Each trace needs its own geographic subplot to use a different projection. The geo and geo2 domains place the two maps side by side.

projection_comparison <- world_map |>
    add_trace(
        data = world_countries, type = 'choropleth', geo = 'geo2',
        geojson = world_geojson, featureidkey = 'properties.NAME', locations = ~name,
        z = rep(1, nrow(world_countries)), text = ~name, hoverinfo = 'text',
        colorscale = list(c(0, 'lightgray'), c(1, 'lightgray')),
        showscale = FALSE, marker = list(line = list(color = 'white', width = 0.3)),
        inherit = FALSE
    ) |>
    layout(
        geo = list(domain = list(x = c(0, 0.48), y = c(0, 1)),
                    projection = list(type = 'equal earth')),
        geo2 = list(domain = list(x = c(0.52, 1), y = c(0, 1)),
                    projection = list(type = 'mercator'), visible = FALSE),
        annotations = list(
            list(x = 0.23, y = 1, text = 'Equal Earth', showarrow = FALSE),
            list(x = 0.77, y = 1, text = 'Mercator', showarrow = FALSE)
        )
    )
projection_comparison








Equal-area projections support comparisons of geographic extent. Conformal projections preserve local angles and shapes, which can be useful for navigation or local detail. Choose a projection for the task and region, and use the same one for maps that readers need to compare.
The coordinates in our GeoJSON use longitude and latitude in WGS84 (EPSG:4326). This coordinate reference system describes the data; Altair’s project() controls how it is displayed. Changing the display projection does not change the underlying measurements. In GeoPandas, to_crs() actually transforms coordinates; assigning a CRS merely declares what existing coordinates mean.


Encoding country attributes
The grammar of graphics still applies. A nominal variable such as continent gets a categorical color scale, and the country name can appear in a tooltip.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(world_countries, width=500).mark_geoshape().encode(
    color=alt.Color('continent:N').title('Continent'),
    tooltip='name:N'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Plotly’s choropleth color channel uses numeric z values. For categories, we use integer codes and label the colorbar with the original names. A stepped color scale gives each category a distinct color rather than a gradient. This small helper repeats each color up to the next bin boundary.

step_colors <- function(colors) {
    positions <- rep(seq(0, 1, length.out = length(colors) + 1), each = 2)
    positions <- positions[-c(1, length(positions))]
    Map(function(position, color) list(position, color), positions, rep(colors, each = 2))
}
continent_levels <- sort(unique(world_countries$continent))
continent_colors <- c('#4c78a8', '#f58518', '#e45756', '#72b7b2',
                       '#54a24b', '#eeca3b', '#b279a2')
world_map |>
    style(
        z = match(world_countries$continent, continent_levels),
        zmin = 0.5, zmax = length(continent_levels) + 0.5,
        colorscale = step_colors(continent_colors), showscale = TRUE,
        colorbar = list(title = 'Continent', tickvals = seq_along(continent_levels),
                        ticktext = continent_levels),
        customdata = world_countries$continent,
        hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>%{customdata}<extra></extra>'
    )





style() changes trace attributes while keeping the map’s geometry and layout. The numeric codes are lookup positions, not a ranking of the continents.



A choropleth fills geographic regions according to an attribute. Here we start with total population, then replace the color encoding with GDP per person.

Altairggplot



country_map = alt.Chart(world_countries, width=500).mark_geoshape().encode(
    color=alt.Color('pop_est:Q').title('Population estimate'),
    tooltip=['name:N', alt.Tooltip('pop_est:Q', format=',')]
)
country_map




  
  
  
  
  


  
  





country_map.encode(
    color=alt.Color('gdp_per_capita:Q').title('GDP per person (US$)'),
    tooltip=['name:N', alt.Tooltip('gdp_per_capita:Q', format=',.0f')]
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Use the same population estimates and GDP-per-person calculation as in Altair. The sequential palette represents a quantitative variable; the tooltip states the value and its units.

world_map |>
    style(z = world_countries$pop_est, colorscale = 'Blues', showscale = TRUE,
          colorbar = list(title = 'Population estimate'),
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>Population: %{z:,.0f}<extra></extra>')






world_map |>
    style(z = world_countries$gdp_per_capita, colorscale = 'Blues', showscale = TRUE,
          colorbar = list(title = 'GDP per person<br>(US$)'),
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>GDP per person: US$%{z:,.0f}<extra></extra>')








For ordered categories, use an ordinal encoding. Natural Earth’s labels include an ordering number, so the default label order is meaningful here.

Altairggplot



country_map.encode(
    color=alt.Color('economy:O').title('Economy group'),
    tooltip=['name:N', 'economy:O']
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  





country_map.encode(
    color=alt.Color('income_grp:O').title('Income group'),
    tooltip=['name:N', 'income_grp:O']
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






The same category codes now follow a meaningful order. A stepped sequential palette preserves that ordering without implying intermediate categories.

economy_levels <- sort(unique(world_countries$economy))
world_map |>
    style(z = match(world_countries$economy, economy_levels),
          zmin = 0.5, zmax = length(economy_levels) + 0.5, showscale = TRUE,
          colorscale = step_colors(colorRampPalette(c('#deebf7', '#08519c'))(length(economy_levels))),
          colorbar = list(title = 'Economy group', tickvals = seq_along(economy_levels),
                          ticktext = economy_levels),
          customdata = world_countries$economy,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>%{customdata}<extra></extra>')






income_levels <- sort(unique(world_countries$income_grp))
world_map |>
    style(z = match(world_countries$income_grp, income_levels),
          zmin = 0.5, zmax = length(income_levels) + 0.5, showscale = TRUE,
          colorscale = step_colors(colorRampPalette(c('#deebf7', '#08519c'))(length(income_levels))),
          colorbar = list(title = 'Income group', tickvals = seq_along(income_levels),
                          ticktext = income_levels),
          customdata = world_countries$income_grp,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>%{customdata}<extra></extra>')










Focusing on a region
Filtering to a continent lets Altair fit the projection to the remaining geometries. It is different from cropping a world map to a rectangular window.

Altairggplot



africa = alt.Chart(
    world_countries.query('continent == "Africa"'), width=450, height=420
).mark_geoshape().encode(
    color=alt.Color('pop_est:Q').title('Population estimate'),
    tooltip=['name:N', alt.Tooltip('pop_est:Q', format=',')]
)
africa




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Adding a stroke makes adjacent boundaries easier to see, especially when their fill colors are similar.

africa.mark_geoshape(stroke='gray', strokeWidth=0.5)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Filter the attribute table, then replace all row-dependent trace attributes. fitbounds = 'locations' fits the view to the matched African countries.

african_countries <- world_countries |> dplyr::filter(continent == 'Africa')
africa_map <- world_map |>
    style(locations = african_countries$name, text = african_countries$name,
          z = african_countries$pop_est, colorscale = 'Blues', showscale = TRUE,
          colorbar = list(title = 'Population estimate'),
          marker = list(line = list(width = 0)),
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>Population: %{z:,.0f}<extra></extra>') |>
    layout(geo = list(fitbounds = 'locations'))
africa_map





Add a visible border between adjacent regions:

africa_map |> style(marker = list(line = list(color = 'gray', width = 0.5)))

title: 20  Geospatial
text:
20.5 States, provinces, and territories
Filtering country polygons does not reveal administrative boundaries that are absent from the file. This view of Canada and the United States still has only country outlines:

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(
    world_countries.query('name.isin(["Canada", "United States of America"])'),
    width=550
).mark_geoshape(stroke='white')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Filter the same two country names and fit the view to those locations:

north_america <- world_countries |>
    dplyr::filter(name %in% c('Canada', 'United States of America'))
world_map |>
    style(locations = north_america$name, text = north_america$name,
          z = rep(1, nrow(north_america))) |>
    layout(geo = list(fitbounds = 'locations'))








To show states and provinces, load Admin 1 data instead. Natural Earth’s 1:50 million Admin 1 dataset covers selected countries; it is not a complete set of subdivisions for every country in the world.

Altairggplot



world_regions = gpd.read_file('data/geospatial-world-regions.geojson')
world_regions[['name', 'admin', 'iso_a2']].head()

                 name      admin iso_a2
0   Western Australia  Australia     AU
1  Northern Territory  Australia     AU
2     South Australia  Australia     AU
3          Queensland  Australia     AU
4            Tasmania  Australia     AU



alt.Chart(world_regions, width=500).mark_geoshape(stroke='white', strokeWidth=0.3).encode(
    color=alt.Color('admin:N').title('Country'),
    tooltip=['admin:N', 'name:N']
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Extract the properties from the same Admin 1 feature collection. These features use lowercase name, so the matching key becomes properties.name.

regions_geojson <- jsonlite::read_json('data/geospatial-world-regions.geojson')
world_regions <- map_dfr(regions_geojson$features, 'properties')
world_regions |> select(name, admin, iso_a2) |> head()

# A tibble: 6 × 3

1 Western Australia  Australia AU

4 Queensland         Australia AU    
5 Tasmania           Australia AU    
6 Victoria           Australia AU    



country_levels <- sort(unique(world_regions$admin))
regions_map <- plot_ly(
    world_regions, type = 'choropleth', geojson = regions_geojson,
    featureidkey = 'properties.name', locations = ~name,
    z = match(world_regions$admin, country_levels),
    zmin = 0.5, zmax = length(country_levels) + 0.5,
    colorscale = step_colors(hcl.colors(length(country_levels), 'Dark 3')),
    colorbar = list(title = 'Country', tickvals = seq_along(country_levels), ticktext = country_levels),
    text = ~paste(name, admin, sep = '<br>'), hoverinfo = 'text',
    marker = list(line = list(color = 'white', width = 0.3))
) |>
    layout(margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, b = 10, t = 30),
           geo = list(projection = list(type = 'equal earth'), visible = FALSE)) |>
    config(topojsonURL = 'data/plotly-geo/')
regions_map





Country and subdivision names are separate attributes. For data with repeated subdivision names, use a unique regional identifier rather than name alone.




A map of Canada
Select Canada’s provinces and territories using the country code. The dataset includes names, representative point coordinates, and Wikipedia links as well as boundaries.

Altairggplot



canadian_provinces = world_regions.query('iso_a2 == "CA"').copy()

This rotated transverse Mercator view is one option for displaying Canada. Canada also uses Lambert conformal conic and regional UTM coordinate systems; there is no single projection that is best for every Canadian map. The display below is an illustration, not a specification of an official UTM zone.

canada_map = alt.Chart(canadian_provinces, width=500, height=420).mark_geoshape(
    stroke='white'
).project('transverseMercator', rotate=[90, 0, 0])
canada_map.encode(
    color=alt.Color('name:N').scale(scheme='tableau20').title('Province or territory'),

The palette has enough distinct colors for these 13 regions. The href channel makes a region a link; clicking it opens its Wikipedia page.


Keep Canada’s 13 features in a smaller GeoJSON collection and filter its attribute table to match. Plotly uses the central meridian, -90, where Altair specifies a longitude rotation of 90.

canada_geojson <- regions_geojson
canada_geojson$features <- keep(regions_geojson$features, function(feature) {

title: 20  Geospatial
text:
20.6 Choropleths and their pitfalls
We can now color the regions by population, using the new column from the join.

Altairggplot



canada_population_map = alt.Chart(
    canadian_provinces, width=500, height=420
).mark_geoshape(stroke='gray').project('transverseMercator', rotate=[90, 0, 0]).encode(
    color=alt.Color('population:Q').title('Population, 2021'),
    tooltip=['name:N', alt.Tooltip('population:Q', format=',')]
)
canada_population_map




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Replace the category codes with the joined populations, and use a quantitative sequential color scale. The location order is unchanged by the left join.

canada_population_map <- canada_map |>
    style(z = canadian_provinces$population,
          zmin = 0, zmax = max(canadian_provinces$population),
          colorscale = 'Blues',
          colorbar = list(title = 'Population, 2021', tickmode = 'auto'),
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>Population: %{z:,.0f}<extra></extra>',
          marker = list(line = list(color = 'gray', width = 0.5)))
canada_population_map








Always check whether the result makes sense. For these data, Ontario has the largest population, followed by Québec. The northern territories are large on the map but have small populations. A reference map on Wikimedia Commons offers another visual check, provided we account for differences in data dates.

Binning color
We can bin the color scale, as we did with histograms. This can make a map with many small regions easier to scan, but it hides differences within bins and creates abrupt changes at bin boundaries. Close values can fall into different bins, while more distant values can share a color.

Altairggplot



canada_population_map.encode(
    color=alt.Color('population:Q').bin(step=2_000_000, extent=[0, 16_000_000]).title('Population, 2021')
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Use explicit two-million-person bins and the stepped scale. The boundaries are visible in the code, making the binning decision easy to inspect or change. The tooltip still reports the original population, not its bin code.

population_breaks <- seq(0, 16e6, by = 2e6)
population_bins <- cut(canadian_provinces$population, breaks = population_breaks,
                       right = FALSE, labels = FALSE)
bin_labels <- paste0(head(population_breaks, -1) / 1e6, '–',
                      tail(population_breaks, -1) / 1e6, ' million')
canada_population_map |>
    style(z = population_bins, zmin = 0.5, zmax = length(bin_labels) + 0.5,
          colorscale = step_colors(colorRampPalette(c('#deebf7', '#08519c'))(length(bin_labels))),
          colorbar = list(title = 'Population, 2021', tickmode = 'array',
                          tickvals = seq_along(bin_labels), ticktext = bin_labels),
          customdata = canadian_provinces$population,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>Population: %{customdata:,.0f}<extra></extra>')








Compare this with the continuous scale. Changing the bin boundaries changes which differences look important, even though the data have not changed.


Highlighting boundaries on hover (Altair)
Selections from Chapter 19 work with geographic marks too. Here, hovering adds a white outline and draws that region last, keeping its outline visible. We retain a legend so the color scale remains interpretable without a tooltip.

province_hover = alt.selection_point(
    name='province_hover', fields=['name'], on='pointerover', clear='pointerout', empty=False
)
canada_population_map.mark_geoshape(strokeWidth=2).encode(
    color=alt.Color('population:Q').scale(scheme='tealblues').title('Population, 2021'),
    stroke=alt.condition(province_hover, alt.value('white'), alt.value('#222222')),
    order=alt.condition(province_hover, alt.value(1), alt.value(0))
).add_params(province_hover)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






What does the map’s area imply?
A choropleth gives each region visual space according to its geographic area, not its population or contribution to a total. A small, densely populated region can be hard to see; a large, sparsely populated one can dominate the page.

Use rates, proportions, or densities when the question is about intensity rather than totals. Population and population density answer different questions.
Use a sequential scale for ordered quantities, and show missing observations distinctly from genuine zeros.
Consider smaller geographic units when their boundaries and data support the question. Aggregation can conceal substantial variation within a region.
Add proportional symbols or a bar chart when readers need to compare totals.
A cartogram resizes or rearranges regions according to a quantity, trading some geographic familiarity for a more relevant allocation of space.

Even an equal-area projection cannot make geographic area stand in for population. Changing the projection and changing the statistical encoding solve different problems.

title: 20  Geospatial
section: 20.7 The United States: projections and electoral votes
text:
20.7 The United States: projections and electoral votes

Separated regions and composite projections
Alaska and Hawaii are far from the contiguous United States. A single fitted world projection leaves a lot of space between them.

Altairggplot



us_states = world_regions.query('iso_a2 == "US"').copy()
alt.Chart(us_states, width=550).mark_geoshape(stroke='white')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Keep the same 51 regions: the 50 states and the District of Columbia. Reuse the outline map with their GeoJSON features and matching names.

us_states <- world_regions |> dplyr::filter(iso_a2 == 'US')
us_geojson <- regions_geojson
us_geojson$features <- keep(regions_geojson$features, function(feature) {
    feature$properties$iso_a2 == 'US'
})
us_map <- world_map |>
    style(geojson = us_geojson, featureidkey = 'properties.name',
          locations = us_states$name, text = us_states$name,
          z = rep(1, nrow(us_states))) |>
    layout(geo = list(fitbounds = 'locations'))
us_map








albersUsa is a composite projection with repositioned insets for Alaska and Hawaii. It makes a compact overview, but inset positions and scales are not literal geographic relationships.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(us_states, width=550).mark_geoshape(stroke='white').project('albersUsa')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Plotly calls the composite projection 'albers usa'. Its USA scope supplies the standard inset arrangement rather than fitting one continuous world view.

us_albers_map <- us_map |>
    layout(geo = list(scope = 'usa', fitbounds = FALSE,
                      projection = list(type = 'albers usa')))
us_albers_map










Joining election results
The lecture used the 2012 presidential election to compare a winner-by-state map with electoral votes. Our local table combines the state winners and the electoral-vote allocations used in 2012. These are electoral votes, not popular votes.

Altairggplot



election_results = pd.read_csv('data/geospatial-us-election-2012.csv')
us_states = us_states.merge(
    election_results, on='name', how='left', validate='one_to_one'
)
assert len(us_states) == 51
assert us_states['electoral_votes'].notna().all()
assert us_states['electoral_votes'].sum() == 538
us_states[['name', 'winning_party', 'electoral_votes']].head()

         name winning_party  electoral_votes
0      Alaska           Rep                3
1     Alabama           Rep                9
2    Arkansas           Rep                6
3     Arizona           Rep               11
4  California           Dem               55




Join the same election table and check both the number of regions and the total electoral votes:

election_results <- read_csv('data/geospatial-us-election-2012.csv')
us_states <- us_states |>
    left_join(election_results, by = 'name', relationship = 'one-to-one')
stopifnot(nrow(us_states) == 51, !anyNA(us_states$electoral_votes),
          sum(us_states$electoral_votes) == 538)
us_states |> select(name, winning_party, electoral_votes) |> head()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  name       winning_party electoral_votes
  <chr>      <chr>                   <dbl>
1 Alaska     Rep                         3
2 Alabama    Rep                         9
3 Arkansas   Rep                         6
4 Arizona    Rep                        11
5 California Dem                        55
6 Colorado   Dem                         9





The 51 regions include the District of Columbia. Its name differs across sources, so the saved table normalizes it explicitly rather than dropping it during a join.
The original tables are available on Wikipedia’s pages for the Electoral College and 2012 US elections. As with the Canadian population data, table positions and headers should be inspected rather than assumed to remain unchanged.

Altairggplot



party_color = alt.Color('winning_party:N').scale(
    domain=['Dem', 'Rep'], range=['#4c78a8', '#e45756']
).title('Winning party')
election_map = alt.Chart(us_states, width=550).mark_geoshape(
    stroke='white'
).project('albersUsa').encode(
    color=party_color,
    tooltip=['name:N', 'winning_party:N']
)
election_map




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Use the same party labels and blue/red colors. The stepped color scale encodes two categories, not a continuous partisan margin.

party_levels <- c('Dem', 'Rep')
party_colors <- c('#4c78a8', '#e45756')
election_map <- us_albers_map |>
    style(z = match(us_states$winning_party, party_levels), zmin = 0.5, zmax = 2.5,
          colorscale = step_colors(party_colors), showscale = TRUE,
          colorbar = list(title = 'Winning party', tickvals = 1:2, ticktext = party_levels),
          text = paste(us_states$name, us_states$winning_party, sep = '<br>'),
          customdata = us_states$electoral_votes,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>Electoral votes: %{customdata}<extra></extra>',
          marker = list(line = list(color = 'white', width = 0.5)))
election_map








This shows which party won each state, but not how much each state contributed to the result. Adding opacity for electoral votes provides another encoding, yet small states are still difficult to compare.

Altairggplot



election_map.encode(
    opacity=alt.Opacity('electoral_votes:Q').title('Electoral votes'),
    tooltip=['name:N', 'winning_party:N', 'electoral_votes:Q']
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Choropleth marker opacity can vary by location. Rescale electoral votes into an opacity range while retaining the party colors.

election_map |>
    style(marker = list(opacity = scales::rescale(us_states$electoral_votes, to = c(0.3, 1)),
                        line = list(color = 'white', width = 0.5)))










Points instead of regions
Proportional symbols allocate visible size according to a quantity rather than land area. First, overlay neutral circles on the party-colored regions:

Altairggplot



electoral_points = alt.Chart(us_states).mark_circle(stroke='black').encode(
    longitude='longitude:Q', latitude='latitude:Q',
    color=alt.value('white'),
    size=alt.Size('electoral_votes:Q').scale(range=[20, 1500]).title('Electoral votes'),
    tooltip=['name:N', 'winning_party:N', 'electoral_votes:Q']
)
election_map + electoral_points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Add a scattergeo trace to the same geographic subplot. Its longitude and latitude locate the circles, and sizemode = 'area' makes symbol area represent electoral votes. inherit = FALSE keeps choropleth-only attributes out of the new point trace. Hover over a circle for its electoral-vote count.

vote_size_reference <- 2 * max(us_states$electoral_votes) / 40^2
election_map |>
    add_trace(
        data = us_states, type = 'scattergeo', mode = 'markers',
        lon = ~longitude, lat = ~latitude, text = ~name, customdata = ~electoral_votes,
        marker = list(size = us_states$electoral_votes, sizemode = 'area',
                      sizeref = vote_size_reference, color = 'white',
                      line = list(color = 'black', width = 1)),
        hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>Electoral votes: %{customdata}<extra></extra>',
        showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE
    )








Alternatively, keep the geographic background neutral and color the circles. Now size and color describe the same marks. Symbol area, rather than radius, should represent the quantity.

Altairggplot



state_background = alt.Chart(us_states).mark_geoshape(
    fill='lightgray', stroke='white'
)
party_points = electoral_points.mark_circle(stroke='white', strokeWidth=0.5).encode(
    color=party_color
)
map_points = (state_background + party_points).project('albersUsa').properties(width=550)
map_points




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Use the neutral state map as the background. For point traces, Plotly can map the categorical color directly; the named colors keep the parties consistent with the choropleth.

us_albers_map |>
    add_trace(
        data = us_states, type = 'scattergeo', mode = 'markers',
        lon = ~longitude, lat = ~latitude,
        color = ~winning_party, colors = setNames(party_colors, party_levels),
        text = ~paste(name, winning_party, sep = '<br>'), customdata = ~electoral_votes,
        marker = list(size = us_states$electoral_votes, sizemode = 'area',
                      sizeref = vote_size_reference, opacity = 0.8,
                      line = list(color = 'white', width = 0.5)),
        hovertemplate = '%{text}<br>Electoral votes: %{customdata}<extra></extra>',
        inherit = FALSE
    ) |>
    layout(legend = list(title = list(text = 'Winning party')))








The supplied longitude and latitude locate representative points for each region; they are not the locations of individual voters. If a dataset lacks such points, Altair’s geoCentroid expression can calculate a geographic centroid. Check the result: a centroid need not fall inside an irregular or multipart region. Dense clusters of small regions can also cause symbols to overlap.


Linking a map and a bar chart (Altair)
Use the region name as a shared selection key. Hover over a circle to highlight the corresponding state in both views; clearing the hover restores all states.

state_hover = alt.selection_point(
    name='state_hover', fields=['name'], on='pointerover', clear='pointerout'
)
selected_points = party_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(state_hover, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(state_hover)
map_with_selection = (state_background + selected_points).project(
    'albersUsa'
).properties(width=480)
map_with_selection




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




The bar chart makes individual values easier to compare. It has one column per party, with independently ordered state names but a shared quantitative x-scale.

bars = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame(us_states.drop(columns='geometry')), width=200).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('electoral_votes:Q').title('Electoral votes'),
    y=alt.Y('name:N').sort('-x').title(None),
    color=party_color,
    opacity=alt.condition(state_hover, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2)),
    column=alt.Column('winning_party:N').title(None)
).resolve_scale(y='independent')
map_with_selection & bars




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Checking electoral-vote totals
For a direct comparison of the party totals, sum the electoral votes rather than judging colored land area or the number of states won:

Altairggplot



us_states.groupby('winning_party')['electoral_votes'].sum()

winning_party
Dem    332
Rep    206
Name: electoral_votes, dtype: int64





us_states |>
    group_by(winning_party) |>
    summarise(electoral_votes = sum(electoral_votes), .groups = 'drop')

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  winning_party electoral_votes
  <chr>                   <dbl>
1 Dem                       332
2 Rep                       206





The totals are 332 for the Democratic candidate and 206 for the Republican candidate. Neither a winner-by-state map nor this electoral-vote table tells us the popular-vote margin within each state.

title: 20  Geospatial
section: 20.8 Further exploration: a rotating earthquake globe (Altair)
text:
20.8 Further exploration: a rotating earthquake globe (Altair)
An orthographic projection looks like a globe. This example combines a sphere, country polygons, and earthquake locations. A slider rotates all layers together; circle size encodes magnitude and fill encodes depth in kilometers.
The power scale is an illustrative visual choice, not a claim that circle area is proportional to earthquake energy. The data are a historical USGS sample distributed with Vega, not a live earthquake feed.

earthquakes = pd.read_csv('data/geospatial-earthquakes.csv')
globe_rotation = alt.param(
    name='globe_rotation', value=120,
    bind=alt.binding_range(min=-180, max=180, step=5, name='Rotate longitude ')
)
quake_hover = alt.selection_point(
    name='quake_hover', on='pointerover', clear='pointerout', empty=False
)
sphere = alt.Chart(alt.sphere()).mark_geoshape(fill='aliceblue', stroke='black')
globe_countries = alt.Chart(world_countries).mark_geoshape(
    fill='mintcream', stroke='black', strokeWidth=0.35
)
quakes = alt.Chart(earthquakes).mark_circle(opacity=0.4).transform_filter(
    'cos(datum.latitude * PI / 180) * '
    'cos((datum.longitude + globe_rotation) * PI / 180) > 0'
).encode(
    longitude='longitude:Q', latitude='latitude:Q',
    size=alt.Size('magnitude:Q').scale(
        type='pow', exponent=4, domain=[0, 6], range=[1, 1000]
    ).title('Magnitude'),
    fill=alt.Fill('depth:Q').scale(scheme='lightorange', domain=[0, 400]).title('Depth (km)'),
    stroke=alt.value('black'),
    strokeWidth=alt.condition(quake_hover, alt.value(1), alt.value(0)),
    tooltip=['place:N', 'magnitude:Q', 'depth:Q']
).add_params(quake_hover)
alt.layer(sphere, globe_countries, quakes).project(
    type='orthographic', rotate=alt.expr('[globe_rotation, 0, 0]')
).add_params(globe_rotation).properties(width=450, height=450)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




The filter removes points on the far hemisphere, including when rotation crosses the date line. Merely projecting a point to an x/y position does not guarantee that a circle mark will be clipped behind the globe.
